entries.headline: Regular winter swimmers show higher baseline antioxidant enzymes (a hormesis signal), but human evidence for health benefits is small and inconsistent, and cold plunges right after strength training blunt muscle gains.

dose.effective: If you do it: brief immersions (seconds to a few minutes) in cold water, with acclimatization and never alone; keep it away from (at least several hours after) strength sessions.
dose.studied_range: Winter-swimming studies over a season; post-exercise CWI 10 min after each strength session for 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: Cold shock and arrhythmia risk on sudden immersion, especially with heart disease; hypothermia.
dose.timeframe: Antioxidant adaptations seen after a winter season.
dose.notes: Each plunge itself causes acute oxidative stress; adaptation follows repetition.

entries.mechanism: Cold triggers a catecholamine surge and increased metabolic rate (brown-fat thermogenesis), generating a transient ROS pulse that may up-regulate glutathione, SOD and catalase. Post-exercise cooling reduces blood flow and anabolic signalling.
entries.interactions: Blunts adaptations to [resistance-training] if done immediately after.
entries.caveats: Winter swimmers are a self-selected healthy group; most studies are small, single-sex and uncontrolled. Reviews rate many claimed benefits as resting on weak or anecdotal data.
entries.title: Cold-water immersion and winter swimming

entries.headline: Cochrane finds possible benefit only from small, biased trials; the best-designed RCT (MOXI) showed no improvement in semen, DNA fragmentation or live birth.

dose.effective: No dose has proven benefit for live birth. If used, choose a modest-dose product (roughly vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 IU, selenium 100-200 ug, zinc 15-25 mg, folate 400-1000 ug, CoQ10 100-200 mg, L-carnitine 1-2 g) for 3 months, not stacked products.
dose.studied_range: MOXI: vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 mg, selenium 0.2 mg, L-carnitine 1000 mg, zinc 20 mg, folic acid 1000 ug, lycopene 10 mg daily for 3-6 months. Cochrane: 20 different antioxidants in 90 RCTs.
dose.too_much: Stacking several products or megadoses risks reductive stress ([high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]); antioxidants cause more mild GI upset (OR 2.70).
dose.timeframe: Trials use 3-6 months.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: counsel that supplements are of questionable clinical utility. EAU: insufficient evidence for widespread empirical use. Yet in a global survey 85.6% of reproductive specialists prescribed them.

entries.mechanism: Intended to scavenge seminal ROS and support antioxidant enzymes; only helpful if a man actually has oxidative stress and a deficiency.
entries.interactions: Not a substitute for removing the source of ROS ([tobacco-smoking], [varicocele], [genital-tract-infection]). May blunt hormetic benefits of [aerobic-exercise-moderate].
entries.caveats: Cochrane 2022: live birth OR 1.43 but very low certainty and null when high-risk-of-bias trials are removed; MOXI live birth was 15% vs 24% with placebo (not significant, small). A 6-month RCT in men with DFI >=25% also found no DFI change. Supplements may help a subgroup with proven oxidative stress, but no validated test identifies them.

key_numbers.label: Live birth OR (all trials, very low certainty)

entries.title: Combination 'male fertility' antioxidant supplements

entries.headline: Combined with resistance training, 3-5 g/day creatine adds about 1.4 kg lean mass and modest strength in older adults; memory effects are small and contested, the antioxidant role is mechanistic only, and long trials in Parkinson and Huntington disease were null.

dose.effective: 3-5 g/day creatine monohydrate (or about 0.1 g/kg/day), taken with resistance training
dose.studied_range: 3-20 g/day (20 g/day for 5-7 days as an optional loading phase); 10 g/day for 5 years in Parkinson disease; up to 40 g/day in Huntington disease
dose.too_much: No kidney harm in healthy people at studied doses; serum creatinine rises slightly as a by-product, which is not kidney injury. People with kidney disease should involve their doctor. Very high doses cause more gastrointestinal upset.
dose.timeframe: Muscle stores fill in about a week with loading or about 3-4 weeks at 3-5 g/day; lean-mass gains seen over 7-52 weeks of training
dose.notes: Monohydrate is the studied and cheapest form. Vegetarians start with lower stores and may respond more on memory tests. A single 0.35 g/kg dose (about 25 g) was used in the sleep-deprivation study, far above normal use.

entries.mechanism: Creatine and phosphocreatine buffer ATP through creatine kinase, which matters in tissues with high, fluctuating energy demand (muscle, brain). Cell and animal studies suggest direct scavenging of some radicals and indirect protection of mitochondria, but these antioxidant effects have not been shown to matter in humans.
entries.interactions: Its benefit for muscle depends on training; pair with [resistance-training]. No known antagonism with exercise adaptation, unlike [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]. Often combined with [coq10] in sarcopenia proposals without outcome data.
entries.caveats: Persistent myths (kidney damage, dehydration, cramps, hair loss) are not supported by the trial evidence. Water retention adds 1-2 kg body weight early on. Neurodegeneration trials at high doses were negative. Creatine is not a longevity drug: there is no human lifespan or aging-rate data.
entries.debate: For muscle, meta-analyses agree that creatine plus training beats training alone in older adults [lon-devries2014, lon-chilibeck2017]. For cognition, positive meta-analyses report memory gains mainly in older adults [lon-prokopidis2023, lon-xu2024], but a letter argued the Prokopidis analysis double-counted data and may be a false positive [lon-eckert2023], and an earlier systematic review found no effect in young people and inconsistent results across domains [lon-avgerinos2018]. Antioxidant claims rest on mechanistic reviews [lon-sestili2011]. Hopes for neuroprotection were tested and failed in large RCTs [lon-kieburtz2015, lon-hersch2017]. Note that the main safety reviews come from sports-nutrition authors, some with industry ties [lon-kreider2017, lon-antonio2021], although an independent meta-analysis also found no renal harm [lon-desouzaesilva2019].

factors.name: Curcumin supplements (enhanced absorption)
aliases: Curcumin supplements for PCOS and egg quality

entries.headline: Enhanced-absorption curcumin (micellar, cyclodextrin, phytosome, colloidal) modestly lowers CRP (~0.6 mg/L) and MDA and reduces knee-osteoarthritis pain about as much as an NSAID in short trials, but the trial base is small, heterogeneous and low quality, and rare idiosyncratic liver injury is now well documented.

dose.effective: Osteoarthritis: 1500 mg/day Curcuma extract (the ibuprofen-comparison trial) or ~180 mg/day curcumin as Theracurmin, for 4-12 weeks. Biomarkers: ~600 mg/day curcuminoids or more (often with piperine) for at least 4-8 weeks; micellar or gamma-cyclodextrin forms deliver more curcumin per mg.
dose.studied_range: 80 mg/day (nanomicelle) to 8 g/day (standard powder) in trials; single doses up to 12 g tolerated.
dose.too_much: EFSA ADI 3 mg/kg/day (about 210 mg/day at 70 kg), which many products exceed. Liver injury (hepatocellular or cholestatic hepatitis, latency 1-4 months, one US death) has been linked to high-dose, high-bioavailability products and is strongly associated with HLA-B*35:01; 3 of 7 implicated US products also contained piperine. GI upset at gram doses.
dose.timeframe: Pain effects within 2-8 weeks; biomarker changes at 4-12 weeks; fasting plasma curcuminoids reached ~50 nmol/L after 3 weeks of meal-time micellar dosing.
dose.notes: Free (unconjugated) curcumin is barely detectable in blood even with advanced formulations; most 'fold-increase' claims compare total conjugates after enzymatic hydrolysis and use different assays, so brand comparisons are not reliable. Best head-to-head data favour micelles (57-185x) and gamma-cyclodextrin (30-39x); phytosome ~8-29x; piperine adds little to conjugate exposure in the head-to-head study but inhibits drug-metabolising enzymes. Take with meals.

entries.mechanism: Claimed: Nrf2 activation via KEAP1 Cys151 (Michael acceptor), NF-kB inhibition, direct radical scavenging and iron chelation. Reality check: these effects appear in cells at 1-20 uM, whereas oral dosing gives low-nanomolar free curcumin and mostly glucuronide/sulfate conjugates that are inactive in cell assays. Curcumin also degrades rapidly and is a known pan-assay interference compound, so many in-vitro 'hits' are suspect. Clinical effects that do appear (OA pain, CRP) may come from gut-local actions, minor metabolites, or bias, and the mechanism in humans is not established.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [sulforaphane-supplements], [broccoli-sprouts] and [broccoli-seed-powder] on Nrf2; sulforaphane is far more potent and bioavailable, and there are no human data on combining them, so adding curcumin for Nrf2 is likely redundant (inference). Its distinct use case is symptomatic osteoarthritis pain. No human evidence that curcumin blunts training adaptations the way high-dose vitamins C/E do ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]); this is untested rather than disproven. Pharmacokinetic interactions: curcumin inhibits intestinal BCRP (sulfasalazine exposure up 3.2x) and CYP/P-gp in vitro; piperine raises phenytoin levels. Short studies found no change in INR on warfarin or bleeding time on antiplatelets, but caution is still advised with anticoagulants. Belongs to the broader [isolated-polyphenol-supplements] category.
entries.caveats: The field carries an integrity problem: a leading curcumin laboratory has dozens of retracted papers, and one glycaemic meta-analysis was itself retracted. Most positive trials are small, short, single-centre and often from a few research networks; meta-analyses show very high heterogeneity and GRADE certainty is low. Larger or Western trials are frequently null (FAP adenomas, radiation dermatitis, prostate cancer, Alzheimer's disease, micellar curcumin on CRP/lipids). Liver injury is rare but real; stop and test liver enzymes if jaundice, dark urine or fatigue appear. Avoid with gallstones or bile-duct obstruction (curcumin contracts the gallbladder), with marginal iron stores (iron chelation in mice), and in pregnancy (no safety data at supplement doses).

entries.title: Curcumin supplements (enhanced-bioavailability extracts)

entries.headline: One small Iranian RCT (56 completers) found 80 mg/day nanomicelle curcumin for 10 weeks improved sperm count, concentration and motility plus seminal-redox and inflammation markers; there are no human data on DNA fragmentation, varicocele, pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: 80 mg/day curcumin as nanomicelle for 10 weeks in the only RCT.
dose.studied_range: 80 mg/day (single human RCT); animal varicocele studies used 4-100 mg/kg.
dose.too_much: Not established for sperm. In vitro, curcumin added directly to sperm blocks motility and capacitation in a concentration-dependent way (it has been studied as a vaginal contraceptive), although such concentrations are not reached in semen after oral dosing. General supplement risks (liver injury, drug interactions) apply.
dose.timeframe: At least one spermatogenic cycle (~74 days); the RCT ran 10 weeks.
dose.notes: Human DNA-fragmentation benefits come only from adding curcumin to freezing medium in the lab (cryopreservation), not from oral use. Varicocele data are from rats only (mechanistic).

entries.mechanism: Proposed: lowering seminal lipid peroxidation (MDA) and inflammatory cytokines (TNF-a, CRP) and Nrf2-driven antioxidant enzymes in testis. Human mechanistic support is limited to blood TAC/MDA changes in one trial.
entries.interactions: Likely overlaps with other antioxidant approaches such as [n-acetylcysteine]; no head-to-head or combination trials. Redundant with [sulforaphane-supplements] on the Nrf2 axis (inference). Not comparable to culinary [turmeric-curcumin].
entries.caveats: A single small trial from one country, without pregnancy outcomes, cannot support a recommendation; it does not show more pregnancies. The in-vitro anti-motility effect argues against assuming 'more is better'. Check for publication bias as further Iranian trials appear.

key_numbers.label: Dose in the only human RCT
Curcumin in freezing medium that reduced post-thaw DNA fragmentation

entries.title: Curcumin supplements for sperm quality

entries.headline: In PCOS, several small RCTs and meta-analyses show curcumin modestly lowers fasting glucose (~3-4 mg/dL), insulin and HOMA-IR, without consistent effects on lipids, testosterone, LH/FSH or weight, and no trial has measured ovulation, pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: PCOS trials: 500-1500 mg/day standard curcumin or ~80 mg two to three times daily as nanocurcumin, for 8-12 weeks.
dose.studied_range: 80-240 mg/day nanocurcumin to 1500 mg/day standard curcumin; endometriosis-ART trial 120 mg/day nanomicelle for 10 weeks.
dose.too_much: Not established. EFSA ADI (3 mg/kg/day) rests on a multigeneration reproductive-toxicity study (reduced F2 body-weight gain). Mouse oocytes exposed to curcumin showed impaired maturation and embryo development. No human safety data in pregnancy at supplement doses.
dose.timeframe: Metabolic effects at 8-12 weeks; an oocyte matures over ~3 months.
dose.notes: Glycaemic benefit is small compared with metformin; one 200-woman factorial trial found curcumin plus metformin better than either alone. Stopping high-dose supplements once pregnancy is possible is a precautionary inference, not a tested rule.

entries.mechanism: Improved insulin sensitivity and lower inflammation/oxidative stress would plausibly help the ovarian environment in PCOS; animal studies show curcumin can preserve follicle reserve but other animal studies show direct harm to oocytes and embryos, so the net effect on eggs is unknown.
entries.interactions: Additive to metformin in one trial. Alternative or adjunct to [myo-inositol], which has a larger PCOS evidence base; no head-to-head trials. Treat [pcos] and [glycemic-control] first with lifestyle and established drugs. Same liver and drug-interaction cautions as [curcumin-supplements].
entries.caveats: All PCOS and endometriosis trials found here were small and mostly from Iran; meta-analyses pool 3-8 trials with high heterogeneity for HOMA-IR. A small endometriosis-ART trial reported more mature oocytes and good embryos but needs replication; a separate endometriosis RCT found no pain benefit. Oocyte-quality claims rest on conflicting animal data (mechanistic).

key_numbers.label: Fasting glucose change in PCOS (5 RCTs)

entries.title: Curcumin supplements for PCOS and egg quality

entries.headline: The best-proven way to prevent oxidative skin aging: in the Nambour RCT, daily sunscreen stopped measurable photoaging (24% less aging than discretionary use over 4.5 years), cut squamous-cell tumours by 39%, and was followed by half as many melanomas over the next 10 years.

dose.effective: Broad-spectrum SPF 15 or higher applied every morning to the face, neck, arms and hands, as in the Nambour trial; reapply after swimming, heavy sweating or long periods outdoors.
dose.studied_range: SPF 15+ broad-spectrum, daily for 4.5 years, adults 25-75 (photoaging analysis in those under 55); melanoma follow-up 10 years after the trial ended.
dose.too_much: No harm was seen in the trial. All six common organic filters are absorbed into blood above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL screening threshold after one application; the clinical significance is unknown.
dose.timeframe: Photoaging differences after 4.5 years; melanoma differences emerged over the following decade.
dose.notes: Sunscreen filters block photons before they generate ROS; they are not antioxidants. Iron-oxide (tinted) sunscreens also block visible light, which improved melasma in one RCT. Sunscreen is one part of sun protection alongside shade, clothing and timing.

entries.mechanism: Organic and mineral UV filters absorb or scatter UVB and UVA, preventing direct DNA photoproducts and the UVA-driven singlet oxygen and superoxide that lead to 8-oxo-dG, lipid peroxidation and AP-1/MMP-mediated collagen breakdown. Standard filters do little against visible light and near-infrared; adding antioxidants to sunscreen reduced IR-A-induced MMP-1 in one small trial.
entries.interactions: Works on the cause of [uv-sun-exposure]. [topical-vitamin-c] and other topical antioxidants are add-ons, not substitutes. Oral [beta-carotene-supplement] added nothing in the same trial. Sunscreen does not meaningfully lower vitamin D status at normal use ([vitamin-d]).
entries.caveats: The only long-term RCT is Nambour (one Australian community, high UV). The melanoma result rests on 11 versus 22 cases and was borderline (P=0.051). Sunscreen did not reduce basal-cell carcinoma.
entries.debate: Observational meta-analyses of mostly case-control studies found no association between sunscreen use and melanoma (OR 1.10) [skb-silva2018], feeding claims that sunscreen does not prevent skin cancer. Rueegg and colleagues showed that adjusting for sun exposure, sunburn and skin type consistently shifts estimates toward protection, and that the only RCT showed HR 0.49 [skb-rueegg2019, skb-green2011]: sun-seeking, fair-skinned people use more sunscreen, which confounds the observational data. Safety: systemic absorption of organic filters [skb-matta2020] prompted calls for more toxicology, but no harm has been shown. Vitamin D concerns are addressed by [skb-passeron2019].
entries.title: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen

entries.headline: In obese hypertensive adults DASH lowered blood pressure by ~8/7 mmHg, raised plasma antioxidant capacity and prevented the F2-isoprostane rise during an experimental lipid infusion.

dose.effective: 8-10 servings/day of fruit and vegetables, low-fat dairy, whole grains, nuts and legumes, low sodium and sweets.
dose.studied_range: 4 weeks per diet in a 24-person crossover study.
dose.timeframe: 4 weeks.
dose.notes: Blood pressure benefits of DASH are well established in larger trials; oxidative data are small.

entries.mechanism: High potassium, fiber and plant polyphenols; reduced sodium lowers vascular NADPH oxidase activity.
entries.interactions: Overlaps heavily with [high-fruit-vegetable-intake] and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Oxidative-stress data come from one small study.
entries.title: DASH diet

entries.headline: Cochrane (2024, moderate certainty): DHEA probably makes little or no difference to live birth in poor responders (OR 1.30, NS); testosterone pre-treatment looks more promising (OR 2.53). ESHRE does not recommend DHEA.

dose.effective: Not recommended. A typical trial dose was 75 mg/day before and during the IVF cycle.
dose.studied_range: 75 mg/day (Wiser 2010) and similar regimens.
dose.too_much: Androgenic side effects (acne, hair growth); a hormone, use only under medical supervision.
dose.timeframe: Started before the IVF cycle and continued during stimulation in trials.
dose.notes: Network meta-analysis showed higher clinical pregnancy with DHEA (OR 2.46), but the larger Cochrane pooled analysis with live birth as outcome did not.

entries.mechanism: Androgen precursor proposed to increase FSH sensitivity of small antral follicles; not an antioxidant.
entries.interactions: Compare [coq10] in the same poor-responder population.
entries.caveats: Early small trials (e.g. 33 women) overstated benefit.
entries.title: DHEA in poor responders

factors.name: Dietary fiber and the gut microbiome

entries.headline: Most dietary polyphenols reach the colon and only work after gut bacteria convert them, and people differ widely in this; a fiber intake of 25-29 g/day is linked to 15-30% lower mortality and cardiometabolic disease.

dose.effective: 25-29 g fiber/day or more from varied plants (whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruit, nuts).
dose.studied_range: Cohorts (185 studies) and 58 RCTs.
dose.too_much: Increase gradually to limit bloating.
dose.timeframe: Microbiome shifts in days; outcomes long-term.
dose.notes: 'High' vs 'low excretor' and 'producer vs non-producer' metabotypes (urolithins, equol) explain part of why the same food works differently in different people.

entries.mechanism: Microbial catabolism turns anthocyanins, flavan-3-ols, chlorogenic acids and ellagitannins into smaller phenolic acids, valerolactones and urolithins that are absorbed and circulate for up to 48 h; fermentation yields short-chain fatty acids that support barrier integrity and lower inflammation.
entries.interactions: Determines how much benefit you get from [blueberries], [coffee], [cocoa-flavanols], [pomegranate], [walnuts-nuts], and how much glucoraphanin converts to sulforaphane ([sulforaphane-supplements]). Antibiotics abolish microbial glucoraphanin conversion.
entries.caveats: Mechanisms are well described; direct evidence that changing the microbiome lowers systemic oxidative stress in humans is limited.

Anthocyanin relative bioavailability incl. metabolites (13C tracer)

entries.title: Dietary fiber and the gut microbiome

entries.headline: Vaping causes less oxidative stress than smoking but more than not using anything: a single e-cigarette acutely raised 8-iso-PGF2a, and dual use is worse than smoking alone.

dose.effective: Best: use neither. For a smoker who cannot otherwise quit, a complete switch lowers toxicant exposure; dual use should be avoided.
dose.studied_range: Acute single-session crossover; large cross-sectional cohort (PATH); 24-week switching RCT.
dose.too_much: Dual use (vaping plus smoking) had 9% higher F2-isoprostanes than smoking only.
dose.timeframe: Acute effects within minutes; switching changes over weeks.
dose.notes: Long-term data are still limited.

entries.mechanism: Heated propylene glycol/glycerol forms carbonyls (formaldehyde, acrolein), and coils release metals; nicotine activates NOX2. Exposure to radicals is far lower than from combustion.
entries.interactions: Only reduces harm versus [tobacco-smoking] if it fully replaces cigarettes.
entries.caveats: Long-term independent data are limited; the acute study tested one session in healthy adults, and the cohort data are cross-sectional.
entries.title: E-cigarettes (vaping)

entries.headline: Egg freezing works best young and in volume: with 10-15 eggs frozen at 35 or under, cumulative live birth reached ~85% vs a ~36% plateau at 36+, but only 9-38% of women ever return to use their eggs, and success after 40 is low.

dose.effective: Freeze at 35 or younger if possible and aim for about 10-15 mature eggs (often 2+ stimulation cycles); at least 8-10 for reasonable success, and expect lower odds per egg when older.
dose.studied_range: Vitrified mature (MII) eggs; mean freezing age in cohorts 36-38.
dose.too_much: Ovarian hyperstimulation, procedure risks and cost of repeated cycles and storage; diminishing returns after 40.
dose.timeframe: One stimulation cycle takes about 2 weeks; eggs keep for years in liquid nitrogen.
dose.notes: Per-egg efficiency is low (about 6% overall per thawed egg) and falls with age at freezing; freezing age, not using age, sets the odds.

entries.mechanism: Vitrification halts egg ageing: aneuploidy risk is fixed at the age of freezing (see [maternal-age]); about 75-85% of eggs survive warming.
entries.interactions: Planning uses [amh-ovarian-reserve-egg] to predict egg yield; later use often involves [pgt-a-egg] (not proven helpful).
entries.caveats: Outcome data come from small numbers of returning users; models (Goldman, Doyle) are partly extrapolated from fresh IVF.
entries.debate: Advocates argue it extends reproductive autonomy and that women should freeze younger [fer-goold2009, fer-cobo2016review]; clinic authors also note it is most cost-effective at 37-38, when biological success is lower [fer-cobo2016review]. Ethicists warn employer-paid schemes may pressure women [fer-mertes2015], and follow-up shows most eggs are never used (38% return at 10-15 years; 15% in Sweden) [fer-blakemore2021, fer-wennberg2019]. ASRM calls it ethically permissible with honest counselling and says live birth cannot yet be predicted precisely [fer-asrm2024ethics, fer-asrm2021oc].

entries.headline: Eggplant skin's nasunin is a strong superoxide scavenger and iron chelator in test tubes, and the flesh is rich in chlorogenic acid, but there is no human evidence that eggplant lowers oxidative stress.

dose.effective: No human dose for oxidative stress exists; eat it as a normal vegetable with the skin on.
dose.studied_range: One RCT used 1.2 g/day eggplant powder for 12 weeks (blood pressure outcome, attributed to acetylcholine, not antioxidants).
dose.timeframe: Unknown.
dose.notes: Phenol-Explorer has only a Folin value (61 mg/100 g) for whole purple eggplant. Chlorogenic acid is the dominant phenolic (>65% of phenolic acids) but content varies widely by cultivar and fruit segment. Frying in oil soaks up a lot of fat.

entries.mechanism: In vitro: nasunin (delphinidin-3-(p-coumaroylrutinoside)-5-glucoside) scavenges superoxide and inhibits hydroxyl radical generation mainly by chelating ferrous iron; chlorogenic acid is metabolised much like coffee chlorogenic acids.
entries.interactions: Chlorogenic acid overlaps with [coffee], which supplies far more per serving.
entries.caveats: The nasunin data are from rat brain homogenate and ESR assays at micromolar concentrations that dietary anthocyanins do not reach intact in human tissues. A 12-week RCT of eggplant powder lowered blood pressure in stressed adults, but the authors attribute it to choline esters (acetylcholine), not antioxidants.
entries.title: Eggplant (skin: nasunin; flesh: chlorogenic acid)

entries.headline: In a 767-patient JAMA trial with euploid embryos, timing transfer by receptivity testing gave no benefit (live birth 58.5% vs 61.9%); HFEA rates it red and ESHRE does not recommend it.

dose.effective: Not recommended.
dose.studied_range: Endometrial biopsy in a mock cycle, gene-expression panel, then 'personalised' transfer timing.
dose.too_much: Extra biopsy (pain, bleeding, rare perforation), a mandatory freeze-all, delay and cost.
dose.timeframe: Adds at least one mock cycle.
dose.notes: Distinct from standard hysteroscopy or treatment of a diagnosed uterine problem.

entries.mechanism: Proposes that some women have a shifted 'window of implantation' detectable by endometrial transcriptomics.
entries.interactions: Often combined with [pgt-a-egg] and [endometrial-scratch-egg] after failed transfers.
entries.caveats: The non-significant direction of the main trial was toward lower live birth.
entries.debate: The test developer's own RCT reported higher per-protocol cumulative live birth (71.2% vs 55.4%) but no intention-to-treat difference and about 50% dropout [fer-simon2020]; the independent JAMA trial was null [fer-doyle2022]. HFEA red [fer-hfea2026]; ESHRE: not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].
entries.title: Endometrial receptivity testing (ERA and similar)

entries.headline: The 1364-woman PIP trial found identical live birth with and without a scratch (26.1% vs 26.1%); Cochrane 2026 calls the effect unclear (OR 1.12, 0.98-1.28), so at best a small benefit, at the cost of a painful extra procedure.

dose.effective: Not recommended for routine use (ESHRE). Trials used a pipelle biopsy in the luteal phase of the cycle before transfer.
dose.studied_range: One or two pipelle passes, day 3 of the preceding cycle to day 3 of the transfer cycle (PIP).
dose.too_much: Median pain 3.5/10; small infection and bleeding risk.
dose.timeframe: Cycle before embryo transfer.
dose.notes: HFEA amber for most IVF patients, grey for recurrent implantation failure.

entries.mechanism: Hypothesis: controlled injury triggers a local inflammatory and wound-healing response (cytokines, macrophages) that improves endometrial receptivity.
entries.interactions: Often offered alongside [endometrial-receptivity-egg] or [immune-addons-egg] after failed transfers; none has been shown to add up.
entries.caveats: Early small trials were strongly positive; several trials have had data-integrity questions. Benefit, if any, is a few percentage points.
entries.debate: The IPD meta-analysis of 13 integrity-checked RCTs found higher live birth (OR 1.29, 1.02-1.64) [fer-vanhoogenhuijze2023], but its sensitivity analyses crossed 1 and it was publicly criticised [fer-aktoz2024]. The large pragmatic PIP trial was flat [fer-lensen2019] and Cochrane 2026 rates the effect unclear [fer-perera2026]. HFEA rates it amber [fer-hfea2026]; ESHRE does not recommend routine use [fer-eshre2023addons].
entries.title: Endometrial scratching before IVF

entries.headline: Endometriosis is an inflammatory, pro-oxidant condition linked to fewer and less mature eggs and lower oocyte mitochondrial content, but women with endometrioma have similar IVF live birth rates (OR 0.98) once eggs are retrieved.

dose.effective: Specialist management; surgery for endometrioma before IVF did not improve live birth (OR 0.90) and may reduce ovarian reserve.
dose.notes: Discuss fertility preservation and surgery timing with a reproductive specialist.

entries.mechanism: Peritoneal and follicular inflammation, iron from repeated bleeding (free-iron Fenton chemistry) and granulosa-cell ROS impair follicle development and oocyte maturation.
entries.interactions: Antioxidant supplements have been tried, but none has convincing live-birth data ([female-antioxidant-supplements]).
entries.caveats: Evidence on egg quality is mostly from small biological studies; the main clinical effect is fewer oocytes and more cancelled cycles rather than lower live birth per transfer.

entries.title: Endometriosis

entries.headline: Higher blood ergothioneine (mainly from mushrooms) is linked to 14% lower mortality per SD in a Swedish cohort, and the body has a dedicated transporter for it, but supplement trials are tiny and show only trends.

dose.effective: No proven supplement dose; eating mushrooms regularly is the practical source
dose.studied_range: Supplements 5-25 mg/day for weeks; 25 mg three times weekly for one year in an MCI pilot
dose.too_much: EFSA judged synthetic ergothioneine safe at proposed levels, including in pregnancy and for young children (NOAEL 800 mg/kg/day in animals)
dose.timeframe: Blood levels rise within days and the compound is retained for weeks
dose.notes: Mushrooms are by far the richest food source; mushroom intake was linked to modestly lower all-cause mortality in cohort studies.

entries.mechanism: A sulfur-containing histidine derivative made only by fungi and some bacteria. Humans absorb and concentrate it through the OCTN1 (SLC22A4) transporter in red cells, immune cells and other tissues. It scavenges radicals and chelates metals, and may act mainly under oxidative stress.
entries.interactions: Comes packaged with fibre and other compounds in mushrooms; overlaps with diet-pattern benefits such as [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Blood ergothioneine is a marker of a health-conscious diet, so cohort links may be confounded. Supplement trials measured biomarkers in small groups; the MCI pilot had 19 participants.
entries.debate: Halliwell and Ames argue ergothioneine may be a 'longevity vitamin' because the body actively concentrates it and levels fall with age and cognitive decline [lon-halliwell2018, lon-ames2018, lon-cheah2016]; the Malmo cohort found strong links with lower mortality [lon-smith2020]. But the cohort authors identified it as a marker of a healthy food pattern, the mushroom-mortality meta-analysis showed only a small association (RR 0.94) and a null NHANES estimate [lon-ba2021], and supplementation produced mostly non-significant biomarker changes [lon-cheah2017]. The only cognitive trial is a 19-person pilot [lon-yau2024].

key_numbers.label: All-cause mortality HR per SD higher ergothioneine

factors.name: Evening and night-time light (room light, screens, light while sleeping)

entries.headline: Ordinary room light before bed delayed melatonin onset in 99% of people and shortened melatonin by about 90 minutes, half-maximal suppression occurs at only ~25 lux, sleeping with a light or TV on was linked to 17-33% more weight gain and obesity, and one night at 100 lux raised next-morning insulin resistance.

dose.effective: In the 3 hours before bed keep light at the eye below about 10 lux melanopic EDI (dim, warm lamps below eye level); keep the bedroom as dark as possible (≤1 lux melanopic EDI; blackout curtains or an eye mask); reduce screen brightness and use low-melanopic (warm) display settings, or stop screens before bed.
dose.studied_range: Room light <200 lux vs <3 lux for 8 h before bed; 10-2,000 lux for 5 h; ~4 h of e-reader use for 5 nights; 100 lux during one night of sleep; habitual bedroom light ≥3 lux.
dose.too_much: Sleeping with a TV or ceiling light on; bright overhead lighting or full-brightness screens late in the evening.
dose.timeframe: Melatonin suppression within minutes to hours; circadian delay after a few evenings; metabolic effects after one night.
dose.notes: Brightness matters more than screen colour filters: in one trial, iPhone Night Shift did not improve sleep, and blue-blocking glasses have indeterminate effects on sleep. See also [morning-light]. Melatonin supplements are covered under [melatonin].

entries.mechanism: Melanopsin-driven signals from the retina inhibit pineal melatonin synthesis and phase-delay the clock. Melatonin is a direct radical scavenger and induces antioxidant enzymes and DNA repair; suppressing it, plus sympathetic activation during lit sleep, worsens insulin sensitivity. Follicular fluid melatonin protects oocytes from oxidative stress in laboratory studies.
entries.interactions: Delays the melatonin rise that makes [late-eating] worse for glucose; adds to [shift-work-circadian]; contributes to [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Health-outcome links (obesity, diabetes, mortality) are observational and confounded by urban living, income, sleep and mental health. Sperm data are one small cross-sectional study of men at a fertility clinic and one ecological study of outdoor light at night; we did not create a separate sperm factor. No human study has tied evening light to egg quality, although melatonin protects oocytes in laboratory work.
entries.debate: Laboratory trials consistently show melatonin suppression and circadian delay [kcc-gooley2011, kcc-phillips2019, kcc-chang2015, kcc-schollhorn2023], and one night of lit sleep impaired insulin sensitivity [kcc-mason2022]; cohorts link light at night to obesity, diabetes and mortality [kcc-park2019, kcc-obayashi2013, kcc-windred2024a, kcc-windred2024b]. A letter argued the e-reader findings overstate real-life relevance and the authors defended them [kcc-zeitzer2015, kcc-changczeisler2015]; screen-colour fixes have weak support (Night Shift [kcc-duraccio2021]; blue-blocking glasses indeterminate [kcc-singh2023]); and cohort authors disclose lighting-industry funding [kcc-windred2024a]. Sperm associations [kcc-green2020, kcc-tian2024] are preliminary.

entries.headline: Fat mass tracks systemic oxidative stress. BMI was one of the strongest independent correlates of urinary F2-isoprostanes in 2,828 Framingham participants, through adipose NADPH oxidase and inflammation.

dose.effective: Reducing excess fat mass (see lifestyle area for specifics).
dose.timeframe: Not specified in these studies
dose.notes: Mechanistic and cross-sectional human evidence. Intervention data are covered by the lifestyle area.

entries.mechanism: In expanded adipose tissue, free fatty acids activate NADPH oxidase and antioxidant enzymes fall, raising ROS. This disrupts adipokines (lower adiponectin, higher IL-6, MCP-1 and PAI-1) and drives systemic low-grade inflammation through NF-kB. Nutrient excess also raises mitochondrial superoxide.
entries.interactions: Compounds [glycemic-control] and [chronic-inflammation]. Supplements do not offset it.
entries.caveats: Most human data are associations. The causal chain is supported by mouse NOX-inhibitor experiments.
entries.title: Excess body fat (especially visceral adiposity)

entries.headline: Obese men are more often infertile and have lower IVF live-birth rates; the BMI-SDF link is real but smaller and less consistent than for smoking or varicocele.

dose.effective: Aim for BMI under 30, ideally 18.5-25; waist reduction matters more than the scale number.
dose.studied_range: BMI categories from <18.5 to >=40.
dose.too_much: Risk rises steeply above BMI 35-40 (odds of oligo/azoospermia 2.04 in morbid obesity). Impaired glucose tolerance was linked to +13.8 points SDF.
dose.timeframe: Lifestyle weight loss over 3-6 months has improved semen in trials.
dose.notes: Very underweight (BMI <18.5) also trends toward worse semen.

entries.mechanism: Excess adipose tissue raises aromatase activity (lower testosterone, higher estradiol), systemic inflammation and insulin resistance, increases scrotal fat and temperature, and raises seminal ROS.
entries.interactions: Improves with [weight-loss], [aerobic-exercise-moderate] and [mediterranean-diet]. Often co-occurs with poor sleep and sugary drinks.
entries.caveats: In the SDF meta-analysis only class I obesity showed a small, borderline increase (SMD 0.23). Confounding by diet, activity and diabetes is substantial.

ART live birth per cycle, obese men

entries.title: Obesity and metabolic dysfunction

entries.headline: Obesity (BMI >= 30) is associated with about 15% lower IVF live birth (RR 0.85), worse with PCOS, and with an inflamed, lipid-rich follicular environment.

dose.effective: Aim for BMI under 30 and ideally 18.5-24.9; in PCOS, even 5% weight loss improved hormones and cycles.
dose.studied_range: BMI categories 18.5-24.9 vs >= 30 kg/m2 in meta-analysis.
dose.too_much: Underweight (BMI < 18.5) and very low energy availability also impair ovulation (see [vigorous-exercise-low-energy]).
dose.timeframe: Follicular environment reflects the preceding ~3 months.
dose.notes: Donor-egg data did not change the overall conclusion, suggesting both egg and uterine effects.

entries.mechanism: Higher follicular fluid insulin, triglycerides, lactate and CRP; lipid accumulation in oocytes causes ER stress, reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and cumulus-cell apoptosis (lipotoxicity).
entries.interactions: Compounds [pcos] and [glycemic-control]. Weight-loss evidence is in [weight-loss]. Vigorous exercise was not harmful in women with BMI >= 25 ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]).
entries.caveats: Associations are confounded by PCOS and metabolic disease. Weight-loss RCTs before IVF have not raised IVF live birth (see [weight-loss]).

entries.title: Obesity (BMI 30 or higher)

factors.name: Exercise snacks and vigorous intermittent lifestyle activity (VILPA)

entries.headline: In non-exercisers, three 1-2 minute bursts of vigorous everyday activity a day (stairs, fast uphill walking, carrying loads) were associated with 38-40% lower mortality and 48-49% lower cardiovascular death, and small RCTs show stair or sprint 'snacks' raise VO2peak modestly (about 4% for sprint snacks); the cohort data may overstate the benefit.

dose.effective: 3-5 bouts a day of about 1 minute of vigorous effort (fast stair climbing, e.g. 60 steps; brisk uphill walking; 20-second sprints), totalling about 3-5 min/day; or 6 x 1-min hard intervals before meals.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: 0 to ~10 VILPA bouts/day (median 3-5); RCTs: 3 x 60-step stair climbs or 3 x 20-s sprints, 3 days/week for 6 weeks.
dose.too_much: None known; the mortality curve flattened beyond about 8 bouts/day.
dose.timeframe: VO2peak gains in 6 weeks; glucose effects the same day.
dose.notes: A practical entry point for people who do not exercise. Benefit for cardiovascular events was clearer in women than men in UK Biobank.

entries.mechanism: Brief vigorous efforts produce the same metabolic, calcium and ROS signals as interval training (AMPK, PGC-1alpha), raise heart rate near maximum, and improve post-meal glucose uptake.
entries.interactions: A stepping stone to [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and [cardiorespiratory-fitness]; breaks up [sedentary-time]; pre-meal snacks complement [post-meal-walking].
entries.caveats: VILPA data come from wrist accelerometers in UK Biobank volunteers (healthier than average) and one smaller US sample; people able to climb stairs fast may simply be healthier. RCTs are small (9-28 people) and short.
entries.debate: The UK Biobank analyses report large, near-linear benefits for mortality, cancer and cardiovascular events [exr-stamatakis2022, exr-stamatakis2023, exr-stamatakis2025, exr-ahmadi2023]. A US national replication found a similar 44% lower mortality, but when people with prevalent heart disease or cancer were excluded the confidence intervals mostly crossed 1, consistent with reverse causation [exr-koemel2026]. Training studies confirm fitness gains but they are modest and small [exr-jenkins2019, exr-little2019], and pre-meal snacks improved glucose in only 9 people [exr-francois2014]. Proponents frame snacks as proof-of-concept rather than a replacement for guidelines [exr-islam2022]. The related 'weekend warrior' pattern is better supported: concentrating activity into 1-2 days gave similar mortality and cardiovascular associations to spreading it out [exr-odonovan2017, exr-dossantos2022, exr-khurshid2023, exr-kim2025].

MACE HR, women with 3.4 min/day VILPA

factors.name: Exogenous ketones (ketone esters, ketone salts, MCT/C8 oil)

entries.headline: A ketone-ester drink raises blood BHB to ~2-4 mmol/L within an hour, and salts or C8 oil raise it much less. Acute doses lower glucose by ~0.5 mmol/L and give a small cognitive benefit, but they do not improve exercise performance, and the anti-inflammatory story is contradictory in humans.

dose.effective: Ketone monoester ~0.3-0.5 g/kg (about 12-27 g BHB) gives a peak BHB of ~2.8-4 mmol/L for 2-4 h. Ketone salts ~12-24 g BHB give ~1 mmol/L. C8 (tricaprylin) 20 mL twice daily gives ~0.3-0.5 mmol/L. A 15 g twice-daily MCT drink was used in the 6-month MCI trial.
dose.studied_range: Single doses up to 714 mg/kg monoester; 25 mL (26.8 g) monoester three times daily for 28 days in healthy adults; 12 g BHB before meals for 14 days in obesity; 30 g/day MCT for 6 months.
dose.too_much: Gut upset (nausea, cramps, diarrhoea) at high doses, worse with salts and MCT. Salts carry a large sodium/potassium load and half the BHB is the less useful L-isomer. Avoid with SGLT2 inhibitors or type 1 diabetes without medical advice.
dose.timeframe: Peak at 30-60 min, back to baseline within 3-4 h; no lasting ketosis without repeated dosing.
dose.notes: A meal cuts the peak by about a third. Ketone esters taste harsh and cost several dollars per serving at retail (a market observation, not from a study). They give ketones without carbohydrate restriction, so they do not reproduce the low-insulin, weight-loss and low-glucose milieu of the diet.

entries.mechanism: Supplies D-BHB directly. In the short term it lowers hepatic glucose output, free fatty acids and lipolysis (HCAR2), and gives the brain an alternative fuel. HDAC inhibition and NLRP3 blockade are cell and mouse findings. In humans, a single dose increased monocyte caspase-1 activation, while 14 days of pre-meal dosing decreased it.
entries.interactions: No human trials measure oxidative-damage markers. It does not replace [ketogenic-diet] for epilepsy. Glucose lowering adds to diabetes drugs. For athletes, pre-race ketone drinks impaired a time trial; post-session ester during overload training is the one positive signal.
entries.caveats: A meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found no performance effect (g = -0.05). The cognitive meta-analysis effect is small (SMD 0.29) across heterogeneous trials. Most trials are industry-linked, small and short. Vendor claims about 'burning fat' are backwards: exogenous BHB suppresses lipolysis.

key_numbers.label: Peak BHB, ketone salts (same BHB dose)

entries.title: Exogenous ketones (ketone esters, ketone salts, MCT/C8 oil)

entries.headline: Outside testosterone shuts down the brain's signal (LH/FSH) to the testes and can drop sperm counts to zero; recovery takes months to over a year.

dose.effective: Any exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroid, including gels, injections and 'cycles'.
dose.studied_range: Androgen regimens used for male contraception reliably suppress sperm output.
dose.too_much: Long-term, high-dose and long-acting preparations recover slowest.
dose.timeframe: Median recovery to 20 million/mL about 3.4 months after contraceptive-style androgen use; after steroid abuse, often 6-12+ months, sometimes incomplete.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: do not prescribe testosterone to men who want current or future fertility. Do not stop abruptly without medical advice; urologists can use hCG, SERMs or aromatase inhibitors to restart production.

entries.mechanism: Negative feedback suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH; intratesticular testosterone collapses, halting spermatogenesis (endocrine, not primarily oxidative).
entries.interactions: Overrides any benefit from diet or supplements. Often combined with other harmful exposures in body-building (high-dose supplements, stimulants).
entries.caveats: Not an SDF factor in the usual sense: it mainly lowers sperm number, often to azoospermia. Included because it is the most common avoidable cause of severe male-factor infertility in young men.
entries.title: Exogenous testosterone (TRT) and anabolic-androgenic steroids

entries.headline: In the 200-man EUROLIVE RCT, oxidized LDL fell linearly with olive-oil phenolic content at 25 mL/day; EU law authorises an LDL-protection claim for oils supplying 5 mg hydroxytyrosol and derivatives per 20 g, and PREDIMED's EVOO arm cut major CVD events by ~30%.

dose.effective: 20-25 g (about 2 tablespoons) per day of a high-phenolic EVOO meeting >= 5 mg hydroxytyrosol + derivatives per 20 g.
dose.studied_range: 25 mL/day for 3 weeks (EUROLIVE); ~1 L/week per household in PREDIMED for years.
dose.too_much: Calories (about 120 kcal per tablespoon).
dose.timeframe: Measurable LDL changes within 3 weeks.
dose.notes: Use as the main culinary fat, raw on food or for moderate-heat cooking; phenolics decline with storage, light and heat. Refined olive oil has a fraction of the phenolics.

entries.mechanism: Hydroxytyrosol and its secoiridoid precursors (oleacein/3,4-DHPEA-EDA, oleuropein aglycone) bind to LDL and protect its lipids from oxidation; high oleic acid content makes membranes and LDL less oxidizable than PUFA-rich oils; modest Nrf2 and anti-inflammatory effects.
entries.interactions: Best evidence when it replaces butter, refined seed oils or [oxidized-frying-oils]. Improves carotenoid absorption from [tomatoes-lycopene] and [leafy-greens]. Core component of [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Short trials use LDL oxidation markers rather than outcomes; PREDIMED was re-analysed after randomisation irregularities (results held). Phenolic content varies enormously between oils and labels rarely state it. In the 50-person OLIVAUS crossover, 60 mL/day of high- vs low-polyphenol oil for 3 weeks gave no significant between-treatment difference, with oxLDL falling only within the high-polyphenol arm (more in abdominal obesity), so effects in healthy people are modest. The throat sting of fresh oil comes from oleocanthal, a COX inhibitor with ibuprofen-like activity in vitro; its clinical relevance at culinary doses is unknown.

entries.headline: In PCOS, intermittent fasting lowered weight (-4.25 kg) and free androgen index and raised SHBG, but no more than calorie restriction; in lean women a 72-h fast made 2 of 7 cycles anovulatory, and fasting beyond the overnight period in late pregnancy rapidly produces ketosis.

dose.effective: With PCOS and excess weight: an 8-10 h eating window or daily calorie restriction for 8+ weeks, whichever is easier to keep. Without excess weight: avoid deliberate energy deficit while trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: 72-h follicular-phase fasts; 5-12 weeks of 6-10 h TRE in PCOS; Ramadan in pregnancy.
dose.too_much: Energy availability below ~30 kcal/kg lean mass/day disrupts LH pulses; multi-day fasts in lean women can block ovulation. In pregnancy avoid fasting beyond the overnight period (18-h fasts cause ketonaemia).
dose.timeframe: Androgen and menstrual changes in PCOS over 5-8 weeks; follicle effects within one cycle.
dose.notes: Normal-weight women tolerated a 3-day fast without cycle disruption; lean women (<=20% body fat) did not.

entries.mechanism: In insulin-resistant PCOS, lower insulin raises SHBG and lowers ovarian androgen output. In lean women, energy deficit slows GnRH/LH pulsatility (hypothalamic suppression). In pregnancy, 'accelerated starvation' raises maternal ketones that cross the placenta.
entries.interactions: Works through the same route as [weight-loss] in [pcos]. Stacking fasting with heavy training risks [vigorous-exercise-low-energy]. Prenatal nutrient needs (e.g., [folic-acid]) are harder to meet in short eating windows.
entries.caveats: PCOS evidence is five small studies; the only RCT comparing early TRE with calorie restriction (Talebi 2024) found no difference. Ramadan pregnancy meta-analyses show no birth-weight effect but are observational and lack mortality data; the IQ-ketone link (Rizzo 1991) is correlational.

key_numbers.label: Weight change with IF in PCOS (meta-analysis)
Energy availability threshold for LH disruption

entries.title: Fasting, ovulation, PCOS and pregnancy

entries.headline: No trial shows fasting improves sperm; a 48-h fast cut LH by ~64% and lowered testosterone, 16:8 TRE lowered testosterone in trained men, and a retrospective IVF study found lower progressive motility (30% vs 38%) in samples produced during Ramadan.

dose.effective: None established. If overweight, the benefit comes from losing weight by any method; daily 12-14 h overnight fasts appear harmless.
dose.studied_range: 48-h fasts, 8 weeks of 16:8 TRE, Ramadan (dawn-to-sunset fasting for a month), three 5-day FMD cycles.
dose.too_much: Multi-day fasts suppress the reproductive axis within 48 h; avoid them during the ~74-day window before conception attempts or semen analysis.
dose.timeframe: Hormone changes within 48 h; semen effects would need one spermatogenic cycle (~74 days).
dose.notes: Ramadan meta-analysis found no average change in testosterone, LH or FSH, so daily dawn-to-dusk fasting is probably neutral for hormones.

entries.mechanism: Acute energy deficit slows hypothalamic GnRH/LH pulsatility and lowers testosterone and IGF-1; dehydration and circadian disruption during Ramadan may affect semen volume and motility.
entries.interactions: Weight loss in men with obesity improves semen quality; see [weight-loss] and [excess-adiposity]. Poor sleep during late-night eating periods overlaps with [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Human sperm data are a 21-man 1986 study, a 97-man retrospective IVF cohort, and an 18-man FMD pilot. Rodent studies of fasting and sperm are not transferable.
entries.title: Fasting and sperm (Ramadan, TRE, multi-day fasts)

entries.headline: Three monthly 5-day cycles (~1,100 then ~700 kcal/day, low protein) lowered weight, trunk fat, blood pressure and IGF-1 vs usual diet in one 100-person trial; no direct oxidative stress endpoints, and the lead developer holds a commercial interest.

dose.effective: 5 consecutive days per month of a plant-based, low-protein, low-sugar, higher-unsaturated-fat diet (~1,100 kcal on day 1, ~700 kcal on days 2-5), for 3 cycles.
dose.studied_range: 3 monthly cycles in generally healthy adults; 3 cycles over 4 months in men with poor semen quality.
dose.too_much: Same exclusions as fasting: pregnancy, eating disorders, underweight, diabetes medication without supervision.
dose.timeframe: Changes measured after 3 cycles (3 months).
dose.notes: Benefits were concentrated in people with elevated baseline risk; low protein is probably what lowers IGF-1.

entries.mechanism: Mimics fasting signals (low insulin, IGF-1 and amino acids) while supplying some food; in mice, cycles triggered regeneration on refeeding and extended lifespan.
entries.interactions: Effects overlap with [weight-loss]; IGF-1 lowering is also achieved by moderate protein reduction under [calorie-restriction].
entries.caveats: Small number of trials, largely from one group with a commercial product; the 2.5-year 'biological age' reduction is an exploratory secondary analysis.
entries.title: Fasting-mimicking diet (5-day low-calorie, low-protein cycles)

entries.headline: Age is by far the dominant, non-modifiable driver of egg quality: fecundity falls from about 32 and faster after 37, and the share of women with no chromosomally normal embryo rises from 2-6% (age 26-37) to 33% at 42 and 53% at 44.

dose.effective: Not modifiable. The practical lever is time: ACOG/ASRM advise expedited evaluation after 6 months of trying from age 35, and immediate evaluation over 40.
dose.studied_range: Aneuploidy data from embryos of women aged ~22-47; egg chromosome-segregation data from ages 9-43.
dose.timeframe: Gradual decline from the early 30s, steep after ~37; no lifestyle change reverses it.
dose.notes: Lifestyle can avoid adding damage on top of age, but no diet or supplement has been shown to restore the chromosomal quality of older eggs in humans. Egg freezing at a younger age and IVF with PGT-A or donor eggs are the only interventions that address age directly.

entries.mechanism: Eggs are arrested in meiosis for decades. Cohesin that holds sister chromatids together is laid down before birth and is not renewed, so it erodes with age, causing chromosome mis-segregation (aneuploidy). In parallel, oocyte mitochondria become less efficient (less ATP, more mtDNA instability), CoQ10-synthesis enzymes and NAD+ levels decline (animal data), and spindle assembly becomes error-prone.
entries.interactions: Age magnifies almost every other harm: [tobacco-smoking] and [excess-adiposity] effects are layered on a declining baseline. Diet associations such as [mediterranean-diet] were seen only in women under 35 in one cohort. Supplements aimed at mitochondria ([coq10], [nmn-nad]) target the age mechanism but have no human live-birth proof.
entries.caveats: Aneuploidy also rises slightly in the very young (U-curve), but this is a minor effect compared with the rise after the mid-30s. Ovarian reserve tests (AMH, antral follicle count) predict egg number and response to stimulation, not egg quality; a woman with high AMH at 42 still has age-typical aneuploidy rates. Claims that any supplement 'reverses egg ageing' are not supported by human data.

factors.name: Fever and acute febrile illness (including flu, COVID-19)

entries.headline: A fever of 39-40 C for even 2 days can raise DNA fragmentation and cut sperm count for 2-3 months before recovering.

dose.effective: Body temperature around 38.5-40 C for 1 day or more.
dose.studied_range: Case report: 2 days at 39-40 C followed for 79 days.
dose.timeframe: DFI up 24-36% at days 15-37, back toward baseline by about day 79; plan semen tests or ART cycles at least ~3 months after a high fever if possible.
dose.notes: Fever control with paracetamol/acetaminophen is reasonable; there is no evidence that it prevents the sperm effect.

entries.mechanism: Whole-body hyperthermia warms the testes, impairing late spermatogenesis and chromatin protamination and increasing heat-shock and apoptotic signalling.
entries.interactions: Same mechanism as [sauna]. A semen test taken within 3 months of a fever may overstate long-term problems.
entries.caveats: Evidence is mostly case reports and small series; the effect is temporary.
entries.title: Fever and acute febrile illness (including flu, COVID-19)

entries.headline: Hair-loss-dose finasteride (1 mg) left semen unchanged in 181 young men, but prostate doses (finasteride 5 mg, dutasteride 0.5 mg) cut total sperm count about 30%, and subfertile men on finasteride saw counts rise on average 11.6-fold after stopping.

dose.effective: Finasteride 1 mg/day (hair loss) or 5 mg/day (prostate); dutasteride 0.5 mg/day.
dose.studied_range: Finasteride 1 mg/day for 48 weeks (RCT); finasteride 5 mg and dutasteride 0.5 mg for 1 year (RCT); mean 1 mg/day for ~57 months (subfertile men).
dose.too_much: Prostate doses and dutasteride have larger effects (semen volume -29.7% on dutasteride); men who are already oligospermic appear most vulnerable even at 1 mg.
dose.timeframe: Counts fell by 26 weeks; recovery after stopping over months (one spermatogenic cycle is ~74 days).
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Men with low counts who are trying to conceive and use finasteride for hair loss can ask about pausing it; a repeat semen analysis about 3 months after stopping shows whether it was a factor.

entries.mechanism: Blocking conversion of testosterone to DHT (by 73% with finasteride 5 mg and 94% with dutasteride) reduces prostate and seminal-vesicle secretions and modestly impairs epididymal sperm maturation; testosterone itself rises slightly [med-amory2007].
entries.interactions: Unlike [testosterone-anabolic-steroids], 5-ARIs do not shut down LH/FSH. Often used alongside [alpha-blockers-sperm] for prostate enlargement, which adds ejaculatory problems.
entries.caveats: The dramatic recovery data come from 27 men who presented with infertility, a selected group; healthy men on 1 mg show no average change.
entries.debate: In healthy young men, 1 mg finasteride did not affect spermatogenesis [med-overstreet1999]; in subfertile men on similar doses, counts rose sharply after stopping [med-samplaski2013], suggesting a vulnerable subgroup. Prostate doses produced mild, mostly reversible falls [med-amory2007].

factors.name: Fisetin (senolytic flavonol supplement; traces in strawberries)

entries.headline: Fisetin cleared senescent cells and extended lifespan in one mouse study, but the NIA Interventions Testing Program found no lifespan extension and no placebo-controlled senolytic trial in humans has reported results; food supplies milligrams, while trials test about 1.4 g doses.

dose.effective: None established.
dose.studied_range: Senolytic trials: 20 mg/kg/day for 2 consecutive days (about 1.4 g for a 70 kg adult), repeated intermittently; one small continuous trial used 200 mg/day for 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: High-dose human safety data are limited; flavonols alter the bioavailability of some drugs (see [quercetin]).
dose.notes: All flavonols and flavones together averaged about 17 mg/day in a Japanese diet, so eating strawberries cannot approach trial doses.

entries.mechanism: In cell and mouse models fisetin triggers apoptosis of senescent cells by disabling their anti-apoptotic defences, lowering the inflammatory SASP. Any antioxidant action in vivo is weak and short-lived.
entries.interactions: Same flavonol class as [quercetin]. The human senolytic data so far come from dasatinib plus quercetin, a drug combination, not from fisetin.
entries.caveats: The widely quoted mouse lifespan result was not reproduced by the multi-site ITP. The Mayo AFFIRM-LITE trial (started 2018) is still listed as enrolling in 2026. Senescent cells also help wound healing, so clearing them is not risk-free. The only completed RCTs are a small trial in obese men measuring adipokines and an unrelated stroke trial.

entries.title: Fisetin (senolytic flavonol supplement; traces in strawberries)

entries.headline: The largest male supplement trial (FAZST, 2370 couples) found folic acid plus zinc did nothing for semen or live birth, and slightly raised DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: Not recommended for male fertility.
dose.studied_range: 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg elemental zinc daily for 6 months.
dose.too_much: SDF 29.7% vs 27.2% with placebo (+2.4 points); more GI symptoms. Long-term zinc above ~40 mg/day can cause copper deficiency.
dose.timeframe: 6 months studied.
dose.notes: Correcting a genuine zinc or folate deficiency via diet is still sensible.

entries.mechanism: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism and DNA methylation; zinc stabilises sperm chromatin and is an antioxidant enzyme cofactor. High doses did not help replete men.
entries.interactions: High-dose folate overlaps with [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail] concerns.
entries.caveats: Population was general infertility patients, not selected for deficiency.
entries.title: Folic acid + zinc

entries.headline: Folic acid is mandatory preconception care (400-800 ug/day prevents neural tube defects) and is also consistently associated with better fertility: 15% higher fecundability and 20 percentage points higher IVF live birth at > 800 ug/day supplemental folate.

dose.effective: 400-800 ug/day folic acid, started before conception (ideally 3 months ahead) and continued through early pregnancy.
dose.studied_range: Supplemental folate < 400 to > 800 ug/day (cohorts).
dose.too_much: Higher doses only on a clinician's advice for specific indications.
dose.timeframe: Before conception for neural tube protection; 3 months covers follicle development.
dose.notes: Usually taken as a prenatal multivitamin. Diet folate (leafy greens, legumes) is good but does not replace the supplement.

entries.mechanism: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism: DNA synthesis and repair, methylation and homocysteine clearance. Elevated homocysteine in follicular fluid is linked to poorer embryo quality.
entries.interactions: Core of [profertility-diet]; may buffer the [outdoor-air-pollution] association in one cohort.
entries.caveats: Fertility benefits are observational; the neural-tube benefit is RCT-proven and reason enough to take it.
entries.title: Folic acid / folate

entries.headline: Ejaculating every 1-2 days keeps sperm fresher: each extra day of abstinence adds about 0.65 points of SDF, and a second sample 3 hours after the first cut SDF from 35% to 24%.

dose.effective: Ejaculate (intercourse or otherwise) every 1-2 days through the fertile window and beyond. For ART with high SDF, ask about a sample after 1 day or a second sample 1-4 hours after a first ejaculation.
dose.studied_range: Abstinence from 1-4 hours to 7+ days; 2-day cut-off in RCT meta-analysis.
dose.too_much: Volume and total count fall with very frequent ejaculation, but for natural conception daily intercourse is not harmful.
dose.timeframe: Immediate: works on the next ejaculate.
dose.notes: Diagnostic labs usually specify 2-7 days of abstinence and SDF guidelines suggest 2-5 days before a test; follow the lab's instructions when testing, and use short abstinence for conception attempts and ART samples.

entries.mechanism: Shortens the time sperm sit in the epididymis, where defective sperm and leukocytes generate ROS and stored sperm accumulate oxidative DNA damage.
entries.interactions: Cheapest and fastest lever; a non-invasive alternative to [testicular-sperm-icsi]. Works alongside slower changes that act on sperm production.
entries.caveats: One large meta-analysis of risk factors found no significant abstinence effect, and absolute reductions in healthy men are small (about 2-3 points). The biggest drops are in men with high baseline SDF or abnormal semen.

SDF in second sample 3 h later

entries.title: Frequent ejaculation (short abstinence, 1-2 days)

entries.headline: Doubling produce from 5.8 to 12 servings/day for 2 weeks reduced lymphocyte 8-OHdG and urinary isoprostanes, but another controlled trial found 600 g/day had no effect on oxidative DNA damage in healthy non-smokers; cohorts show lower mortality up to ~800 g/day.

dose.effective: At least 5 servings (400-500 g)/day, ideally up to ~800 g, from diverse botanical families.
dose.studied_range: 600 g/day for 24 days; 12 servings/day for 14 days.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Diversity across plant families mattered in the positive trial; benefit was larger in people with low baseline carotenoids.

entries.mechanism: Many compounds acting through different routes (Nrf2 electrophiles, gut metabolites, vitamin C/carotenoids, nitrate, fiber, potassium).
entries.interactions: The null Danish trial suggests healthy people with adequate defences may already be near a ceiling for oxidative DNA damage.
entries.caveats: Oxidative-marker trials conflict; cohort benefits may partly reflect healthier lifestyles.

entries.title: High fruit and vegetable intake

entries.headline: Low-pesticide fruit and vegetables (2.8+ servings a day) are linked to much higher sperm counts; high-residue produce is not.

dose.effective: At least 3 servings/day; wash produce and favour lower-residue choices.
dose.studied_range: <1.1 to >=2.8 servings/day of low-to-moderate-residue produce.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Benefit is likely part of the overall dietary pattern.

entries.mechanism: Food-level vitamin C, folate, carotenoids and polyphenols support seminal antioxidant defences without the megadoses that cause reductive stress.
entries.interactions: See [pesticides] and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Total fruit and vegetable intake was unrelated to semen in the same study; the finding depended on pesticide residue classification.

key_numbers.label: Higher total count, >=2.8 servings/day low-residue produce

factors.name: G6PD deficiency (oxidant drug and fava bean sensitivity)

entries.headline: An X-linked enzyme defect carried by roughly 400-500 million people; carriers are usually well but can hemolyze after fava beans, high-risk drugs (dapsone, primaquine, rasburicase, methylene blue) or very high IV vitamin C, so knowing your status changes what you must avoid.

dose.effective: One G6PD activity test (or genotype) before high-risk drugs or IV vitamin C infusions, especially with African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern or Asian ancestry. If deficient: avoid fava beans and CPIC high-risk drugs.
dose.studied_range: CPIC 2022 classification of drugs by systematic review: high risk (dapsone, methylene blue, pegloticase, primaquine, rasburicase, tafenoquine, toluidine blue), medium (nitrofurantoin), low-to-no risk (vitamin C at standard doses, vitamin K, many sulfonamides).
dose.too_much: Very high-dose IV vitamin C (gram-level infusions) can trigger hemolysis in deficient people; methylene blue, sometimes sold as a 'mitochondrial' or nootropic supplement, is classed high risk.
dose.timeframe: Hemolysis typically starts within 1-3 days of the trigger and resolves after it is removed.
dose.notes: Activity tests can read falsely normal during or right after a hemolytic episode; heterozygous women may have intermediate activity and still hemolyze.

entries.mechanism: G6PD makes NADPH through the pentose phosphate pathway; NADPH keeps glutathione reduced. Red cells have no other NADPH source, so oxidant drugs, fava-bean glycosides (vicine, convicine) or infection-related oxidants overwhelm glutathione, oxidize hemoglobin into Heinz bodies and destroy the cells.
entries.interactions: Pro-oxidant effects of megadose vitamin C (see [vitamin-c-supplement]) and of high-dose antioxidant stacks ([high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]) matter here because ascorbate can act as an oxidant in the presence of iron and oxygen. Infections ([febrile-illness]) are themselves triggers.
entries.caveats: Most carriers are lifelong asymptomatic; this is about avoiding specific triggers, not about general oxidative stress. Ordinary dietary antioxidants and standard-dose vitamin C are not a concern.
entries.debate: Regulatory warnings conflict and evidence for many listed drugs is sparse; CPIC authors disagreed about the strength of the nitrofurantoin evidence [tst-gammal2023], while older reviews list a broader range of triggers [tst-cappellini2008]. CPIC classes standard-dose vitamin C as low-to-no risk [tst-gammal2023], but a systematic review of IV vitamin C flags hemolysis at very high doses and supports pre-infusion G6PD testing [tst-alangari2026].
entries.title: G6PD deficiency (oxidant drug and fava bean sensitivity)

entries.headline: Garlic supplements lower blood pressure in hypertensives (about -8.7/-6.1 mmHg) and a meta-analysis of 12 small RCTs reports lower MDA and higher antioxidant enzymes, but these markers are weak and the trials low quality.

dose.effective: Culinary: 1-2 cloves/day crushed and left 10 min before cooking; supplement trials used aged garlic extract or powder.
dose.studied_range: 80-4000 mg/day garlic preparations for 2-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Supplements can increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Red onions are a major dietary source of quercetin (onion chromatography total ~140 mg/100 g in Phenol-Explorer).

entries.mechanism: Organosulfur compounds (allicin breakdown products, S-allylcysteine) activate Nrf2 and raise hydrogen sulfide signalling; onion quercetin.
entries.interactions: Another mild Nrf2 inducer; much weaker than sulforaphane.
entries.caveats: TAC and TBARS-type MDA are non-specific oxidative markers; effect sizes in the meta-analysis (Hedges' g up to 13.8) are implausibly large, a sign of small heterogeneous studies.

key_numbers.label: Onion (red), total polyphenols, chromatography (sum of compounds)

entries.title: Garlic and onions

entries.headline: Active infection (e.g. Chlamydia, Mycoplasma) and white cells in semen raise ROS and SDF; treating a proven infection can lower SDF by about a third.

dose.effective: Leukocytospermia is defined as >=1 million white cells/mL; even 0.2-1 million/mL has been linked to higher ROS and SDF.
dose.studied_range: Antibiotic courses guided by culture/PCR; follow-up about 4 months.
dose.timeframe: In one study SDF fell from 37.7% to 24.2% after ~3.8 months of treatment; pregnancy rates were higher in couples who tried after rather than during treatment.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: if round cells exceed 1 million/mL, distinguish white cells from immature germ cells before treating. Treat confirmed infection; do not give empiric antibiotics for every abnormal semen test.

entries.mechanism: Activated neutrophils and macrophages produce superoxide via NADPH oxidase (NOX2) at rates far above sperm, overwhelming seminal antioxidants and attacking sperm membranes and DNA.
entries.interactions: [febrile-illness] from the same infection adds thermal damage. Antioxidants are not a substitute for treating infection.
entries.caveats: A large meta-analysis found overall effects of Chlamydia and HPV on SDF negligible, so the strongest data are from symptomatic or culture-positive cases. Evidence comes from small observational studies.
entries.title: Genital tract infection and leukocytospermia

factors.name: GLP-1 drugs (semaglutide, tirzepatide)
aliases: GLP-1 drugs before conception (PCOS, contraception, washout)

entries.headline: Semaglutide and tirzepatide cut body weight by about 15-21% in 68-72-week trials and lower CRP and malondialdehyde in meta-analyses of RCTs, but roughly a quarter to a third of the weight lost is lean mass unless resistance training is added.

dose.effective: Semaglutide 2.4 mg once weekly (obesity dose); tirzepatide 5, 10 or 15 mg once weekly, reached by gradual dose escalation.
dose.studied_range: Semaglutide 2.4 mg/week for 68 weeks (STEP 1); tirzepatide 5-15 mg/week for 72 weeks (SURMOUNT-1); liraglutide 1.2-3 mg/day in older and fertility studies.
dose.too_much: Lean mass made up about 35% of weight lost on semaglutide and 25% on tirzepatide; older or frail people risk sarcopenia. GI side effects are the main reason for stopping (4.5% vs 0.8% on placebo for semaglutide).
dose.timeframe: Weight and inflammatory markers fall over months, with weight plateauing around 1-1.5 years; in STEP 4, switching to placebo after 20 weeks regained 6.9% of body weight by week 68.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. To protect muscle, pair the drug with resistance training (lean-mass share fell to ~17.5% with lifestyle plus resistance training) and adequate protein. Women: see the egg entry for contraception and the label's 2-month semaglutide washout before trying to conceive.

entries.mechanism: Most of the redox benefit likely comes from losing visceral fat, which lowers adipose NADPH oxidase activity, inflammatory cytokines and insulin resistance; GLP-1 receptor signalling may also have direct anti-inflammatory effects. In a 40-RCT meta-analysis the CRP fall tracked blood-pressure and insulin-resistance improvement rather than HbA1c [med-bray2021]. The drugs slow gastric emptying, which is why they can change absorption of oral medicines [med-fda-zepbound2023].
entries.interactions: Delivers the benefits of [weight-loss] in people with [excess-adiposity]; improves [glycemic-control]. Combine with [resistance-training] and adequate protein to limit lean-mass loss. Alternative or add-on to [metformin] in [pcos]. In obese men with low testosterone it raised testosterone and preserved sperm, unlike [testosterone-anabolic-steroids]. Very-low-calorie intake on these drugs overlaps with [calorie-restriction].
entries.caveats: The MDA (lipid peroxidation) result rests on only 3 trials in the 2026 meta-analysis; IL-6 and TNF-alpha effects were not significant. Weight is regained after stopping (STEP 4). Long-term data on muscle function and bone in younger people are limited. Supply via compounded or unregulated products is outside the evidence base.
entries.debate: Inflammation/oxidative stress: one meta-analysis calls the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant evidence strong [med-bray2021], while a 2026 update finds consistent CRP and adiponectin effects but variable IL-6/TNF-alpha and a thin MDA evidence base [med-kanbay2026]. Lean mass: reviewers argue the loss is proportional and adaptive, with better muscle quality [med-neeland2024], and a 2026 meta-analysis found the lean-mass share similar to diet-based weight loss [med-eisa2026]; another 2026 systematic review found muscle-related losses exceeded prespecified benchmarks in about two thirds of incretin trials [med-batsis2026]. Sperm: a small RCT found GLP-1 treatment maintained diet-induced sperm-count gains [med-andersen2022] and semaglutide improved morphology in hypogonadal diabetic men [med-gregoric2025], but systematic reviews note no change in healthy men and too few trials to judge [med-deameh2026, med-peel2026].

entries.title: GLP-1 drugs (semaglutide, tirzepatide)

entries.headline: In PCOS with obesity GLP-1 drugs add modest weight loss (BMI -1.4 kg/m2 in 11 RCTs) but a fertility benefit is unproven; tirzepatide cut oral-contraceptive peak levels by 59%, and the semaglutide label says stop at least 2 months before trying to conceive.

dose.effective: Semaglutide or liraglutide in PCOS trials, usually 12-26 weeks before ovulation induction or IVF, followed by a drug-free gap.
dose.studied_range: Liraglutide 1.2 mg/day with metformin for 12 weeks then a 4-week washout before IVF (pilot RCT); 11 RCTs of GLP-1 add-on in PCOS.
dose.too_much: Continuing into pregnancy: the labels warn of possible fetal harm (from animal data) and human data on continued use are limited. Oral contraceptives may fail during tirzepatide start-up and dose escalation.
dose.timeframe: Semaglutide: discontinue >=2 months before a planned pregnancy (label). Tirzepatide: use non-oral or back-up contraception for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase (label).
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Plan the washout and contraception with the prescriber; weight loss itself can restore ovulation, so unplanned pregnancies occur. Stop the drug and inform the prescriber if pregnancy is found.

entries.mechanism: Weight loss and lower insulin reduce ovarian androgen excess and can restore ovulation; GLP-1 receptors are also present in reproductive tissues. Delayed gastric emptying lowers and delays absorption of oral contraceptive hormones, most with tirzepatide after the first doses [med-fda-zepbound2023, med-skelley2024].
entries.interactions: An option alongside [metformin] and lifestyle in [pcos] and [excess-adiposity]; produces [weight-loss]. St John's wort is another cause of oral-contraceptive failure ([supplement-drug-interactions]). Folic acid ([folic-acid]) should start before the washout ends.
entries.caveats: Fertility trials are small, short and mostly use liraglutide; there are no large trials of semaglutide or tirzepatide with live birth as the outcome.
entries.debate: Benefit: a pilot RCT found higher IVF pregnancy rates with liraglutide plus metformin than metformin alone despite similar weight loss [med-salamun2018], and GLP-1 agonists beat metformin for weight and insulin sensitivity in PCOS [med-han2019]; but the 2026 guideline-informing meta-analysis found only modest weight loss and insufficient evidence for reproductive outcomes [med-forslund2026]. Safety: large cohorts found no excess malformations versus insulin [med-cesta2024] and no consistent safety signal [med-ozbek2026], with preterm-birth signals confined to women with diabetes [med-hviid2026]; an AJOG review argues malformation data cannot be trusted without glycaemic-control data and recommends contraception for all users [med-drummond2025].
