entries.headline: 3 g of glycine at bedtime reduced next-day fatigue in small sleep-restriction studies, and a high-glycine diet extended mouse lifespan by only 4-6%; there are no human aging-outcome trials.

dose.effective: 3 g taken about an hour before bed (sleep studies)
dose.studied_range: 3 g/night in sleep studies; about 100 mg/kg/day (about 7 g at 70 kg) as part of GlyNAC; 8% of diet in mice
dose.too_much: Well tolerated at gram doses in trials; long-term safety of multi-gram daily use has not been formally assessed
dose.timeframe: Sleep effects measured over 1-3 nights
dose.notes: Glycine is abundant in collagen and gelatin. For glutathione support, see [glynac].

entries.mechanism: Glycine is one of the three amino acids of glutathione, and red-cell glycine is low in older adults. In rats it promotes sleep by acting on NMDA receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, widening skin blood vessels and lowering core temperature. In mice it may also offset methionine excess, which is one proposed reason the ITP glycine diet extended life.
entries.interactions: Combined with [n-acetylcysteine] it forms [glynac]. Any glutathione effect is likely limited to people with low baseline status.
entries.caveats: Sleep data come from small, short studies, mostly from one research group. The mouse lifespan effect was small and the dose (8% of the diet) is not comparable to supplement use.
entries.debate: The ITP glycine result is one of the more rigorous mouse lifespan studies (three sites, both sexes) but the effect was small [lon-miller2019]. Human sleep evidence is a few small trials from one group [lon-bannai2012] with a rat mechanism [lon-kawai2015]; no independent replication or critique was found, which reflects how little the question has been studied.
entries.title: Glycine

entries.headline: In small trials from one Baylor group, about 7 g glycine plus 9 g NAC daily restored glutathione and improved many aging markers in older adults, but a 114-person industry RCT at lower doses found no rise in glutathione.

dose.effective: Glycine 1.33 mmol/kg/day + cysteine 0.81 mmol/kg/day as NAC (about 100 mg/kg glycine + 130 mg/kg NAC, roughly 7 g + 9 g/day at 70 kg)
dose.studied_range: Weight-based doses for 2-24 weeks in the Baylor trials; 2.4, 4.8 or 7.2 g/day total (1:1) for 2 weeks in the Nestle trial
dose.too_much: Long-term safety beyond 24 weeks not established; NAC carries the same tumour-promotion caution in mice as [n-acetylcysteine]
dose.timeframe: Changes reported at 16-24 weeks; benefits faded within 12 weeks of stopping
dose.notes: Relevant mainly to older adults with low glutathione; young adults already have normal glutathione synthesis. Over-the-counter GlyNAC products usually supply far less than the trial doses.

entries.mechanism: Supplies both limiting precursors (cysteine and glycine) for glutathione synthesis, which is reduced with aging. Older adults in the original study had about half the red-cell glutathione and synthesis rate of young adults, and 2 weeks of precursors restored both and lowered F2-isoprostanes.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [n-acetylcysteine] and [glycine]. Probably redundant in people with high protein intake and normal glutathione. Not a substitute for oral or IV glutathione, see [iv-glutathione].
entries.caveats: The positive trials are tiny (8 older adults open-label; 24 in the RCT), come from a single group, and measured many outcomes, which raises the chance of false positives. The striking mouse lifespan gain (24%) came from a single-lab study in one inbred strain, not the multi-site ITP design. No hard outcomes.
entries.debate: The Baylor group reports broad benefits: corrected glutathione, lower oxidative stress, better mitochondrial fuel oxidation, insulin sensitivity, gait speed and strength [lon-sekhar2011, lon-kumar2021, lon-kumar2023], and longer life in mice [lon-kumar2022]. A larger Nestle-run RCT in 114 healthy older adults found GlyNAC at up to 7.2 g/day for 2 weeks did not raise glutathione or the GSH:GSSG ratio; only a post-hoc subgroup with high oxidative stress and low glutathione responded [lon-lizzo2022]. The doses and duration were lower than in the Baylor trials, so the two are not a direct contradiction, but the null primary result shows benefit is not universal. Both sides have commercial interests: Nestle Health Science holds patents and licences on glycine-plus-NAC use [lon-lizzo2022].

entries.headline: Four cups a day of decaffeinated green tea cut urinary 8-OHdG by 31% in heavy smokers over 4 months, and 4 cups/day lowered plasma MDA/HNE in metabolic syndrome; across 145 RCTs, flavan-3-ol foods including tea lower blood pressure by about 3/2 mmHg and improve FMD, while evidence on oxidative damage in healthy non-smokers stays weak.

dose.effective: About 4 cups (~1 L) per day of brewed green tea.
dose.studied_range: 4 cups/day for 8 weeks to 4 months.
dose.too_much: Brewed tea is considered safe at usual intakes (90-300 mg EGCG/day; heavy drinkers up to ~866 mg/day); rare idiosyncratic liver injury reported. See [green-tea-extract] for the supplement risk.
dose.timeframe: Weeks to months.
dose.notes: EGCG bioavailability is low and variable; plasma half-life ~3.4 h. Ring-fission valerolactone metabolites appear 3-15 h later.

entries.mechanism: Catechins (EGCG, EGC, EC) and their microbial valerolactone metabolites; at physiological doses mild Nrf2 signalling and effects on endothelium rather than plasma radical scavenging.
entries.interactions: Flavan-3-ols overlap with [cocoa-flavanols]. Tea with meals reduces non-heme iron absorption (relevant to [iron-excess] and to iron-deficient people). Unlike high-dose vitamins C and E, 980 mg/day of green-tea polyphenols did not appear to blunt antioxidant-enzyme adaptation in sprinters.
entries.caveats: The smoker trial used decaf tea and showed no benefit for black tea. Smokers have high baseline oxidative damage, so the effect may not generalise. Concentrated extracts are a different exposure: free EGCG exposure rose by more than 60% after 4 weeks of 800 mg once-daily dosing, and in a 12-month RCT in 1021 women, high-dose green tea extract caused moderate or worse liver-test abnormalities in 5.1% (see [green-tea-extract]).

entries.headline: 30 g/day of milled flaxseed for 6 months lowered systolic blood pressure by about 10 mmHg (15 mmHg in hypertensives) in a 110-patient RCT, one of the largest blood-pressure effects of any food; lignans and ALA both appear to contribute.

dose.effective: 30 g/day milled flaxseed (roughly 3-4 tablespoons).
dose.studied_range: 30 g/day in foods for 6 months.
dose.timeframe: Months.
dose.notes: Use milled seed; enterolignans rose 2-50-fold on the milled-flax diet.

entries.mechanism: Secoisolariciresinol diglucoside is converted by gut bacteria to enterodiol and enterolactone; ALA and its oxylipins also lower blood pressure. Plasma ALA tracked systolic and diastolic pressure, lignans tracked diastolic.
entries.interactions: ALA overlaps only partly with [omega3-fish]. Lignans also come from [whole-grains]. In PREDIMED, lignan intake was among the subclasses most strongly linked to lower mortality.
entries.caveats: One main RCT, in peripheral artery disease patients; replication in the general population is limited. Enterolactone production depends on the microbiome.
entries.title: Ground flaxseed (lignans plus alpha-linolenic acid)

entries.headline: Claims that touching the ground supplies 'antioxidant electrons' have no credible mechanism and rest on small, mostly unblinded studies by proponents.

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress. Walking barefoot outdoors is harmless and pleasant if you enjoy it.
dose.studied_range: Small studies of grounding mats/patches over nights to weeks.
dose.notes: No validated oxidative biomarker improvement in rigorous trials.

entries.mechanism: Proposed mechanism (free electrons neutralizing radicals) is not physiologically plausible: radical chemistry occurs inside cells and is buffered by enzymes and glutathione.
entries.interactions: None.
entries.caveats: The main review is by advocates; independent replication is lacking.
entries.title: Grounding / earthing

factors.name: Growth hormone for poor responders in IVF

entries.headline: Growth hormone adds about 1.4 eggs in poor responders, and Cochrane pooling suggests more live births (OR 1.77) but at very low certainty; the only placebo-controlled trial focused on live birth (LIGHT) found 14.5% vs 13.7%, and ESHRE does not recommend it.

dose.effective: Not recommended routinely. Trials used about 4-12 IU/day subcutaneously during stimulation.
dose.studied_range: Various regimens, often started in the preceding luteal phase.
dose.too_much: Expensive (often the costliest drug in the cycle); fluid retention, joint pain.
dose.timeframe: During ovarian stimulation.
dose.notes: Not on the HFEA rating list.

entries.mechanism: GH and IGF-1 enhance granulosa-cell FSH sensitivity and steroidogenesis; proposed to improve egg competence and mitochondrial function.
entries.interactions: Same population as [dhea], [coq10] and [prp-ovarian-egg]; none has proven live-birth benefit.
entries.caveats: Small, heterogeneous trials; LIGHT stopped early (113 women), so it was underpowered.
entries.debate: Cochrane pooled 8 small poor-responder trials and found more live births (OR 1.77, 1.17-2.70) but rated it very low certainty [fer-sood2021]; the placebo-controlled LIGHT trial found no difference [fer-norman2019]. ESHRE lists GH among adjuncts not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].

factors.name: GSTM1 / GSTT1 null genotype and isothiocyanate handling

entries.headline: Roughly half of people lack both GSTM1 copies; null carriers handle broccoli's sulforaphane differently and in one cohort gained the most lung-cancer protection from isothiocyanates, but results conflict and the advice (eat crucifers) is the same whatever the genotype.

dose.effective: No test needed. Whatever the genotype, regular cruciferous vegetables (for example 1/2 cup broccoli sprouts or a serving of crucifers most days) are the lever.
dose.studied_range: Crossover feeding with standard and high-glucosinolate broccoli; urinary isothiocyanate cohort of 18,244 men; case-control meta-analysis of 6,934 men for infertility.
dose.timeframe: Sulforaphane pharmacokinetics differ within hours; any cancer association reflects years of intake.
dose.notes: Consumer 'detox' panels often report GSTM1 status; it should not drive supplement purchases.

entries.mechanism: GSTM1 and GSTT1 conjugate isothiocyanates and electrophilic toxins to glutathione for excretion. Null carriers may keep sulforaphane in circulation longer (more Nrf2 activation) or form less of the conjugated metabolites, depending on the study.
entries.interactions: Relevant to [broccoli-sprouts], [cruciferous-other] and [sulforaphane-supplements]; may modify the effect of [tobacco-smoking] carcinogens.
entries.caveats: Associations with male infertility and endometriosis come from case-control studies with population heterogeneity and possible publication bias; no intervention study uses genotype to change outcomes.
entries.debate: In Shanghai men, isothiocyanate protection was concentrated in GSTM1-null and double-null carriers [tst-london2000], whereas a crossover study suggested GSTM1-positive people retain different sulforaphane metabolites that might give them more benefit [tst-gasper2005], and a 114-person feeding study found genotype made little difference to excretion [tst-steck2007]. GSTM1 null was associated with male infertility in a meta-analysis [tst-wu2013], but a broad meta-analysis of endometriosis polymorphisms found GSTT1, not GSTM1, among the more robust signals [tst-mear2020].

entries.headline: Chronic periodontitis is associated with lower systemic antioxidant capacity and higher malondialdehyde, and periodontal treatment lowers oxidative markers.

dose.effective: Brush twice daily, clean between teeth daily, and get professional cleaning and periodontal treatment if gums bleed or recede.
dose.studied_range: Non-surgical periodontal therapy studies with >=6 weeks follow-up.
dose.timeframe: Markers improved within 6 weeks to months after treatment.
dose.notes: Smoking and diabetes strongly worsen periodontitis.

entries.mechanism: Chronic bacterial infection recruits neutrophils that release superoxide, hypochlorous acid and other oxidants locally, with spill-over systemic inflammation.
entries.interactions: Worsened by [tobacco-smoking] and poor [glycemic-control].
entries.caveats: Most data are from saliva and gum fluid; systemic effects are less consistent and few trials are randomized.
entries.title: Gum disease (periodontitis)

entries.headline: Toxic metals deplete glutathione and drive oxidative damage; even at normal background levels, urinary cadmium tracked oxidative DNA damage in non-smokers.

dose.effective: Do not smoke (the main cadmium source); test well water for arsenic; check old homes for lead paint and pipes; choose low-mercury fish (salmon, sardines) over high-mercury species (swordfish, king mackerel, shark).
dose.studied_range: Observational studies at background and occupational exposure levels.
dose.too_much: Occupational exposures and contaminated water are the main high-dose risks.
dose.timeframe: Body burdens of cadmium and lead decline slowly (years).
dose.notes: Chelation 'detox' for people without documented poisoning is not supported.

entries.mechanism: Cadmium, lead and arsenic bind thiol groups, deplete glutathione and inhibit antioxidant enzymes; redox-active metals (iron, copper) generate hydroxyl radical via Fenton chemistry; arsenic can generate H2O2.
entries.interactions: Cadmium exposure is largely from [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: Spot-urine biomarker studies are prone to confounding: in one study the strongest metal associations were for essential selenium and copper.
entries.title: Heavy metals: lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury

entries.headline: Higher follicular-fluid mercury (above ~0.5 ug/L) and lead were associated with lower IVF live birth (lead RR 0.68) in a small study; cadmium exposure comes mainly from smoking.

dose.effective: Favour smaller, lower-mercury fish over large predatory fish (e.g. shark, swordfish); do not smoke (main cadmium source).
dose.studied_range: Follicular fluid Hg, Pb, Cd, As in 56 IVF patients.
dose.too_much: Follicular fluid Hg > ~0.51 ug/L associated with lower biochemical pregnancy and live birth.
dose.notes: Keep eating fish: the omega-3 benefit is real; choose low-mercury species.

entries.mechanism: Metals bind thiol groups, deplete glutathione and inactivate antioxidant enzymes; cadmium and lead can displace essential metals and promote Fenton-type ROS generation.
entries.interactions: Trades off against [omega3-fish] (fish is the main source of both); [tobacco-smoking] supplies cadmium.
entries.caveats: One small cohort; associations were non-linear and imprecise.

factors.name: Heavy vigorous exercise & low energy availability (women)

entries.headline: In lean women, 5 or more hours a week of vigorous exercise was associated with about 32% lower monthly chance of conception; exercising to exhaustion or on most days was linked to 2-3 times the odds of fertility problems.

dose.effective: If trying to conceive and lean, cap vigorous exercise below ~5 h/week and swap some for moderate activity; eat enough to keep regular cycles.
dose.studied_range: Vigorous activity 0 to >= 5 h/week (Danish cohort); frequency/intensity categories (Norwegian cohort).
dose.too_much: >= 5 h/week vigorous: FR 0.68 in lean women; exercising most days: 3.2-fold odds of fertility problems; exercising to exhaustion: 2.3-fold.
dose.timeframe: Cycle recovery after restoring energy balance can take months.
dose.notes: Missed or irregular periods in an active woman are a red flag for low energy availability (hypothalamic suppression).

entries.mechanism: Low energy availability suppresses GnRH pulsatility (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea), lowering estrogen and ovulation; this is an energy-signalling problem more than an oxidative one.
entries.interactions: No adverse association in women with BMI >= 25, for whom activity helps ([aerobic-exercise-moderate], [weight-loss]). Different from acute oxidative damage after ultra-endurance events ([overtraining-ultraendurance]); in general health, vigorous exercise in normal amounts is beneficial ([hiit-vigorous-exercise]).
entries.caveats: Observational and self-reported; vigorous exercise was not associated with worse IVF outcomes in the EARTH cohort.
entries.title: Very intense exercise and low energy availability (RED-S)

factors.name: Herbs and spices (oregano, rosemary, cloves, cinnamon, etc.)

entries.headline: Their biggest proven effect is in the pan: a polyphenol-rich spice mix cut malondialdehyde in cooked burgers by 71% and in the eaters' urine by 49%, and herb marinades cut heterocyclic amines in grilled steak by 57-88%.

dose.effective: Generous use in cooking, especially in meat dishes and marinades (about a tablespoon of dried herbs per meal); 14 g spice blend in a meal in one trial.
dose.studied_range: Single meals; marinating steaks 1 h before grilling at 204 °C.
dose.too_much: None established at culinary amounts.
dose.timeframe: Same meal.
dose.notes: Per gram, dried cloves, oregano and other herbs top every polyphenol table, but servings are small.

entries.mechanism: Rosmarinic acid, carnosic acid and carnosol inhibit lipid oxidation and Maillard/HCA chemistry in food and in the stomach, so fewer oxidized lipids are absorbed; a spice blend also lowered postprandial insulin and triglycerides.
entries.interactions: Counteracts [high-temperature-cooking] and [processed-red-meat] oxidation products. Here direct scavenging is plausible because the reaction happens in the food and gut, where concentrations are high.
entries.caveats: Meal studies are tiny (n=6-11) and short.

factors.name: HFE hemochromatosis (C282Y homozygosity) and iron overload

entries.headline: About 1 in 156 people of northern European descent are C282Y homozygotes; untreated iron loading caused documented organ disease in about 28% of homozygous men (about 1% of women in one cohort, more in UK Biobank), and regular blood removal to a ferritin below 50-100 ug/L prevents it.

dose.effective: Test transferrin saturation and ferritin; if TSAT >45% (women) or >50% (men) with ferritin >200/300 ug/L, genotype HFE. In C282Y homozygotes, phlebotomy (typically 400-500 mL blood) to ferritin <50 ug/L during induction, then maintenance at <100 ug/L.
dose.studied_range: Diagnostic thresholds and phlebotomy targets from EASL 2022 and ACG 2019 guidelines; outcomes from cohorts of 31,192 (Melbourne) and 451,243 (UK Biobank) people.
dose.too_much: Over-phlebotomy to iron deficiency causes fatigue and anemia; ferritin targets exist for that reason. Avoid iron supplements and iron-fortified 'antioxidant' blends, and avoid high-dose vitamin C supplements, which increase non-heme iron absorption.
dose.timeframe: Iron accumulates over decades (disease usually after 40 in men, after menopause in women); induction phlebotomy takes months, then lifelong maintenance.
dose.notes: Ferritin above 1,000 ng/mL at diagnosis marks higher risk of advanced liver fibrosis. C282Y/H63D compound heterozygotes rarely develop disease without fatty liver, diabetes or excess alcohol. High ferritin with normal TSAT is usually fatty liver, alcohol or inflammation, not hemochromatosis.

entries.mechanism: Loss of HFE function lowers hepcidin, so the gut absorbs and macrophages release too much iron; transferrin saturates and non-transferrin-bound iron enters liver, pancreas, heart and joints. Labile iron catalyzes Fenton chemistry (Fe2+ + H2O2 -> hydroxyl radical), driving lipid peroxidation, fibrosis and cell death.
entries.interactions: Alcohol and fatty liver multiply liver damage, see [alcohol] and [excess-adiposity]. Iron supplements and multivitamins with iron are contraindicated (see [iron-excess], [multivitamin-mineral]); megadose [vitamin-c-supplement] raises iron absorption. Diabetes in homozygotes interacts with [glycemic-control].
entries.caveats: Genotype alone is not disease: penetrance is incomplete and much lower in women, who lose iron through menstruation and pregnancy. Heterozygotes (single C282Y) do not need treatment. Consumer genotyping that reports HFE should be confirmed clinically with iron studies before any action.
entries.debate: UK Biobank found C282Y homozygosity caused substantial incident morbidity in both men (15.7% vs 5.0%) and women (10.1% vs 3.4%) and argued for expanded early case-finding [tst-pilling2019], whereas an earlier cohort found documented disease in only 1.2% of homozygous women [tst-allen2008] and USPSTF judged evidence insufficient to estimate benefit from population genetic screening [tst-whitlock2006]. Ferritin's accuracy for detecting overload is rated very low certainty [tst-garciacasal2021].

key_numbers.label: Liver disease odds in homozygotes (UK Biobank)

entries.title: HFE hemochromatosis (C282Y homozygosity) and iron overload

entries.headline: In type 2 diabetes, urinary 8-iso-PGF2α tracked glucose variability (r = 0.86) and post-meal glucose, not HbA1c. Hyperglycaemia drives mitochondrial superoxide and AGE formation.

dose.effective: Limit post-meal glucose excursions and keep glucose in the normal range (see food and lifestyle areas).
dose.timeframe: Acute: postprandial window (hours); chronic: years
dose.notes: Dietary AGEs from dry-heat cooking add to the endogenous load (10- to 100-fold more than uncooked).

entries.mechanism: Excess glucose makes the mitochondrial ETC overproduce superoxide, which activates the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways. AGEs bind RAGE, activating NOX and NF-kB. Postprandial hyperglycaemia and hyperlipidaemia transiently raise oxidative stress and impair endothelial function.
entries.interactions: Compounds [excess-adiposity]. Antioxidants taken with a meal can attenuate postprandial oxidative stress, but this has not translated into supplement benefits.
entries.caveats: The Monnier study is small (21 patients). The extent to which glucose swings matter in non-diabetic people is less established.
entries.title: High blood glucose and post-meal glucose spikes

entries.headline: Type 2 diabetes was associated with ~75% higher urinary 8-iso-PGF2a, which tracked day-to-day glucose swings (r = 0.86) more than HbA1c; reducing glucose spikes is a meaningful lever.

dose.effective: Keep fasting glucose and HbA1c in the normal range (individualized targets with diabetes); limit post-meal spikes with fibre-rich whole foods, fewer refined carbohydrates, and a short walk after meals.
dose.studied_range: Case-control comparison using continuous glucose monitoring.
dose.too_much: Large post-meal excursions and sustained hyperglycemia.
dose.timeframe: Glucose swings respond within days; HbA1c over ~3 months.
dose.notes: Exercise and weight loss are the main non-drug tools.

entries.mechanism: High glucose overloads mitochondria, causing superoxide overproduction that activates the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways; AGE-RAGE binding further activates NADPH oxidase and NF-kB.
entries.interactions: Improved by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [resistance-training], [weight-loss] and [short-sleep] correction.
entries.caveats: Monnier 2006 was small (21 patients); the 'swings matter more than average glucose' idea is supported mechanistically but outcome trials targeting variability are limited.
entries.title: Blood-sugar control and diabetes

entries.headline: Women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes have 24-36% lower fecundability; in mice, maternal diabetes damages oocyte mitochondria and raises egg aneuploidy.

dose.effective: Good glycaemic control before conception (managed with the diabetes team); weight loss and physical activity for insulin resistance.
dose.timeframe: Preconception optimisation over at least 3 months covers one full cycle of follicle growth.
dose.notes: Preconception glucose control is also critical for reducing birth-defect risk.

entries.mechanism: Hyperglycaemia increases mitochondrial superoxide and advanced glycation end-products; in diabetic mice oocytes show abnormal mitochondrial structure, lower ATP and TCA metabolites, spindle defects and aneuploidy, and the defective mitochondria are passed to the embryo.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [excess-adiposity] and [pcos].
entries.caveats: Oocyte mechanism data are from animals; human data are fecundability associations.
entries.title: Diabetes and insulin resistance

entries.headline: Higher ferritin consistently predicts type 2 diabetes (about +22% per 100 ug/L) and Mendelian randomization supports a causal diabetes link, but the heart-disease side of the 'iron hypothesis' failed: genetic data even suggest slightly less coronary disease with higher iron, and the one phlebotomy RCT (FeAST) was null on its primary outcome.

dose.effective: No target has been validated by trials. Practical reading: ferritin roughly 30-200 ug/L (women) or 30-300 ug/L (men) with normal transferrin saturation is unremarkable; persistently high ferritin together with high transferrin saturation warrants medical evaluation for haemochromatosis rather than self-treatment.
dose.studied_range: FeAST lowered mean ferritin from ~123 to ~80 ng/mL by phlebotomy over ~4.5 years.
dose.too_much: Pathological overload (haemochromatosis, transfusion) damages liver, pancreas, heart, joints and gonads.
dose.timeframe: Ferritin falls over months with phlebotomy or donation; disease associations accrue over years.
dose.notes: Ferritin is also an acute-phase protein: inflammation, obesity, fatty liver, alcohol and infection all raise it, so a single high value often reflects inflammation rather than iron. Check CRP and transferrin saturation alongside.

entries.mechanism: Iron stored in ferritin is safe; danger comes from the small labile iron pool that catalyses Fenton chemistry and drives ferroptosis (iron-dependent lipid peroxidation when GPX4/glutathione defences fail). Hepatic and pancreatic iron may impair insulin secretion and action. Serum ferritin itself partly leaks from damaged cells, which ties it to oxidative stress independently of stores.
entries.interactions: Blood donation lowers stores [blood-donation]. Red meat raises heme iron intake [processed-red-meat]. Interpreting ferritin requires accounting for [chronic-inflammation], [excess-adiposity] and alcohol; high ferritin co-travels with [glycemic-control] problems. Avoid iron pills when stores are high [iron-excess].
entries.caveats: Observational ferritin-disease links are heavily confounded because ferritin rises with inflammation and fatty liver. Do not induce iron deficiency in pursuit of 'low ferritin': [iron-deficiency] carries real harms. Haemochromatosis genetics is covered elsewhere.
entries.debate: Supporting a harmful role: Sullivan's hypothesis [nut-sullivan1981], ferritin-diabetes meta-analyses [nut-jiang2019, nut-kunutsor2013, nut-zhao2012], MR showing iron raises diabetes risk [nut-wang2021, nut-liu2024] and shortens lifespan [nut-daghlas2021], and FeAST's secondary cancer reduction [nut-zacharski2008]. Against: prospective studies found no ferritin-CHD association [nut-danesh1999, nut-sempos2000], FeAST was null on its primary endpoints [nut-zacharski2007] with an editorial calling the evidence far from ironclad [nut-hu2007] and another doubting the cancer result [nut-edgren2008], MR suggests higher iron is mildly protective for coronary disease [nut-gill2017, nut-liu2024] and hypercholesterolemia [nut-gill2019], and ferritin may mostly mark cell damage [nut-kell2014, nut-depalma2010]. Reviewers have long called the iron-heart question unresolved [nut-wood2004].

entries.headline: Pooled over 78 RCTs, antioxidant supplements did not lower mortality and slightly raised it in low-bias trials (RR 1.04). A 20,536-person trial of vitamin E + C + beta-carotene found no effect at all. Around exercise they block training benefits.

dose.effective: None.
dose.studied_range: e.g. vitamin E 600 mg + C 250 mg + beta-carotene 20 mg/day (HPS); vitamin C 1,000 mg + E 400 IU/day (exercise studies)
dose.too_much: Any dose at these levels: no benefit; beta-carotene, vitamin A and vitamin E components carry the documented harms.
dose.timeframe: Exercise-blunting effect within 4 weeks; mortality signal over years
dose.notes: Raising blood vitamin levels does not mean oxidative damage was reduced; HPS raised levels 'substantially' with zero outcome change.

entries.mechanism: Suppresses ROS signals needed for adaptation (insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial biogenesis, endogenous antioxidant enzyme induction). In tumours, lowering ROS can release p53-dependent brakes and increase metastasis (mouse data). Endogenous enzymatic defences do not respond to extra dietary antioxidants once someone is replete.
entries.interactions: Antagonises the adaptive (hormetic) benefits of exercise. Contains [vitamin-e-supplement] and [beta-carotene-supplement] harms. Redundant with endogenous defences.
entries.caveats: Marketing often cites ORAC or 'total antioxidant capacity' values, which USDA abandoned in 2012 because they have no demonstrated in-vivo relevance.
entries.title: High-dose 'antioxidant formula' supplements (vitamin C + E + beta-carotene/A, etc.)

entries.headline: Too much antioxidant can loosen sperm chromatin: one study saw DFI fall 19% but decondensation rise 23%, and high doses damaged sperm DNA in mice.

dose.effective: Avoid taking several fertility products at once or doses well above the RDA (e.g. vitamin C >1 g, zinc >40 mg, folic acid >1 mg) without a specific indication.
dose.studied_range: Antioxidant vitamins with zinc and selenium for 90 days (human); dose-escalation of vitamin C, zinc, folate, carnitine (mice).
dose.too_much: This factor is the 'too much' end of [male-antioxidant-combination].
dose.timeframe: Over one spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: FAZST's small SDF increase with 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg zinc is consistent with this concern.

entries.mechanism: Sperm chromatin compaction depends on oxidative formation of protamine disulphide bridges in the epididymis, and capacitation needs a controlled ROS burst. Excess reductants (especially vitamin C) can reduce these disulphide bonds and blunt physiological ROS signalling.
entries.interactions: Opposes the benefits sought from [male-antioxidant-combination] and [vitamin-c-e-combined]; also relevant to [l-carnitine].
entries.caveats: Human evidence is one small uncontrolled study plus indirect trial data; the mouse data may not transfer. Plausible but unproven.
entries.title: Megadose or stacked antioxidants ('reductive stress')

factors.name: High-dose antioxidant supplements during training (vitamin C/E, resveratrol, NAC)

entries.headline: Gram-level vitamin C plus vitamin E, and 150-250 mg/day resveratrol, blunted molecular and some functional training adaptations in several RCTs (e.g. 45% smaller VO2max gain with resveratrol; lean-mass gain 1.4% vs 3.9% with C+E in older men), although meta-analyses find no significant loss of VO2max, endurance or strength overall.

dose.effective: Avoid routine supplementation at about 500-1000 mg/day vitamin C plus 235-400 IU vitamin E, or 150-250+ mg/day resveratrol, during training blocks. Get antioxidants from food. Correct true deficiencies (e.g. low vitamin C or low glutathione status) under guidance.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin C 500-1000 mg/day plus vitamin E 117.5-400 IU (4-12 weeks); resveratrol 150-250 mg/day (4-8 weeks); NAC 1200-2400 mg/day orally or IV infusion; quercetin ~1000 mg/day.
dose.too_much: 1000 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E/day removed the insulin-sensitivity gain of 4 weeks' training in one trial; 1000 mg C plus 235 mg E blocked mitochondrial-protein gains and blunted bone-density gains in older men.
dose.timeframe: Effects appeared within 4-12 weeks of combined training and supplementation.
dose.notes: Timing has not been directly tested: blunting occurred both with daily dosing and when doses were taken just before and after sessions, so moving the pill a few hours away from workouts is not proven to help. Food-level intakes (fruit, vegetables, tea, cocoa) have not shown this effect. Acute NAC or other antioxidants before a single competition is a different question from chronic use during training.

entries.mechanism: Exercise ROS (largely NOX2-derived H2O2) act as second messengers that activate Nrf2, PGC-1alpha, MAPKs (p38, JNK, ERK) and insulin-signalling adaptations. Flooding cells with reducing agents can blunt this signal, reducing induction of SOD2, GPx, COX4 and mitochondrial biogenesis and hypertrophy signalling. Redundant pathways mean the blunting is partial and inconsistent.
entries.interactions: Directly undermines [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and [resistance-training]. See the general supplement entries [vitamin-c-supplement], [vitamin-e-supplement], [isolated-polyphenol-supplements], [n-acetylcysteine] and [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Trials are small (11-54 people), use different doses and outcomes, and many find molecular blunting without performance loss. Isoflavones may even help lean-mass gains. NAC may help people with low glutathione.
entries.debate: Pro-blunting: vitamin C/E abolished insulin-sensitivity gains [exr-ristow2009], blocked mitochondrial-protein increases [exr-paulsen2014a, exr-gomezcabrera2008], blunted hypertrophy signalling [exr-paulsen2014b], lean-mass gains [exr-bjornsen2016] and bone gains in older men [exr-stunes2017]; resveratrol blunted VO2max, blood pressure and lipid improvements [exr-gliemann2013] and HIIT power gains [exr-scribbans2014], and impaired training effects on muscle oxidative and inflammatory markers [exr-olesen2014]; NAC infusion blunted adaptive signalling [exr-petersen2012]. Against: other RCTs found no effect on endurance adaptation or insulin sensitivity [exr-yfanti2010, exr-yfanti2011] or only partial cellular effects [exr-morrison2015]; a meta-analysis of 18 RCTs found no significant effect on VO2max (SMD -0.14), endurance, lean mass or strength [exr-clifford2020], and a strength-specific review found no effect on strength [exr-dutra2020]. Critics argued the resveratrol data do not show 'mainly negative' effects [exr-smoliga2013], and a polyphenol meta-analysis found resveratrol's harm non-significant (SMD -0.54) and isoflavones possibly helpful [exr-martineznegrin2022]. Underneath sits the question of whether exercise ROS are necessary at all: without any supplement, men with the smallest exercise-induced oxidative stress adapted least [exr-margaritelis2018], while reviews still weigh how essential the ROS signal is versus redundant pathways [exr-powers2024, exr-merry2016b]. A 'personalised' camp argues antioxidants help only deficient people: NAC improved performance only in men with low glutathione [exr-paschalis2018, exr-margaritelis2018b]. Narrative reviews converge on 'no benefit, possible harm' for chronic megadoses [exr-merry2016b, exr-mason2020, exr-higgins2020, exr-nikolaidis2012].

entries.headline: EFSA (2018) concluded that 800 mg EGCG/day or more from supplements significantly raises liver transaminases in RCTs; extracts also cause rare severe liver injury, especially in multi-ingredient products.

dose.effective: No oxidative-stress benefit beyond brewed tea has been shown.
dose.studied_range: Supplements supply 5-1000 mg EGCG/day.
dose.too_much: >= 800 mg EGCG/day as a supplement (EFSA). Multi-ingredient products caused more severe injury.
dose.timeframe: Liver injury latency averaged ~6 months for green-tea-only products and ~6 weeks for multi-ingredient ones.
dose.notes: Brewed tea at traditional intakes is considered safe.

entries.mechanism: At high concentrations EGCG becomes pro-oxidant (generating H2O2) and hepatotoxic; patient susceptibility factors appear important.
entries.interactions: Do not combine with other hepatotoxic supplements.
entries.caveats: Absolute risk is low given wide use, but the dose threshold is clear from trials.

factors.name: High-temperature dry cooking of meat (HCAs, PAHs, AGEs)

entries.headline: Grilling, broiling and pan-frying meat until well done or charred forms heterocyclic amines (HCAs) and PAHs, and people in the top intake category have about 15-20% higher odds of colorectal adenoma in meta-analyses; dry heat also multiplies food AGEs 10-100-fold, but the largest cohort and the most rigorous low- vs high-AGE diet trials found no effect.

dose.effective: Cook meat to a safe internal temperature without charring: moderate pan or grill heat (about 160-180 °C rather than 200-250 °C), turn every minute, cut off blackened parts, microwave patties 1-3 min first and pour off the juice, marinate before grilling, and use moist heat (stewing, braising, poaching, steaming) for much of your meat.
dose.studied_range: Cooking-chemistry studies at 160-250 °C; adenoma meta-analyses comparing top vs bottom HCA intake; AGE trials from a single meal to 1 year with 2.7- to 5-fold differences in CML intake.
dose.too_much: Regular well-done or very-well-done grilled red meat: each 10 g/day was linked to 29% higher odds of colorectal adenoma in one case-control study (rare/medium meat: 10%, not significant).
dose.timeframe: Cancer associations reflect years of habit; AGE-diet trials looked for effects over 2 weeks to 1 year.
dose.notes: Poultry and fish form HCAs too (grilled chicken breast is often high). Vegetables, grains and fruit form essentially no HCAs. PAHs come mostly from fat dripping onto flames and from smoke, so leaner cuts, a raised grill rack and removing char help. Brown, crusty grain and nut products are the biggest AGE sources in LC-MS databases, not only meat.

entries.mechanism: Above about 150 °C, creatine/creatinine, free amino acids and sugars in muscle react to form HCAs such as PhIP and MeIQx; CYP1A2 N-hydroxylation and NAT2/SULT esterification turn them into DNA-binding species. PAHs such as benzo(a)pyrene form from fat pyrolysis; CYP1A1/1B1 activation to diol epoxides and quinone redox cycling produce DNA adducts and ROS. Maillard chemistry forms AGEs (CML, CEL, MG-H1); absorbed AGEs can bind RAGE and activate NADPH oxidase and NF-kB, although how much dietary AGE reaches tissues is debated.
entries.interactions: Adds to the risks of [processed-red-meat]. Reduced by [marinating-meat] and [herbs-spices]. Endogenous AGE formation from [glycemic-control] and [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] probably matters more than dietary AGEs. Related starchy-food chemistry is covered under [acrylamide].
entries.caveats: HCA exposure estimates come from questionnaires about doneness and cooking method, which are crude. Typical HCA intakes are far below the doses that cause tumours in rodents. Most low-AGE trial benefits come from one research group using an ELISA-based food database; independent groups using mass-spectrometry databases and blinded designs mostly found no effect. The egg link is indirect: AGEs in follicular fluid track poorer IVF outcomes and a small PCOS crossover found a high-AGE diet raised testosterone and oxidative stress, but no trial has tested cooking method on egg quality.
entries.debate: HCA epidemiology: meta-analyses of mostly case-control data find modest positive associations with colorectal adenoma and cancer [kcc-martinezgongora2019, kcc-chiavarini2017], and the NIH-AARP cohort linked MeIQx and DiMeIQx to colorectal cancer [kcc-cross2010], but the 165,717-person Multiethnic Cohort found no association for meat or HCAs [kcc-ollberding2012], and Sugimura argued that HCA content in ordinary meals is too low to explain human cancer alone [kcc-sugimura2004]. Dietary AGEs: the Vlassara/Uribarri group reported large improvements in insulin resistance and 8-isoprostanes on low-AGE diets [kcc-vlassara2016, kcc-uribarri2011] and a blinded crossover from another group found better insulin sensitivity [kcc-decourten2016], whereas 6-week, 2-week and 4-week trials found no effect on endothelial function, inflammation or glucose metabolism [kcc-semba2014, kcc-baye2017, kcc-linkens2022], habitual AGE intake measured by LC-MS/MS was not linked to microvascular or glucose outcomes [kcc-linkens2022b, kcc-linkens2023], and systematic reviews rate the evidence as low quality [kcc-kellow2013, kcc-clarke2016].

entries.headline: Cycling 5 or more hours a week is linked to lower sperm concentration; moderate cycling is not a concern.

dose.effective: Under about 5 hours/week is fine; above that, use a well-fitted saddle, padded shorts and rest days.
dose.studied_range: Cycling >=5 h/week vs no regular exercise (2261 men); 16 weeks of intensive road training (24 cyclists).
dose.too_much: Intensive training raised seminal inflammatory cytokines, with some semen changes persisting 30 days after stopping.
dose.timeframe: Recovery may need more than 30 days; plan ~3 months.
dose.notes: Combine with general exercise advice ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]).

entries.mechanism: Perineal pressure, scrotal heat and friction, plus inflammation and oxidative stress from very high training loads.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [everyday-scrotal-heat].
entries.caveats: Observational; the training study comes from a group with several retracted papers.

factors.name: Home water filtration (reverse osmosis, activated carbon)

entries.headline: Where tap water carries PFAS, reverse-osmosis and well-maintained carbon filters remove much of it and home-filter users in a contaminated county had lower serum PFAS, but real-world filter testing is thin, short-chain PFAS slip through more easily, and there is no human evidence that filtering changes microplastic body burden.

dose.effective: Most worthwhile when local water reports show PFAS, especially in the ~10-100 ng/L range or above (where water clearly raises blood levels, most consistently PFHxS). Options: under-sink reverse osmosis, or a carbon-block filter certified for PFOA/PFOS reduction; change cartridges on schedule.
dose.studied_range: Lab and certification tests of point-of-use devices; only five real-life tap studies; observational serum comparisons.
dose.timeframe: Serum PFAS falls slowly after exposure stops (roughly 13-26% per year for PFHxS, PFOS, PFOA).
dose.notes: Neglected activated-carbon cartridges can release captured PFAS back into water. Below ~10 ng/L the benefit for blood levels is uncertain. Filtering does not affect PFAS from food or consumer products.

entries.mechanism: Reduces intake rather than acting on oxidative stress directly: activated carbon adsorbs long-chain PFAS, ion-exchange resins bind anionic PFAS, and reverse osmosis membranes reject most PFAS molecules.
entries.interactions: Pairs with [pfas] serum testing; the elimination side (donation, sequestrants) is covered there. For bottled water vs tap and plastics see [microplastics].
entries.caveats: Serum benefit is shown only by observational comparisons in a heavily contaminated area. Device performance varies by product, PFAS chain length and maintenance.
entries.debate: Benefit size depends on water levels: a 2026 evidence summary found clear water-to-blood links at 10-100 ng/L but inconsistent ones below ~10 ng/L [env-tefera2026], whereas a California study found detectable PFAS in general public supplies raised serum PFHxS ~80% [env-fillman2026]. Filters: home-filter users had lower serum PFAS [env-cuffney2023], and stopping contaminated water lowers serum over years [env-li2018], but a review warns real-world performance is poorly characterized and short-chain PFAS are harder to remove [env-mackeown2024].

factors.name: Hormonal contraception and return of fertility

entries.headline: About 83% of women conceive within 12 months of stopping contraception of any type; injectables delay return of normal fertility by about 5-8 cycles, the patch about 4, the pill or ring about 3, IUDs and implants about 2, and total years of use do not matter.

dose.effective: Not applicable; the question is the delay after stopping.
dose.studied_range: 22 studies of 14,884 women; prospective cohort of 17,954 women trying to conceive.
dose.too_much: Injectable progestin (DMPA) has the longest delay (FR 0.65).
dose.timeframe: Pill, ring: ~3 cycles; patch: ~4; injectable: 5-8; IUD and implant: ~2.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Plan stopping injectables several months before wanting to conceive. Start folic acid before stopping contraception (see folic-acid).

entries.mechanism: Hormonal methods suppress ovulation; the delay reflects time for the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis to resume normal cycles, longest with depot injections that persist in the body. No evidence that past use damages eggs.
entries.interactions: Oral contraceptive efficacy is reduced by St John's wort ([supplement-drug-interactions]) and during tirzepatide initiation ([glp1-agonists]). [folic-acid] should begin before stopping.
entries.caveats: Neither study measured egg quality directly; return of fertility is the outcome.
entries.debate: A meta-analysis found no significant delay overall or by method [med-girum2018], whereas a large prospective cohort found short method-specific delays, longest after injectables [med-yland2020]; both agree long-term use does not reduce eventual fertility.

key_numbers.label: Fecundability ratio after injectables vs barrier

entries.title: Hormonal contraception and return of fertility

entries.headline: The one add-on with a plausible live-birth gain: Cochrane finds about 21% higher live birth (RR 1.21; ~33% to 37-44%) but also 45% more multiple pregnancies, so ESHRE recommends it only with single embryo transfer; HFEA rates it amber.

dose.effective: Hyaluronan 0.5 mg/mL in the transfer medium, with single embryo transfer.
dose.studied_range: 0.5 mg/mL ('functional') vs 0-0.125 mg/mL controls.
dose.too_much: Multiple pregnancy RR 1.45 when more than one embryo is transferred.
dose.timeframe: Embryo is placed in the medium minutes to hours before transfer.
dose.notes: Benefit seen with women's own eggs, not clearly with donor eggs.

entries.mechanism: Hyaluronan is abundant in uterine fluid at implantation; proposed to help embryo-endometrium adhesion via CD44 and to make the medium more viscous.
entries.interactions: Multiple-pregnancy risk interacts with the number of embryos transferred.
entries.caveats: Many trials are older, small and industry-linked; the effect appears in autologous fresh transfers more than frozen ones.
entries.debate: Cochrane (moderate certainty) and a 2022 meta-analysis find a live-birth gain with women's own eggs [fer-heymann2020, fer-heymann2022], and ESHRE recommends it [fer-eshre2023addons]. HFEA judges the evidence conflicting and rates it amber [fer-hfea2026], and in Cochrane's low-risk-of-bias subset the miscarriage benefit disappears [fer-heymann2020].

entries.headline: Being dehydrated increased muscle H2O2 after resistance exercise in one small study; there is no evidence that drinking extra water beyond thirst lowers oxidative stress.

dose.effective: Drink to thirst; aim for pale-yellow urine; replace fluids lost in heavy sweating.
dose.studied_range: One crossover study with 24 h fluid restriction.
dose.too_much: Overdrinking (hyponatremia) is a risk in endurance events.
dose.notes: 'Alkaline' or 'structured' water claims have no support.

entries.mechanism: Dehydration raises cell stress and may increase ROS production in exercising muscle.
entries.interactions: Relevant to [overtraining-ultraendurance] and [sauna].
entries.caveats: Evidence is a single small study; 'flushing out toxins' with water is not a real antioxidant mechanism.
entries.title: Hydration

entries.headline: Molecular hydrogen scavenges hydroxyl radicals in lab and animal studies, but human trials are small and show at most modest effects on lipids, not established oxidative-stress benefits.

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress. Trials used ~0.5-1.5 L/day of hydrogen-rich water.
dose.studied_range: Pilot RCTs of weeks to 6 months.
dose.too_much: Appears safe.
dose.notes: Hydrogen escapes quickly from water once opened.

entries.mechanism: H2 reacts selectively with hydroxyl radical and peroxynitrite; may also signal via Nrf2. Doses from drinking water are tiny and transient.
entries.interactions: No known interactions.
entries.caveats: Most trials are small and come from a few research groups; the telomere result came from a 40-person pilot with many outcomes, and the lipid meta-analysis pooled only 7 small studies.
entries.title: Hydrogen-rich water / molecular hydrogen

factors.name: ICSI when sperm are normal (non-male-factor ICSI)

entries.headline: With normal sperm count and motility, ICSI did not beat conventional IVF in a 1064-couple Lancet RCT (live birth 35% vs 31%, NS; fertilisation failure 5% vs 6%), yet US registry data show two-thirds of non-male-factor cycles use it; ESHRE and ASRM advise against routine use.

dose.effective: Use conventional IVF when semen is normal; reserve ICSI for male factor, prior fertilisation failure, PGT cycles or very few eggs.
dose.studied_range: Sibling and randomised comparisons with WHO-normal semen.
dose.too_much: Extra cost and lab time; skips natural sperm selection at the egg's surface.
dose.timeframe: Fertilisation day.
dose.notes: Distinct from ICSI for genuine male factor, where it is the standard of care.

entries.mechanism: ICSI bypasses sperm binding and penetration; it rescues fertilisation when sperm cannot do this, but adds nothing when they can.
entries.interactions: Often combined with [sperm-selection-icsi-sperm]; high SDF is not by itself an indication for ICSI over IVF.
entries.caveats: Observational data even suggest slightly lower live birth with ICSI in non-male-factor cycles, but confounding is likely.
entries.debate: Some clinicians use ICSI routinely to avoid the small risk of total fertilisation failure; the Dang RCT found no difference in failure or live birth [fer-dang2021], and registry data found no benefit and slightly lower live birth (aRR 0.95) [fer-boulet2015]. ASRM and ESHRE advise against routine use [fer-asrm2020icsi, fer-eshre2023addons].

factors.name: Immunological tests and treatments (IVIG, intralipids, steroids, NK-cell testing)

entries.headline: No good evidence that 'immune' testing or treatment helps IVF: HFEA rates IVIG and steroids red (no proven benefit plus real risks such as thrombosis, infection and preterm birth) and intralipids grey; ESHRE recommends against all of them.

dose.effective: Not recommended outside research or a diagnosed autoimmune disease treated for its own sake.
dose.studied_range: IVIG 0.2-0.5 g/kg infusions; intralipid 20% infusions; prednisolone/dexamethasone around implantation.
dose.too_much: IVIG is a blood product (thrombosis, kidney injury, allergy); steroids raise infection risk, blood pressure and possibly preterm birth; intralipids can cause allergy in soy/egg-allergic people.
dose.timeframe: Given before and after embryo transfer.
dose.notes: Uterine or blood natural-killer-cell tests have no validated link to IVF outcome.

entries.mechanism: Premise that maternal immune cells (especially NK cells) reject the embryo; immune rejection of the fetus 'rarely, if ever, happens' according to HFEA.
entries.interactions: Often sold after recurrent implantation failure; ESHRE's RIF recommendations do not support immunomodulators [fer-eshre2023rif].
entries.caveats: Positive small trials and meta-analyses exist but are low quality.
entries.debate: A meta-analysis mixing RCTs and case-control studies reported higher live birth with IVIG (RR 1.62) [fer-li2013] and a 102-woman RCT reported higher live birth with intralipid (28.8% vs 10%) [fer-singh2019]. Cochrane is uncertain about glucocorticoids (OR 1.37, 0.69-2.71) [fer-boomsma2022]; HFEA (red/grey) and ESHRE reject these treatments [fer-hfea2026, fer-eshre2023addons, fer-eshre2023rif].
entries.title: Immunological tests and treatments (IVIG, intralipids, steroids, NK-cell testing)

entries.headline: Fitness is one of the strongest predictors of survival: each 1-MET higher VO2max (about 3.5 mL/kg/min) is associated with 11-17% lower mortality, and the least fit have about 4x the risk of the most fit, with no upper limit; but genetic analyses question how much of this is caused by fitness itself.

dose.effective: Aim to move out of the bottom fifth for your age and sex, then keep improving: each +1 MET counts. Combine 150+ min/week of aerobic activity with 1-2 weekly interval sessions (e.g. 4 x 4 min at 85-95% HRmax); add sessions or intensity if fitness does not budge.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: fitness from under 5 to over 14 METs on treadmill tests; training studies: 60-300 min/week for 6-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: No upper limit of benefit was seen for measured fitness, even at the 98th percentile (elite).
dose.timeframe: VO2max rises measurably within 4-8 weeks of training; fitness change over years tracks mortality.
dose.notes: The lowest mortality in 750,302 veterans was at about 14 METs (roughly 49 mL/kg/min). In older adults (70-77 years), being moderately fit gave most of the benefit. 'Non-responders' to standard programs responded when weekly time or intensity was raised.

entries.mechanism: Training raises stroke volume, blood and haemoglobin volume, capillary density and muscle mitochondrial content (PGC-1alpha), via the same redox-signalling and hormesis pathways as [aerobic-exercise-moderate]. High fitness travels with lower blood pressure, visceral fat, insulin resistance and inflammation, all chronic ROS sources.
entries.interactions: Built by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and even [exercise-snacks]; strength gains appear to feed fitness ([resistance-training]). Lower body fat raises VO2max per kg ([weight-loss]).
entries.caveats: Baseline fitness and trainability partly reflect genes, body composition and health status, so people with undiagnosed disease test as 'unfit'. Most data come from people referred for treadmill tests. VO2max in mL/kg/min also falls with fat mass, so part of the signal is adiposity.
entries.debate: Proponents point to large, consistent cohorts with graded associations and no upper limit [exr-mandsager2018, exr-kokkinos2022, exr-kodama2009, exr-han2022, exr-lang2024], an AHA call to treat fitness as a vital sign [exr-ross2016], and evidence that improving fitness over time tracks lower mortality [exr-imboden2019]. Skeptics note that a two-sample Mendelian randomization found genetically predicted VO2max was not causally associated with longevity, while activity, lean mass and lower fat did raise VO2max [exr-kjaergaard2025], that genetic analyses point from strength to fitness rather than the reverse [exr-norris2024], that the certainty of the meta-analytic evidence is very low to moderate [exr-lang2024], and that the only long-term exercise RCT in older adults did not reduce mortality significantly [exr-stensvold2020]. In older adults, benefit may plateau above moderate fitness [exr-tari2025]. Trainability is also debated: non-response to standard doses disappears at higher doses [exr-montero2017] or intensities [exr-ross2015].

entries.headline: I3C (200-400 mg/day) and DIM reliably shift estrogen metabolism toward 2-hydroxylation, and I3C regressed cervical precancer in one 30-woman trial, but no trial shows fewer cancers, DIM lowered active tamoxifen metabolites, and high-dose I3C caused liver tumours in male mice and uterine cancer in female rats.

dose.effective: No outcome-based dose; 200-400 mg/day I3C or 300 mg/day DIM shifted estrogen metabolites.
dose.studied_range: I3C 200-1200 mg/day; DIM 150 mg twice daily for up to 12 months.
dose.too_much: Do not combine with tamoxifen (endoxifen fell). NTP found carcinogenicity at high gavage doses. DIM plasma levels plateau above about 1000 mg I3C.
dose.timeframe: Estrogen metabolite shift within 1 month.
dose.notes: I3C itself never reaches the blood; it condenses in stomach acid, and DIM is the only product detected in plasma. Eating crucifers gives a much smaller version of the same shift.

entries.mechanism: Acid-condensation products of I3C (chiefly DIM) activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and induce CYP1A enzymes that hydroxylate estradiol at C-2 rather than C-16; they are also weak Nrf2 inducers.
entries.interactions: Synergistic or additive with isothiocyanates (sulforaphane, PEITC) in cell Nrf2 assays. Food sources overlap [cruciferous-other] and [broccoli-mature]. Drug interaction with tamoxifen.
entries.caveats: The urinary 2:16-hydroxyestrone ratio is a surrogate with an uncertain link to cancer risk. The cervical trial is small and unreplicated. Higher catechol-estrogen levels could have long-term downsides. Marketing for 'estrogen detox' outruns the data.

key_numbers.label: Complete CIN regression on I3C (8 of 17) vs placebo (0 of 10)
Plasma DIM Cmax plateau (1000 mg I3C)

factors.name: Indoor combustion: wood stoves, fireplaces, gas cooking

entries.headline: Wood smoke at smoky-home levels raised airway oxidative stress in one chamber study but had no systemic effect in another; gas cooking is linked to childhood asthma, though the quality of that evidence is debated.

dose.effective: Use range hoods vented outdoors when cooking (especially on gas), keep wood stoves well-sealed and burning cleanly, avoid open fireplaces as daily heat, and ventilate.
dose.studied_range: Chamber studies: 3-4 h at 220-354 µg/m³ wood-smoke particles.
dose.too_much: Exposure in poorly vented homes with daily solid-fuel burning (much higher in low-income countries using biomass).
dose.timeframe: Airway markers changed within hours.
dose.notes: Electric or induction cooking removes the NO2 source.

entries.mechanism: Combustion particles and gases (NO2, aldehydes, PAHs) generate airway ROS and inflammation; NO2 is itself an oxidant.
entries.interactions: Similar pathways to [outdoor-air-pollution]; mitigated by [hepa-air-purifier] for particles.
entries.caveats: Controlled wood-smoke studies are small and inconsistent. The gas-stove literature is mostly cross-sectional; a 2013 meta-analysis found OR 1.32 for asthma while a 2023 review judged the evidence too low-quality for causal conclusions.
entries.title: Indoor combustion: wood stoves, fireplaces, gas cooking

entries.headline: In randomized sham-controlled crossover trials, running HEPA purifiers cut indoor PM2.5 by about half and lowered oxidative and inflammatory markers (8-isoprostane, myeloperoxidase) and blood pressure within days.

dose.effective: Run a HEPA purifier sized for the room (check its clean-air delivery rate) continuously in the bedroom and main living space when outdoor or indoor PM2.5 is elevated, with windows closed.
dose.studied_range: Trials: 48 h to 1 week of real vs sham purification in dormitories with outdoor PM2.5 roughly 40-100 µg/m³.
dose.timeframe: Effects within 48 h to 1 week; they disappear when purification stops.
dose.notes: Benefits are largest where indoor air is polluted; in clean-air regions the gain is small.

entries.mechanism: Removes redox-active particles before they reach the lungs, reducing airway NADPH-oxidase activation, inflammatory cell activation and systemic lipid peroxidation.
entries.interactions: Counters [outdoor-air-pollution] and [indoor-combustion-smoke]; does not remove gases like NO2 unless the unit has activated carbon.
entries.caveats: Trials were short, in young healthy Chinese students exposed to high pollution; long-term clinical outcomes are not yet shown.
entries.title: Indoor HEPA air purification

entries.headline: Industrial trans fats raise LDL, lower HDL, promote systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction, and carry a higher coronary risk per gram than any other fat.

dose.effective: As close to zero as possible from partially hydrogenated oils.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts and controlled feeding studies.
dose.too_much: Any regular intake from partially hydrogenated oils.
dose.timeframe: Years.
dose.notes: Now banned or restricted in many countries; still present in some imported or older products.

entries.mechanism: Altered lipoprotein metabolism and inflammatory signalling (NF-kB), endothelial dysfunction.
entries.interactions: Often co-occurs with [oxidized-frying-oils] in fried fast food.
entries.caveats: The oxidative-stress component is one part of a broader cardiometabolic harm.
entries.title: Industrial trans fats

entries.headline: Intermittent fasting helps mainly by making people eat less: across 99 RCTs it beat ad libitum eating, but matched calorie restriction about equally (Cochrane: -0.56 kg difference over 3-12 months), and calorie-matched trials show no fasting-specific drop in oxidative stress markers.

dose.effective: Any form you can sustain that produces a modest energy deficit: an 8-10 h daily eating window, alternate-day fasting (~500 kcal or zero on fast days), or 2 days/week of 500-600 kcal (5:2). See [time-restricted-eating], [alternate-day-fasting], [five-two-diet].
dose.studied_range: Daily fasts of 12-20 h, 24-36 h alternate-day fasts, 2 days/week at ~25% of needs, for 3 weeks to 12 months.
dose.too_much: Daily eating windows under ~6 h and multi-day fasts increase lean-mass loss; not for pregnancy, eating disorders, underweight, type 1 diabetes, or insulin/sulfonylurea users without medical adjustment.
dose.timeframe: Weight and insulin changes within 4-12 weeks; oxidative stress markers follow weight loss.
dose.notes: Fasting length matters physiologically (ketones barely rise before ~20 h), but for health outcomes the total energy deficit matters far more than the pattern.

entries.mechanism: Energy deficit and weight loss lower insulin, adipose inflammation and mitochondrial ROS production. Longer fasts add a metabolic switch to fatty acids and ketones; beta-hydroxybutyrate can inhibit class I HDACs and induce FOXO3A and metallothionein (mouse data). Early eating windows align intake with circadian insulin sensitivity.
entries.interactions: Effects largely overlap with [calorie-restriction] and [weight-loss]; benefits are biggest with [excess-adiposity] and [glycemic-control] problems. Pair with [resistance-training] and adequate protein to limit lean loss. Diet quality still matters: fasting does not offset [overfeeding] on eating days. Late, short windows can shorten sleep; see [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Most claims about autophagy, 'cellular cleanup' and longevity come from rodents. Calorie-matched trials (Templeman 2021, Liu 2022, Peters 2025) found no fasting-specific benefit. Only modified alternate-day fasting for BMI reached high-quality evidence in an umbrella review, and IF is associated with fat-free mass loss. The early eTRF oxidative stress result (n = 8) was driven partly by worsening on the control schedule.

ADF vs continuous restriction, weight (network meta-analysis)

entries.headline: Two RCTs in poor responders found no gain in euploid embryos (one null on every outcome, one with ~1.5 more mature eggs over three retrievals); HFEA rates it red for safety and lack of evidence, and ESHRE does not recommend it.

dose.effective: Not recommended outside research.
dose.studied_range: Autologous PRP injected transvaginally into each ovary, usually 1-3 months before stimulation.
dose.too_much: Needle injection under anaesthesia: infection, bleeding, anaesthetic risk; no standard preparation.
dose.timeframe: Claims of effect within 1-3 months; not borne out in RCTs.
dose.notes: Marketed for low AMH, perimenopause and premature ovarian insufficiency.

entries.mechanism: Platelet growth factors (PDGF, VEGF, TGF-beta) are claimed to activate dormant follicles or improve the ovarian microenvironment; no human evidence of new or better eggs.
entries.interactions: Does not change [maternal-age]-driven aneuploidy; compare [growth-hormone-ivf-egg] and [dhea] in the same poor-responder population.
entries.caveats: Most supporting studies are uncontrolled case series.
entries.debate: The double-blind Barrenetxea RCT found slightly more cumulative mature eggs (10.45 vs 8.91) but identical euploid blastocysts [fer-barrenetxea2024]; the PROVA RCT found no effect at all [fer-herlihy2024]. Cochrane rates the evidence very low certainty [fer-vaidakis2024]; HFEA red [fer-hfea2026prp]; ESHRE not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].

factors.name: Intrauterine hCG infusion before embryo transfer

entries.headline: Cochrane found a live-birth benefit only for day-3 (cleavage-stage) transfers with at least 500 IU and no evidence for blastocyst transfer, today's norm; ESHRE does not recommend it.

dose.effective: Not recommended. The only positive subgroup used >=500 IU before cleavage-stage transfer.
dose.studied_range: 100-1000 IU urinary or recombinant hCG infused minutes to days before transfer.
dose.timeframe: Embryo-transfer cycle.
dose.notes: Not on the HFEA rating list.

entries.mechanism: hCG made by the embryo signals to the endometrium (angiogenesis, immune tolerance, decidualisation); infusion aims to mimic this early.
entries.interactions: Irrelevant to most current cycles, which use blastocyst transfer.
entries.caveats: Most trials at high risk of bias, with very high heterogeneity.
entries.debate: Cochrane rated the cleavage-stage >=500 IU benefit as moderate quality [fer-craciunas2018]; ESHRE judged the evidence conflicting and does not recommend it [fer-eshre2023addons].
entries.title: Intrauterine hCG infusion before embryo transfer

entries.headline: Pooled small trials suggest higher pregnancy after implantation failure, but the only low-risk-of-bias trial showed no clear effect on live birth (OR 1.10, 0.38-3.14); HFEA rates intrauterine PRP red for every indication.

dose.effective: Not recommended outside research.
dose.studied_range: 0.5-1 mL autologous PRP infused into the uterus 1-2 days before transfer or in the proliferative phase.
dose.too_much: Infection, bleeding, allergic reaction; preparations unstandardised.
dose.timeframe: Embryo-transfer cycle.
dose.notes: Marketed for thin endometrium, recurrent implantation failure and Asherman's syndrome.

entries.mechanism: Growth factors claimed to thicken the endometrium and promote angiogenesis and receptivity.
entries.interactions: Usually offered alongside other implantation add-ons ([endometrial-scratch-egg], [immune-addons-egg]).
entries.caveats: Positive pooled results come from high-risk-of-bias trials.
entries.debate: Including all trials, Cochrane found higher live birth/ongoing pregnancy (OR 2.38) but rated it very low certainty and the low-risk trial was null [fer-vaidakis2024]. HFEA red [fer-hfea2026prp]; ESHRE not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].
entries.title: Intrauterine platelet-rich plasma

entries.headline: IV glutathione is cleared from blood with a half-life of ~14 minutes; oral glutathione raised blood stores 17-35% in one 6-month RCT, but no trial shows clinical benefit for oxidative stress.

dose.effective: Not recommended. Oral trial used 250-1000 mg/day for 6 months; levels returned to baseline within a month of stopping.
dose.studied_range: IV: single 2 g/m² infusion pharmacokinetics; oral: 6-month RCT.
dose.too_much: No benefit shown; usual infusion risks apply to IV use.
dose.timeframe: IV effect gone within about an hour; oral effect builds over months and reverses within a month.
dose.notes: Cells make their own glutathione from cysteine, glycine and glutamate; exercise, sleep and not smoking support it.

entries.mechanism: Exogenous glutathione is broken down in plasma and by gamma-glutamyl transferase into amino acids; cells resynthesize glutathione internally.
entries.interactions: Lifestyle factors that preserve glutathione: avoiding [tobacco-smoking] and [alcohol], [short-sleep] correction.
entries.caveats: Biomarker increases do not equal health benefit; no outcome trials.
entries.title: Intravenous (IV) or oral glutathione

entries.headline: Even mild iodine deficiency matters around conception: women with very low urinary iodine took longer to conceive (46% lower fecundability per cycle), and children of mildly deficient UK mothers had higher odds of low verbal IQ (OR 1.58); but excess iodine can also tip the thyroid into dysfunction.

dose.effective: RDA 150 ug/day (220 pregnancy, 290 lactation). Iodised salt, dairy, eggs and seafood are main sources. The American Thyroid Association recommends a 150 ug/day iodine supplement (as potassium iodide) before and during pregnancy and lactation.
dose.studied_range: Observational urinary iodine:creatinine ratios (<50 to >150 ug/g).
dose.too_much: UL 1100 ug/day (IOM) or 600 ug/day (EFSA). Kelp supplements, amiodarone and contrast media can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism in susceptible people.
dose.timeframe: Thyroid stores build over months; fetal brain depends on maternal thyroxine in the first trimester.
dose.notes: At risk: vegans and people avoiding dairy, fish and iodised salt (sea salt and specialty salts are usually not iodised), pregnancy, regions without salt iodisation (e.g. UK).

entries.mechanism: Iodine is the substrate for thyroid hormones, which set mitochondrial metabolic rate and drive fetal brain development. Thyroid hormone synthesis itself uses H2O2 (thyroid peroxidase), protected by selenium-dependent GPx.
entries.interactions: Selenium supports thyroid peroxidase protection and deiodinases [selenium-supplement]. Delivered by most prenatal multivitamins [multivitamin-mineral].
entries.caveats: Fertility data come from a single cohort of 501 women; no RCT tests iodine for conception or child IQ in mildly deficient populations.
entries.debate: Observational data link mild deficiency to child cognition [nut-bath2013] and slower conception [nut-mills2018], prompting calls for action [nut-stagnarogreen2013] and supplement recommendations [nut-alexander2017, nut-korevaar2026]. The counterweight is that iodine has a U-curve too: excess can trigger thyroid dysfunction [nut-sohn2024], and the Mills result needs replication, as the authors themselves note [nut-mills2018].

entries.title: Iodine status

entries.headline: Iron deficiency is one of the world's leading nutritional harms: even without anaemia it causes fatigue (iron cut fatigue scores 48% vs 29% placebo in women with ferritin <50 ug/L), and in pregnancy anaemia is linked to ~30% more low birthweight and ~60% more preterm birth.

dose.effective: Treat documented deficiency: typical oral regimens give 40-100 mg elemental iron once daily or on alternate days for about 3 months, then recheck ferritin; 80 mg/day for 12 weeks was used in the fatigue RCT. Prevention: RDA 8 mg/day (men, postmenopausal women), 18 mg/day (menstruating women), 27 mg/day (pregnancy); vegetarians need ~1.8x more because non-heme iron is less bioavailable.
dose.studied_range: Oral iron 60-80 mg/day in most adult trials; prenatal 30-60 mg/day.
dose.too_much: Continuing high-dose iron after repletion pushes stores up [iron-excess]; IOM UL 45 mg/day (GI effects) applies to healthy people, not to supervised treatment.
dose.timeframe: Haemoglobin rises within 2-4 weeks; ferritin repletion takes ~3 months; fatigue improved by 12 weeks.
dose.notes: At-risk groups: heavy menstrual bleeding, pregnancy, infants and adolescents, vegans/vegetarians, frequent blood donors, endurance athletes, coeliac disease and other GI disease, bariatric surgery, chronic PPI use. In men and postmenopausal women, unexplained iron deficiency needs investigation for GI blood loss.

entries.mechanism: Iron is needed for haemoglobin, myoglobin, mitochondrial cytochromes and iron-sulfur clusters, catalase and many DNA-synthesis enzymes. Deficiency impairs oxygen delivery and mitochondrial energy production, immunity and brain neurotransmitter synthesis. It is not an 'antioxidant' state: anaemia is itself associated with oxidative stress in red cells.
entries.interactions: Frequent donation can cause it [blood-donation]. Vitamin C-rich foods with meals raise non-heme absorption [vitamin-c-foods]; tea and coffee with meals reduce it [green-tea] [coffee]. For fertility relevance see [iron-egg].
entries.caveats: Ferritin is the best single test but is falsely raised by inflammation; in that setting transferrin saturation <20% helps. Cognitive benefits of iron in non-anaemic people are less certain than fatigue benefits.
entries.debate: That deficiency harms health is not contested [nut-pasricha2021]. Debate centres on thresholds and on non-anaemic deficiency: fatigue benefits appeared in an RCT [nut-vaucher2012] and a 2025 meta-analysis found psychiatric and cognitive gains only in iron-deficient participants [nut-fiani2025], while an earlier review judged cognitive trials small and weak [nut-falkingham2010]. In pregnancy, Cochrane supports routine iron [nut-finkelstein2024] but also notes more haemoglobin above 130 g/L [nut-penarosas2015], and high maternal haemoglobin/ferritin are themselves linked to gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia [nut-young2023, nut-khambalia2016].

key_numbers.label: Fatigue reduction, iron vs placebo (ferritin <50 ug/L)

entries.title: Iron deficiency (with or without anaemia)

entries.headline: Pathological iron overload (thalassaemia, haemochromatosis) causes hypogonadism in about half of affected men and more sperm DNA damage; in ordinary men, higher seminal iron tracks with poorer motility, but there is no evidence that normal dietary iron harms sperm.

dose.effective: Men do not need iron supplements unless deficient; men with known iron overload need chelation or phlebotomy started early.
dose.studied_range: Median ferritin 2251 ug/L in thalassaemic men; observational seminal iron levels.
dose.too_much: Iron overload disorders: hypogonadism in ~47% of men, azoospermia in ~18% of those assessed.
dose.timeframe: Earlier chelation was associated with less sperm DNA damage.
dose.notes: Relevant mainly to men with thalassaemia, transfusion dependence or untreated haemochromatosis.

entries.mechanism: Iron deposits in the pituitary and testis; free iron catalyses Fenton chemistry and lipid peroxidation in polyunsaturated-rich sperm membranes; ferroptosis markers (low GPX4) appear in poor-motility sperm.
entries.interactions: Do not take iron-containing multivitamins without need [iron-excess]. Antioxidant supplements have not been tested in this group [male-antioxidant-combination].
entries.caveats: Evidence comes from tiny case series and case-control studies; seminal iron correlations are confounded by infection and leukocytes.
entries.debate: A systematic review of iron-overload disorders documents frequent hypogonadism and sperm abnormalities [nut-carlomagno2026], and a small study linked overload to sperm DNA damage [nut-perera2002]. Seminal iron correlates with poorer sperm quality [nut-ammar2019], but no study shows that dietary iron in non-overloaded men affects sperm; this extrapolation is unsupported.

key_numbers.label: Hypogonadism in men with iron overload
Median ferritin, thalassaemic men with sperm DNA damage

entries.title: Iron overload and sperm

entries.headline: In the Nurses' Health Study II, women taking iron supplements had 40% less ovulatory infertility, but two newer cohorts of 4662 pregnancy planners found no consistent link except in women prone to deficiency; correcting deficiency matters, extra iron does not.

dose.effective: Check ferritin before trying to conceive; if low, treat (see [iron-deficiency]). Prenatal vitamins typically supply 27 mg/day, matching the pregnancy RDA.
dose.studied_range: Dietary and supplemental non-heme iron intakes in cohorts; heme iron showed no association.
dose.too_much: IOM UL 45 mg/day outside treatment; high ferritin in pregnancy is associated with gestational diabetes.
dose.timeframe: Repletion takes about 3 months, similar to the ~3-month follicle development window.
dose.notes: Heavy menstrual bleeding and short cycles are common causes of low iron in women trying to conceive.

entries.mechanism: Iron supports mitochondrial energy production and oxygen delivery to developing follicles. At the other extreme, iron overload in follicular fluid (seen in endometriosis) triggered granulosa-cell ferroptosis and poor oocyte maturation in mouse models, a mechanistic warning against excess.
entries.interactions: Usually delivered via prenatal multivitamins together with folic acid [folic-acid] [multivitamin-mineral]. Endometriosis creates local iron overload [endometriosis].
entries.caveats: Observational and self-reported; women who take supplements differ in many ways. No RCT of iron for fertility in non-anaemic women exists.
entries.debate: Positive: NHS II found iron supplements lowered ovulatory infertility (RR 0.60) [nut-chavarro2006]. Null-to-modest: PRESTO and Snart Foraeldre found no consistent association, with benefit limited to supplement users in North America and women with heavy menses [nut-hahn2019]. Mechanistic data point the other way for local excess [nut-ni2022], and iron-overload disorders cause amenorrhoea [nut-carlomagno2026].
entries.title: Iron status and ovulatory fertility

entries.headline: Polyphenols reach only about 0-4 µmol/L in plasma, mostly as metabolites. Effects in human trials are small and mostly on biomarkers, and no outcome benefit is established for capsules.

dose.effective: Not established for outcomes.
dose.studied_range: Tens to hundreds of mg/day in short biomarker studies
dose.timeframe: Transient plasma exposure after each dose
dose.notes: Bioavailability varies over 100-fold by compound (urinary recovery 0.3-43%); isoflavones and gallic acid are best absorbed, proanthocyanidins and anthocyanins worst.

entries.mechanism: Direct scavenging in plasma is implausible at these concentrations. Likely actions are mild electrophilic Nrf2 activation, modulation of NF-kB and endothelial signalling, and local effects in the gut, where much of the dose and its microbial metabolites act.
entries.interactions: May act additively with other Nrf2 activators in vitro; human interaction data are lacking. The rise in plasma antioxidant capacity after polyphenol foods is mostly uric acid.
entries.caveats: Cell-culture 'antioxidant' effects are often artefacts of polyphenols oxidising in culture media. Whole foods with the same polyphenols carry fibre and other components.
