factors.name: Mustard powder on cooked crucifers (myrosinase add-back)

entries.headline: Sprinkling 1 g powdered brown mustard on 200 g cooked broccoli raised sulforaphane metabolite excretion about 4.5-fold, and mustard-seed myrosinase doubled conversion of a broccoli seed extract (40% vs 19%).

dose.effective: About 1 g (roughly 1/2 teaspoon) powdered brown mustard per 200 g cooked broccoli, stirred in after cooking.
dose.studied_range: 1 g mustard powder with 200 g cooked broccoli (12 adults, crossover); mustard-seed powder with a glucoraphanin-rich seed extract (16 adults, crossover).
dose.timeframe: Same meal.
dose.notes: Add after cooking, once the food has cooled below steaming; heat inactivates mustard myrosinase too. Raw daikon radish (used to make Qidong's sulforaphane-rich beverage) or a pinch of broccoli seed powder works on the same principle.

entries.mechanism: Exogenous plant myrosinase hydrolyses glucoraphanin that survives cooking into sulforaphane in the meal and upper gut, instead of leaving it to variable colonic bacteria; then Nrf2 activation.
entries.interactions: Turns cooked [broccoli-mature] and [cruciferous-other] into meaningful sulforaphane sources and can boost glucoraphanin-only [sulforaphane-supplements]; same redundancy considerations as other Nrf2 inducers.
entries.caveats: Two small pharmacokinetic trials; no outcome data.

key_numbers.label: Urinary SF-NAC, cooked broccoli + 1 g mustard
Seed extract conversion with mustard myrosinase

entries.title: Mustard powder on cooked crucifers (myrosinase add-back)

entries.headline: Widely used in PCOS, but the Cochrane review rated the evidence very low quality and could not show a live-birth benefit (OR 2.42, 95% CI 0.75-7.83); the 2023 PCOS guideline review calls it limited and inconclusive.

dose.effective: Trials commonly used 4 g/day myo-inositol with 400 ug folic acid (e.g. the now-retracted Pacchiarotti trial); no dose is proven to raise live birth.
dose.studied_range: 11 of 13 Cochrane trials used myo-inositol as pre-treatment before IVF; 2 during ovulation induction.
dose.too_much: Mild GI effects; fewer GI effects than metformin.
dose.timeframe: Pre-treatment before IVF stimulation in most trials.
dose.notes: D-chiro-inositol may help ovulation per the guideline review, but evidence is very uncertain. One widely cited myo-inositol plus melatonin RCT (526 women) was retracted in 2026.

entries.mechanism: Inositol phosphoglycans act as second messengers for insulin and FSH signalling; may improve insulin sensitivity in PCOS.
entries.interactions: Alternative to or adjunct with metformin; often combined with [melatonin] and [folic-acid].
entries.caveats: Industry-linked trials, poor reporting and a retraction. Not relevant for women without PCOS.

key_numbers.label: Live birth, MI vs standard (2 RCTs)

entries.title: Myo-inositol (in PCOS)

entries.headline: NAC raises glutathione and improved performance and oxidative markers only in people with low baseline glutathione. In replete people it blunts muscle repair signalling. In mouse cancer models it accelerated tumour growth and metastasis.

dose.effective: 1,200 mg/day (600 mg twice daily) for 30 days in people with low baseline glutathione
dose.studied_range: 1,200 mg/day for 30 days (performance trial); short courses in exercise-recovery studies
dose.too_much: No defined toxicity threshold at these doses, but caution in people with active or past cancer (mouse data) and around training (blunted adaptation).
dose.timeframe: Glutathione restored within 30 days in deficient individuals
dose.notes: Benefit depends on baseline redox status; there is no routine clinical test, and this is a research approach.

entries.mechanism: Supplies cysteine, the limiting substrate for glutathione synthesis via glutamate-cysteine ligase. By raising GSH it can blunt redox-sensitive signalling (Akt/mTOR, NF-kB) needed for repair, and in tumour cells it can increase glutathione-dependent migration.
entries.interactions: Combined with glycine as [glynac]. Redundant with a high-protein diet rich in sulfur amino acids, and with Nrf2 activators that induce GCL. Antagonises exercise adaptation like [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Popular as a 'master antioxidant' supplement. Human outcome data in healthy people are lacking, and the tumour-promotion findings come from mice with existing tumours.
entries.title: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)

entries.headline: NAC 600 mg/day for 3 months lowered SDF and improved motility in an uncontrolled study; no placebo-controlled live-birth data.

dose.effective: 600 mg/day for 3 months (studied dose).
dose.studied_range: 600 mg/day in 50 men with asthenoteratozoospermia.
dose.too_much: Higher doses add GI upset; no proven extra benefit.
dose.timeframe: 3 months.

entries.mechanism: Cysteine donor for glutathione synthesis; also reported to induce Nrf2 target genes in sperm.
entries.interactions: Part of many combination products.
entries.caveats: Before-after design without placebo. Some widely cited NAC/selenium RCTs come from an author several of whose other papers have been retracted; they are not used here.
entries.title: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)

entries.headline: In PCOS, NAC added to clomiphene improved ovulation and pregnancy vs placebo in small, biased trials, but it was inferior to metformin and live-birth data are thin.

dose.effective: 1.2 g/day (with clomiphene in clomiphene-resistant PCOS) in the original RCT.
dose.studied_range: 1.2 g/day in the main RCT; 8 RCTs (910 women) pooled in meta-analysis.
dose.timeframe: During ovulation-induction cycles.
dose.notes: A glutathione precursor; available as a supplement in some countries and a drug in others.

entries.mechanism: Supplies cysteine for glutathione synthesis; may improve insulin sensitivity.
entries.interactions: Compared against metformin and [l-carnitine] in trials; the NAC-vs-carnitine trial in the Cochrane review was flagged for integrity concerns.
entries.caveats: Many trials come from a few centres; high risk of selection, attrition and reporting bias. The 1.2 g/day trial's 49% vs 1% ovulation contrast is implausibly large.

key_numbers.label: Ovulation, NAC + clomiphene vs placebo + clomiphene

entries.title: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) in PCOS

entries.headline: NR and NMN reliably raise blood NAD+ (NR 1 g/day by about 140%), but most human trials found no gain in insulin sensitivity, muscle mitochondria or muscle function, and NR did not extend mouse lifespan in the ITP.

dose.effective: No dose has a proven clinical benefit; NR 300-1000 mg/day or NMN 250-600 mg/day raise blood NAD+
dose.studied_range: NR 100-2000 mg/day for up to 12 weeks; NMN 250-900 mg/day for up to about 12 weeks
dose.too_much: No serious adverse effects in trials up to NR 2 g/day for 12 weeks; long-term safety beyond months is unknown
dose.timeframe: Blood NAD+ rises within 2 weeks; no clinical effect has been consistently shown at any duration
dose.notes: Blood NAD+ is a marker of intake, not proof of tissue benefit; muscle NAD+ did not rise in some trials. In the US, FDA reversed its 2022 exclusion of NMN from the supplement definition in September 2025.

entries.mechanism: NAD+ is the cofactor for mitochondrial energy metabolism and the substrate of sirtuins and PARPs (DNA repair). NAD+ falls with age in rodent tissues. NR and NMN are vitamin B3 forms that feed NAD+ salvage synthesis. They are not antioxidants, but NAD+/NADH and NADPH balance underlies much of cellular redox control.
entries.interactions: Exercise raises muscle NAD+ synthesis naturally ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]). Plain nicotinamide and niacin also raise NAD+ but were rarely compared head-to-head. The egg-specific evidence is covered on the same page.
entries.caveats: Many trials are small, short, industry-funded and measure surrogate markers. The single strongly positive insulin-sensitivity trial had a large baseline liver-fat imbalance. Positive walking-distance and 'biological age' findings come from one trial that used an online age calculator of uncertain validity.
entries.debate: Supporters cite the Yoshino trial, in which NMN 250 mg/day raised muscle insulin sensitivity in 25 prediabetic women [lon-yoshino2021], a dose-ranging trial showing longer 6-minute walks [lon-yi2023], and anti-inflammatory signals [lon-elhassan2019, lon-brakedal2022]. Critics note the Yoshino groups differed sharply in baseline liver fat [lon-brenner2021], while trials of NR at 1-2 g/day found no improvement in insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial function or body composition [lon-dollerup2018, lon-dollerup2020, lon-remie2020] and a meta-analysis found no benefit for muscle mass or function in older adults [lon-prokopidis2025]. NR also failed to extend lifespan in the rigorous ITP mouse programme [lon-harrison2021]. Several key pharmacokinetic and safety trials were sponsored by the NR manufacturer [lon-trammell2016, lon-conze2019]. Reviews agree the compounds are safe short term and raise NAD+, but benefit is unproven [lon-freeberg2023].

key_numbers.label: Baseline liver fat, NMN vs placebo group

entries.title: NAD+ precursors (NMN, NR)

entries.headline: NAD+ falls in ageing mouse eggs and NMN restored egg quality and fertility in aged mice, but there are no human data on egg quality, pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: No human fertility dose exists; all egg data are from mice.
dose.studied_range: Animal studies only.
dose.too_much: Unknown in pregnancy; safety in early embryos not studied in humans.
dose.notes: Marketed heavily as 'egg rejuvenation'; this is extrapolation from mice.

entries.mechanism: Raises NAD+, a cofactor for sirtuins (e.g. SIRT2) and mitochondrial metabolism; in aged mice restored spindle assembly, mitochondrial function and lowered ROS.
entries.interactions: Shares the mitochondrial-ageing target with [coq10]; sirtuin overlap with [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements].
entries.caveats: Mouse reproductive ageing differs from human (human egg aneuploidy is driven largely by cohesin loss over decades).
entries.title: NMN / NAD+ precursors (NMN, NR)

entries.headline: Shift work is linked to about 17% more cardiovascular events and roughly 10% more type 2 diabetes, and lab studies that flip sleep and meals by 12 hours raise glucose, blood pressure and inflammatory markers within days; night workers show more oxidative damage and lower antioxidant defences, though these data are cross-sectional.

dose.effective: Where possible limit consecutive nights and years of rotating nights; keep the day-sleep room dark and quiet; avoid large meals during the biological night (roughly midnight to 6 am); get bright light during the shift and wear dark glasses on the way home; keep a regular schedule on days off.
dose.studied_range: Lab misalignment for 3-10 days or 3 weeks of 28-hour days; cohorts with up to decades of rotating nights (≥3 night shifts/month).
dose.too_much: CVD risk rose ~7% per additional 5 years of shift work after the first 5 years; CHD risk rose with years of rotating nights and waned after stopping.
dose.timeframe: Glucose and blood-pressure effects within 3 days of misalignment; cardiometabolic disease over years.
dose.notes: Melatonin before day sleep is being tested for DNA repair (borderline result); see [melatonin]. Short or poor sleep often coexists ([short-sleep]).

entries.mechanism: Light at night suppresses melatonin and desynchronises the central clock from peripheral clocks in liver, muscle and fat. Misalignment lowers insulin sensitivity, raises blood pressure and inflammatory cytokines and disturbs clock-controlled antioxidant and DNA-repair genes (including Nrf2 targets and OGG1). Reduced night-time melatonin is proposed to impair repair of 8-oxoguanine.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [short-sleep], [evening-light-exposure] and [late-eating]; worsens [glycemic-control] and weight gain ([excess-adiposity]).
entries.caveats: Shift workers differ from day workers in income, smoking and health (healthy-worker and selection effects). Lower urinary 8-OH-dG during night work is interpreted as reduced repair rather than less damage, which is an assumption. Sperm and egg data are observational: rotating-shift men had ~11% lower sperm concentration and lower fecundity, and women on non-day shifts had 2.3 fewer mature oocytes at IVF, but a large nurse cohort found no effect of shift work on time to pregnancy.
entries.debate: IARC classifies night shift work as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A) [kcc-iarc2019], yet a meta-analysis of 10 prospective studies found no association with breast cancer even after 30 years [kcc-travis2016]. Cardiometabolic associations are consistent [kcc-torquati2018, kcc-gan2015, kcc-gao2020, kcc-vetter2016] and supported by lab misalignment studies [kcc-scheer2009, kcc-morris2015, kcc-morris2016, kcc-buxton2012]. For oxidative stress, a cross-sectional study found worse markers in night workers but no link with social jetlag [kcc-teixeira2019]; the reduced-repair reading of 8-OH-dG [kcc-bhatti2016, kcc-bhatti2017] rests on an untested assumption and the melatonin trial was borderline [kcc-zanif2025]. Fertility: a meta-analysis linked shift work to menstrual disruption and infertility (with very high heterogeneity) [kcc-stocker2014], while nurses showed no effect on time to pregnancy [kcc-gaskins2015].

entries.headline: Daily maximal OTC ibuprofen (1200 mg) halved muscle growth from 8 weeks of strength training in young adults, yet similar doses did not hurt (and seemed to help) older adults; in young men daily ibuprofen produced compensated hypogonadism, and around ovulation NSAIDs can stop the follicle from rupturing.

dose.effective: Occasional use at labelled doses (e.g. ibuprofen 200-400 mg per dose) for pain or inflammation.
dose.studied_range: Ibuprofen 1200 mg/day for 8 weeks (young adults) or 12 weeks (older adults); ibuprofen 1600 mg/day and etoricoxib in women with arthritis.
dose.too_much: Chronic daily high doses are where training and testicular effects appear; GI bleeding, kidney and cardiovascular risks rise with dose and duration.
dose.timeframe: Training effects over 8-12 weeks; hormonal changes in men within weeks; ovulatory effects in the same cycle.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. If you take NSAIDs for a chronic condition and are trying to conceive or training for muscle, discuss timing (avoiding continuous use around ovulation) and alternatives with the prescriber.

entries.mechanism: NSAIDs block COX-1/COX-2 and prostaglandin synthesis. Prostaglandins help drive satellite-cell activity and muscle protein turnover after exercise [med-schoenfeld2012, med-lundberg2018], are needed for follicle rupture at ovulation [med-stone2002], and influence Leydig-cell steroidogenesis; ibuprofen transcriptionally repressed testosterone production in human testis explants [med-kristensen2018].
entries.interactions: May blunt hypertrophy from [resistance-training] in young people (compare [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]). [acetaminophen] is the usual alternative around conception. Fish oil ([omega3-fish]) is sometimes used for inflammatory pain without the ovulation issue.
entries.caveats: Occasional use is unlikely to matter for muscle. The testicular study is short-term with a hormonal (not semen) outcome. Ovulation data come mainly from women with inflammatory arthritis on continuous NSAIDs.
entries.debate: Muscle: maximal OTC ibuprofen blunted hypertrophy and strength in young adults [med-lilja2018], while ibuprofen or acetaminophen enhanced gains in older adults [med-trappe2011]; reviewers suggest age and growth potential explain the split and that occasional use is harmless [med-schoenfeld2012, med-lundberg2018]. Men: ibuprofen induced compensated hypogonadism [med-kristensen2018], but reviews note human semen data on NSAIDs are scarce and effects look smaller than for opioids [med-drobnis2017]. Women: see the egg entry for ovulation and miscarriage debates [med-micu2011, med-li2018, med-chen2024].
entries.title: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, COX-2 inhibitors)

entries.headline: Continuous NSAIDs around ovulation caused luteinized unruptured follicles (the egg is not released) in 35.6% of cycles vs 3.4% untreated in women with arthritis, mostly with the COX-2 drug etoricoxib, while ibuprofen 1600 mg/day caused none; NSAIDs around conception were also linked to miscarriage (aHR 1.89).

dose.effective: Occasional NSAID doses for period pain are not implicated; concern is continuous use spanning ovulation.
dose.studied_range: Continuous periovulatory etoricoxib, diclofenac and ibuprofen 1600 mg/day (arthritis cohort); any NSAID use around conception (miscarriage cohort).
dose.too_much: Continuous periovulatory COX-2 inhibitor use; use for >=15 days around conception (aHR 1.85 for miscarriage).
dose.timeframe: Ovulation returns in the next cycle after stopping.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Women with inflammatory conditions planning pregnancy can discuss avoiding continuous NSAIDs around mid-cycle with their rheumatologist.

entries.mechanism: COX-2-derived prostaglandins drive the enzymatic breakdown of the follicle wall at ovulation; blocking them lets the follicle luteinize without releasing the egg [med-stone2002, med-micu2011].
entries.interactions: [acetaminophen] is the usual alternative around conception; relevant to [endometriosis] and inflammatory arthritis, where NSAIDs are common.
entries.caveats: Ovulation data come from women with inflammatory arthritis and small case series; the miscarriage link is observational and confounded by the reasons for taking NSAIDs.
entries.debate: Ovulation: case series and a monitored-cycle cohort show reversible ovulatory failure [med-smith1996, med-micu2011, med-stone2002], but evidence is limited to small samples. Pregnancy: a prospective cohort linked periconceptional NSAIDs to miscarriage, even versus acetaminophen users [med-li2018], while a 2024 meta-analysis found the miscarriage association non-significant (OR 1.20) but birth defects modestly higher (OR 1.19) [med-chen2024].
entries.title: NSAIDs around ovulation and conception

factors.name: Oily fish & omega-3
aliases: Fish and omega-3 fatty acids (food and fish oil/DHA)

entries.headline: Although EPA/DHA are highly peroxidizable, 3.4 g/day fish oil did not raise plasma F2-isoprostanes or MDA vs oleic or linoleic oils; long-chain omega-3s slightly reduce CHD events and lower triglycerides ~15%.

dose.effective: 1-2 servings of oily fish per week (salmon, sardines, mackerel), baked or poached rather than deep-fried.
dose.studied_range: 0.5 to >5 g/day long-chain omega-3 in RCTs (86 trials, 162,796 people).
dose.too_much: Cochrane found little or no effect of increased omega-3 on serious adverse events.
dose.timeframe: Weeks for triglycerides.
dose.notes: Oxidized (rancid) oils and deep-fried fish deliver dietary lipid oxidation products.

entries.mechanism: EPA/DHA alter membrane composition, eicosanoids and resolvins (anti-inflammatory); their double bonds are substrates for lipid peroxidation, so oxidized products in food or capsules matter more than the fats themselves.
entries.interactions: Eat with polyphenol-rich foods and avoid [oxidized-frying-oils]. TBARS rose with fish oil while F2-isoprostanes did not, illustrating how marker choice changes conclusions.
entries.caveats: Cochrane: little or no effect on all-cause mortality (RR 0.97) or total CV events; modest CHD reduction is low-certainty.
entries.title: Oily fish and omega-3 fats

entries.headline: Fish eaters have higher sperm counts, and a small RCT of 1.5 g/day DHA lowered sperm DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: Oily fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel, herring) 2-3 times a week; if supplementing, about 1-1.5 g/day EPA+DHA.
dose.studied_range: 1.5 g/day DHA for 10 weeks (n=74); fish-oil use on >=60 days in 1679 young men; fish-intake quartiles.
dose.too_much: Above ~3 g/day EPA+DHA raises bleeding risk; choose low-mercury fish.
dose.timeframe: 10-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Swap processed meat for fish: the fish-sperm association was strongest when fish replaced processed red meat.

entries.mechanism: DHA is a key structural lipid of sperm membranes; supplementation raised seminal antioxidant capacity. Paradoxically more PUFA means more oxidisable substrate, so benefit depends on adequate antioxidant status.
entries.interactions: Pairs with [walnuts-nuts] (plant omega-3) and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Supplement trials are small; the Danish fish-oil study is cross-sectional; reviews note heterogeneity.

key_numbers.label: Total count, lowest vs highest fish quartile

entries.title: Fish and omega-3 fatty acids (food and fish oil/DHA)

entries.headline: Each 1% higher serum long-chain omega-3 was associated with 8% higher probability of IVF live birth; in mice omega-3-rich diets preserved egg quality into older age.

dose.effective: Eat lower-mercury fatty fish regularly as part of the diet; studies measured serum levels and dietary share rather than a fixed supplement dose (replacing 1% of energy from saturated fat with long-chain omega-3 was associated with RR 2.37 for live birth).
dose.studied_range: Serum omega-3 4.7% median (IQR 3.8-5.8%) of total fatty acids.
dose.too_much: High-mercury fish (see [heavy-metals]).
dose.timeframe: Adopt within the 3-month preconception window.
dose.notes: Human evidence is from observational IVF cohorts; no adequate RCT on live birth.

entries.mechanism: Incorporation into membranes, anti-inflammatory lipid mediators, possible effects on follicular steroidogenesis.
entries.interactions: Trade-off with [heavy-metals]; part of [mediterranean-diet] and [profertility-diet].
entries.caveats: Small cohort (100 women); mouse data on reproductive ageing have not been replicated in humans.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth probability per +1% serum LC omega-3

entries.title: Omega-3 fats (EPA/DHA from fish)

entries.headline: Regular opioid use, including methadone, lowers testosterone by about 165 ng/dL in men, and reviews report lower semen quality and higher sperm DNA fragmentation; direct human semen studies are few and low quality.

dose.effective: Effects described with regular (daily) use of any opioid, including maintenance methadone.
dose.studied_range: Cross-sectional and cohort studies of chronic users; no dose-response trials.
dose.too_much: Higher doses and long-acting opioids appear worse; tramadol and tapentadol may cause less suppression.
dose.timeframe: Hormonal suppression develops with regular use; semen recovery after tapering is expected over months but is poorly studied.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Never stop opioids or methadone abruptly; tapering or switching must be supervised. Men on opioids with low testosterone who want children should not be treated with testosterone, which further suppresses sperm production.

entries.mechanism: Opioids suppress hypothalamic GnRH and hence LH and testosterone, increase aromatase, and act on opioid receptors in the testis and on sperm themselves [med-drobnis2017, med-bawor2015].
entries.interactions: Testosterone replacement ([testosterone-anabolic-steroids]) for opioid-induced low testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis; [glp1-agonists] raised testosterone without suppressing LH/FSH in obese men, though not studied in opioid users. [cannabis] is covered separately.
entries.caveats: Opioid users differ from controls in smoking, illness and other drug use, so semen findings are heavily confounded.
entries.debate: The testosterone effect is consistent across 17 studies, though heterogeneous and low quality [med-bawor2015]; the semen and DNA-fragmentation effects rest mainly on narrative review of small studies [med-drobnis2017]. No published study was found arguing opioids are harmless to sperm; the debate is about magnitude and reversibility.

key_numbers.label: Testosterone difference, opioid users vs controls

entries.title: Opioid painkillers & methadone

factors.name: Oral nicotinamide (vitamin B3 amide) for skin-cancer prevention

entries.headline: In people with at least two previous non-melanoma skin cancers, nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily cut new skin cancers by 23% in a year (ONTRAC), but it did nothing in immunosuppressed transplant recipients (rate ratio 1.0), and the benefit stops when the pills stop.

dose.effective: 500 mg nicotinamide twice daily, taken continuously, in people at high risk (prior keratinocyte cancers or many actinic keratoses).
dose.studied_range: 500 mg twice daily for 12 months in RCTs; more than 30 days in the Veterans Affairs cohort.
dose.too_much: Well tolerated in trials; a meta-analysis found slightly more digestive side effects. Nicotinic acid (niacin) is a different compound and should not be substituted.
dose.timeframe: Actinic keratoses fell from 3 months; no carry-over benefit 6 months after stopping.
dose.notes: Observational VA data suggest the largest benefit (54% lower risk) when started after a first skin cancer. Topical 5% niacinamide is a separate, cosmetic use with modest effects on spots, redness and fine lines in an industry trial.

entries.mechanism: Nicotinamide is an NAD+ precursor. DNA repair after UV consumes NAD+ and cellular energy; nicotinamide enhances repair of UV-induced DNA damage and reduces UV-induced suppression of skin immunity, the proposed basis for fewer actinic keratoses and keratinocyte cancers.
entries.interactions: An add-on to [sunscreen], not a substitute. Shares NAD+ biology with [nmn-nad]. Unlike antioxidant cocktails ([high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]), it has positive RCT data for skin cancer.
entries.caveats: Evidence applies to high-risk people, not the general public. The pivotal trial lasted 12 months; long-term and melanoma data are lacking. It did not work in organ-transplant recipients, the group with the highest risk.
entries.debate: ONTRAC [skb-chen2015] and a meta-analysis (rate ratio 0.50, with heterogeneity explained by risk of bias) [skb-mainville2022] support use, and some guidelines recommend it. The transplant trial was flatly null [skb-allen2023], although it stopped early with only 158 participants. A large Veterans Affairs cohort found 14% lower risk overall and 54% when started early, but no overall benefit in transplant recipients [skb-breglio2025]; being observational, it is open to confounding by who gets prescribed nicotinamide.

key_numbers.label: Risk reduction when started after first skin cancer (cohort)

entries.headline: Switching to organic food reliably cuts urinary pesticide metabolites within days (e.g. organophosphate metabolites down ~60-95%), but health benefits rest on observational cohorts (25% lower cancer in high organic consumers, absolute difference 0.6%) that are heavily confounded.

dose.effective: If budget allows, prioritize organic versions of produce that typically carry high residues; never eat less fruit and vegetables to avoid pesticides.
dose.studied_range: Organic-diet interventions of about 1 week (urinary biomarkers); cohort comparisons of habitual organic intake.
dose.timeframe: Urinary metabolites fall within days; any disease effect would take years and is unproven.
dose.notes: Glyphosate fell with organic food only in people living away from fields; near farms, spray drift dominates.

entries.mechanism: Lowers dietary intake of organophosphate, pyrethroid and neonicotinoid residues, which in animals induce oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation and endocrine disruption.
entries.interactions: Sperm-specific pesticide data are in [pesticides]; fertility diet patterns that favour low-residue produce are in [profertility-diet]. Overall produce intake ([high-fruit-vegetable-intake]) matters more than its organic status.
entries.caveats: Organic buyers are richer, leaner, more active and eat better diets; cohort adjustment cannot remove all of this. No long-term randomized trial with clinical outcomes exists.
entries.debate: Exposure: organic-diet trials consistently lower urinary pesticide metabolites [env-hyland2019, env-gonzalez2023], though glyphosate fell only modestly [env-hyland2023]. Outcomes: NutriNet-Sante linked high organic intake to 25% lower cancer risk [env-baudry2018] and organic produce substitution to lower postmenopausal breast cancer only [env-berlivet2026], but an accompanying commentary questioned whether this justifies the cost [env-hemler2018]. Reviews split: one reports lower cardiometabolic risk in prospective studies [env-poulia2025], another finds data too contradictory for any conclusion [env-komati2025]. Fertility: high-residue produce was linked to 26% lower IVF live birth in women [env-chiu2018] and lower fertilization in male partners [env-kazemi2025], but a 5,234-woman preconception cohort found no link with natural fecundability and evidence of reverse causation [env-wesselink2020].

factors.name: Other berries & cherries (strawberry, raspberry, chokeberry, blackcurrant, cranberry, cherries)

entries.headline: Berry RCTs pooled together show small improvements in LDL, systolic blood pressure, glucose and TNF-alpha, and anthocyanin foods improve flow-mediated dilation; specific oxidative-stress effects are inconsistent.

dose.effective: About 1 cup (150 g) of mixed berries daily, or ~3 servings per week in cohort data.
dose.studied_range: Juices, powders and whole fruit in 22 RCTs (1251 people); cranberry juice dose-response trials.
dose.timeframe: Acute (hours) for FMD; weeks for lipids and blood pressure.
dose.notes: Chokeberry and blackcurrant are far denser in anthocyanins than strawberries, but higher content has not been shown to give proportionally more benefit.

entries.mechanism: Anthocyanin and ellagitannin metabolites; vitamin C in strawberries.
entries.interactions: Substitutes for [blueberries]; not additive beyond plateau.
entries.caveats: Meta-analytic effects are small (LDL -0.21 mmol/L, SBP -2.7 mmHg) and heterogeneous. Cohort link: >3 servings/week of blueberries plus strawberries tended toward lower MI risk in young women (not significant on its own).
entries.title: Other berries & cherries (strawberry, raspberry, chokeberry, blackcurrant, cranberry, cherries)

factors.name: Other crucifers (kale, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower)

entries.headline: Supply other isothiocyanates and indoles plus fiber and vitamins; in large cohorts the top fifth of crucifer intake had about 22% lower total mortality, and a controlled feeding trial lowered IL-6 by 19%, but oxidative-stress trials are few.

dose.effective: 1-2 servings (80-160 g) most days, some raw or lightly cooked; in a feeding trial a double dose (14 g/kg body weight, about 1 kg/day for a 70 kg adult) lowered IL-6.
dose.studied_range: Cohort intakes; feeding studies 7-14 g/kg body weight per day for 14 days.
dose.too_much: Collards, Brussels sprouts and some Russian kale can contain enough goitrin to reduce thyroid iodine uptake if eaten in very large amounts; with adequate iodine, normal intakes show no adverse thyroid effects.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Same cooking rules as broccoli: chop and wait, eat some raw, steam briefly, or add mustard powder after cooking.

entries.mechanism: Isothiocyanates (Nrf2), indoles, fiber and micronutrients; induction of conjugating enzymes such as UGT1A1 and GSTs.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [broccoli-mature]; benefits from [mustard-seed-myrosinase] when cooked. Part of [high-fruit-vegetable-intake] and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Inverse associations with mortality and cancers are observational and mostly rated weak to suggestive in an umbrella review.

IL-6 change, double-dose crucifer diet vs vegetable-free

entries.headline: Fine particles raise oxidative and inflammatory markers within days; each 10 µg/m³ of short-term PM2.5 was linked to ~1.6% higher malondialdehyde. Individually modest, but it affects everyone in polluted areas.

dose.effective: Aim to live and exercise where annual PM2.5 is near the WHO guideline of 5 µg/m³; on high-pollution days (AQI 'unhealthy') move hard exercise indoors or away from traffic, and use HEPA filtration indoors (see [hepa-air-purifier]).
dose.studied_range: Epidemiology across typical urban levels (roughly 10-100 µg/m³ PM2.5).
dose.too_much: WHO 2021: annual PM2.5 above 5 µg/m³ and peak-season 8-h ozone above 60 µg/m³ are associated with harm; no clear safe threshold.
dose.timeframe: Marker changes within hours to days of exposure.
dose.notes: Distance from heavy traffic and indoor filtration are the practical levers for individuals.

entries.mechanism: Particles carry transition metals and quinones that redox-cycle (Fenton chemistry), activate NADPH oxidase in airway and immune cells, and trigger systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. Ozone directly oxidizes lung-lining lipids and proteins.
entries.interactions: Adds to [tobacco-smoking] and [secondhand-smoke]. Reduced by [hepa-air-purifier].
entries.caveats: Effect sizes on systemic markers are small per unit exposure; most evidence is observational. Air pollution is also linked to poorer semen quality (cross-link to sperm area).
entries.title: Outdoor air pollution (PM2.5, ozone, traffic)

entries.headline: Periods of high air pollution are linked to higher SDF (about +9.7 points across studies) even when other semen measures look normal.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure on high-pollution days (air-quality alerts): avoid exercising beside heavy traffic, use HEPA filtration indoors, keep car windows closed in traffic.
dose.studied_range: Episodes at or above US air-quality standard limits (Teplice, Czech Republic); PM and NO2 in later studies.
dose.timeframe: Effects appear in sperm produced during and after exposure (~2-3 months later).
dose.notes: Individual control is limited; the effect size is a population average.

entries.mechanism: Fine particles and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons cause systemic oxidative stress and inflammation, and some PAH metabolites form DNA adducts in germ cells.
entries.interactions: Additive with [tobacco-smoking], which delivers similar compounds at much higher doses.
entries.caveats: Ecological and repeated-measures studies; exposure misclassification likely.
entries.title: Air pollution

entries.headline: Higher traffic-related NO2 exposure is associated with lower AMH and lower IVF live birth (e.g. OR 0.76 per 0.01 ppm after embryo transfer); effect sizes per person are modest and hard to separate from other urban factors.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure where practical: avoid exercising beside heavy traffic, use HEPA filtration indoors on high-pollution days.
dose.studied_range: Residential and IVF-lab NO2, ozone, PM2.5 and PM10 from monitoring models.
dose.too_much: No safe threshold established; associations were per 0.01 ppm (Legro) or 20 ppb (Gaskins) increase in NO2.
dose.timeframe: Exposure in the ~3 months before IVF was studied.
dose.notes: In one IVF cohort the NO2-live birth association was absent in women taking >= 800 ug/day supplemental folate (hypothesis-generating).

entries.mechanism: Inhaled particles and NO2 cause systemic inflammation and oxidative stress; PAHs adsorbed on particles are ovotoxic.
entries.interactions: Possible modification by [folic-acid]. Overlaps with [tobacco-smoking] (shared PAH exposure).
entries.caveats: All observational, with exposure estimated from home address. Individual control is limited; do not let this become a source of anxiety.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth per +0.01 ppm NO2 (post-transfer)
Lower odds of live birth per +20 ppb NO2 (folate < 800 ug/day)

entries.title: Air pollution (NO2, fine particles)

factors.name: Ovarian reserve testing (AMH, antral follicle count)

entries.headline: AMH and antral follicle count predict how many eggs IVF will retrieve (AUC ~0.78 for poor response) but not natural fertility or egg quality: women 30-44 with low AMH conceived as often as those with normal AMH (84% vs 75% by 12 cycles).

dose.effective: Useful before IVF or egg freezing to plan drug dose and expected egg numbers; not a 'fertility test' for women trying naturally.
dose.studied_range: Low AMH commonly <0.7-1.0 ng/mL (5-7 pmol/L); AFC = follicles 2-10 mm on day 2-5 ultrasound.
dose.too_much: Over-interpretation: a low AMH can push people into rushed IVF or costly egg freezing; a normal AMH can falsely reassure.
dose.timeframe: AMH can be drawn any cycle day; falls with hormonal contraception, so retest off it if results drive decisions.
dose.notes: Neither marker adds to age in predicting IVF live birth.

entries.mechanism: AMH is secreted by small growing follicles, so it tracks the number of follicles (quantity), whereas egg quality (euploidy) is driven mainly by age.
entries.interactions: Interpret with [maternal-age]; a young woman with low AMH has fewer but mostly euploid eggs. Relevant to [egg-freezing-egg] planning.
entries.caveats: Assays differ; AMH is high in PCOS and low on the pill.
entries.debate: A pilot cohort found low AMH cut day-specific fecundability (FR 0.38) [fer-steiner2011], but the larger Time to Conceive cohort and EAGeR found no link [fer-steiner2017, fer-zarek2015]; ASRM now says markers poorly predict reproductive potential independent of age [fer-asrm2020reserve]. For menopause, AMH is the best single predictor but too imprecise for individuals [fer-depmann2016, fer-finkelstein2020].

entries.headline: Overeating by ~1000 kcal/day for 28 days raised urinary F2-isoprostanes and muscle protein carbonyls; 6000 kcal/day caused systemic oxidative stress within 2-3 days; BMI is one of the strongest correlates of urinary isoprostanes in the population.

dose.effective: Eat to energy balance; avoid sustained surplus.
dose.studied_range: +1040 kcal/day for 28 days; ~6000 kcal/day for 1 week.
dose.too_much: Any chronic surplus that drives weight gain, especially visceral fat.
dose.timeframe: Oxidative stress rises within days of overfeeding.
dose.notes: Avoiding a surplus probably outweighs any single 'antioxidant food'.

entries.mechanism: Nutrient excess overloads mitochondrial electron transport, increasing superoxide; adipose tissue oxidative stress carbonylated GLUT4, impairing insulin action; adipose inflammation.
entries.interactions: Reversed by [calorie-restriction]; compounded by [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] and [alcohol].
entries.caveats: Overfeeding studies are short and small; the Framingham link is cross-sectional.

key_numbers.label: Weight gain in 1 week at ~6000 kcal/day
Weight gain after 28 days at +1040 kcal/day

entries.title: Excess calories / overfeeding and weight gain

entries.headline: Very long or excessive exercise spikes oxidative damage markers (F2-isoprostanes up ~75% after a 50 km race; up to 7-fold in overreaching), and decades of high-volume endurance training are linked to more coronary calcium and about 2.5x the odds of atrial fibrillation, yet very fit and very active people still have the lowest mortality.

dose.effective: Train within a load you recover from: performance, sleep, mood and (for women) menstrual cycles should not decline over weeks. Build volume gradually and include easy weeks.
dose.studied_range: 50 km ultramarathon (~6.5 h); 12-week resistance block peaking at 14 t/week; 4-week progressive HIIT overload; lifelong volumes above 2000-3000 MET-min/week (roughly 3.5-5+ h/week of running) in coronary studies; 5+ Vasaloppet 90 km ski races.
dose.too_much: Oxidative/metabolic: daily very hard sessions for weeks impaired mitochondria and glucose tolerance. Cardiac: lifelong >2000 MET-min/week linked to more coronary plaque (OR 3.2); 5+ long-distance ski races to higher AF risk (HR 1.29). Male reproductive: chronic high mileage (~100+ km/week) linked to lower testosterone and semen quality ([endurance-hypogonadism-sperm]).
dose.timeframe: Acute marker spikes resolve within about 24 h after an ultramarathon; overreaching markers stayed high 96 h after sessions; cardiac remodelling and calcification reflect years to decades.
dose.notes: Occasional long events are not a health problem for trained people; chronic under-recovery is. Athletes with palpitations or a high calcium score should see a cardiologist rather than stop exercising.

entries.mechanism: Prolonged high oxygen flux plus muscle damage and immune activation (neutrophil NADPH oxidase, myeloperoxidase) overwhelm glutathione and vitamin E; ROS shift from signal to damage, and mitochondrial respiration falls. Repeated atrial stretch, high vagal tone and inflammation may remodel the atria (AF substrate); repeated haemodynamic and inflammatory stress may promote calcified plaque. Low energy availability suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
entries.interactions: Adequate sleep ([short-sleep]) and energy intake matter for recovery; in women see [vigorous-exercise-low-energy], in men [endurance-hypogonadism-sperm] and [cycling]. High-dose antioxidants do not solve this and may hinder adaptation ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]).
entries.caveats: Most oxidative data come from small samples of athletes. Coronary studies are cross-sectional, mostly in men, and measure plaque, not events. Spikes after an event do not prove long-term harm.
entries.debate: The 'extreme exercise J-curve' is contested. Hypothesis papers argue chronic extreme endurance training may cause atrial fibrosis, coronary calcification and arterial stiffening [exr-okeefe2012], and a Copenhagen cohort reported strenuous joggers' mortality was no better than sedentary people's (HR 1.97) [exr-schnohr2015], but that estimate was extremely imprecise (95% CI 0.48-8.14), and much larger cohorts found no excess mortality at 10x the guideline [exr-arem2015], benefit across all running doses [exr-lee2014] and no upper limit for fitness [exr-mandsager2018, exr-kokkinos2022]. Lifelong athletes do have more coronary plaque [exr-aengevaeren2017, exr-merghani2017, exr-mohlenkamp2008]; whether it is more benign (more calcified) [exr-aengevaeren2017, exr-merghani2017] or not [exr-debosscher2023] is disputed. Outcome data so far are reassuring: high-volume men with high CAC did not die more (HR 0.77, NS) [exr-defina2019], and high volume carried similar coronary-event risk but the lowest mortality [exr-berry2025]; Tour de France riders outlived the general population [exr-marijon2013]. For AF, athletes have higher odds (OR 2.46) [exr-newman2021, exr-andersen2013], and population data suggest a J-shape [exr-morseth2016, exr-morseth2018] with higher risk in very active men but lower in women [exr-kunutsor2021, exr-elliott2020], while moderate activity lowers AF [exr-mozaffarian2008, exr-mishima2021].

entries.title: Overtraining, ultra-endurance and lifelong very high exercise volumes

entries.headline: Independent surveys found 50-83% of fish-oil supplements exceeded oxidation limits while an industry-run survey found most compliant; in RCTs, 7 weeks of heavily oxidized fish oil did not raise isoprostanes or HNE, but it lost the LDL-lowering benefit of fresh oil.

dose.effective: Choose plain capsules over flavoured liquids and children's products; prefer brands that publish third-party oxidation results (peroxide value, anisidine value, TOTOX); store closed, cool and dark, refrigerate liquids after opening, and discard any product that smells or tastes strongly fishy or rancid.
dose.studied_range: RCTs: 8 g/day fish oil (1.6 g EPA+DHA) at peroxide values ~4 vs ~18 meq/kg for 3-7 weeks; 30-day capsule trial in 52 women.
dose.too_much: Voluntary industry limits (GOED): PV ≤5 meq O2/kg, p-anisidine ≤20, TOTOX ≤26; pharmacopoeia limits are looser (PV 10, p-AV 30, TOTOX 50).
dose.timeframe: Oxidation accumulates during storage and after opening; lipid effects seen within 4-7 weeks.
dose.notes: Fishy taste is masked in flavoured products, which also interfere with standard oxidation assays. Eating oily fish avoids the issue ([omega3-fish]).

entries.mechanism: EPA and DHA have five and six double bonds and oxidize readily to hydroperoxides (measured as peroxide value) and then aldehydes and ketones (anisidine value). Oxidized lipids may reduce the omega-3 biological activity and, in theory, add dietary lipid peroxides; in practice, gut and liver metabolism appear to handle the amounts in capsules without raising systemic oxidative-stress markers.
entries.interactions: Relevant to anyone taking fish oil for [omega3-fish] benefits. Antioxidants added by manufacturers (tocopherols, rosemary extract) slow oxidation in the bottle; taking [vitamin-e-supplement] does not fix an already rancid oil.
entries.caveats: Lab methods and limits differ; several surveys had commercial affiliations on both sides. Human trials are short, small and in healthy people.
entries.debate: Albert and colleagues found 83% of New Zealand products over the peroxide limit and most below label EPA/DHA [kcc-albert2015], and a Canadian survey found 50% over limits [kcc-jackowski2015] (most authors were affiliated with an omega-3 company); a US analysis of three top sellers also found excess oxidation [kcc-mason2017]. The industry association GOED re-tested 47 New Zealand products and found 72-86% compliant [kcc-bannenberg2017]. On health effects, oxidized oil did not raise isoprostanes, HNE or CRP [kcc-ottestad2012], but it blunted lipid benefits in two trials [kcc-rundblad2017, kcc-garciahernandez2013].

NZ products compliant with PV limit (industry)

entries.headline: Ozone is a strong oxidant and a regulated air pollutant; 'ozone therapy' is marketed as hormetic, but a Cochrane review could draw no firm conclusions even for its best-studied use (diabetic foot ulcers).

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress.
dose.studied_range: Clinical trials of ozone for wounds and other conditions; small and high risk of bias.
dose.too_much: Inhaled ozone is toxic to the lungs; WHO's peak-season 8-h outdoor guideline is 60 µg/m³.
dose.notes: Intravenous and blood-handling procedures carry their own procedural risks.

entries.mechanism: Ozone reacts with lipids to form ozonides, aldehydes and H2O2; proponents claim this triggers Nrf2-mediated hormesis.
entries.interactions: Opposite of [outdoor-air-pollution] advice: ozone exposure is a recognized harm.
entries.caveats: Hormesis claims are mechanistic; human outcome evidence is poor.
entries.title: Ozone therapy (autohemotherapy, ozone saunas)

entries.headline: SDF rises steadily with age, with a clear jump after 50 (about +12.6 points on average), alongside more new mutations in offspring.

dose.effective: Not modifiable, but relevant to timing: SDF climbs from the 20s with no threshold; effects are largest from about age 45-50.
dose.studied_range: Men aged 20-80.
dose.too_much: Age >=50 associated with the largest SDF increase.
dose.timeframe: Lifelong, gradual.
dose.notes: Older men gain the most from removing other risk factors, because damage is additive. Partner's age matters too: older eggs repair paternal DNA damage less well.

entries.mechanism: Age-related decline in testicular antioxidant defence and mitochondrial function, more oxidative stress, less efficient apoptotic culling of damaged germ cells, and accumulating replication errors in spermatogonial stem cells.
entries.interactions: Combined with older maternal age, high SDF has a bigger effect on embryo quality and miscarriage (see [testicular-sperm-icsi]).
entries.caveats: Age is confounded with weight, illness and varicocele duration; the absolute risk to any one child remains low.
entries.title: Paternal age

entries.headline: In the lab, many lubricants (K-Y, Astroglide, olive oil, saliva) cut sperm motility and some raise DNA fragmentation, while isotonic 'sperm-friendly' gels (e.g. Pre-Seed) do not; yet in two cohorts (6,467 and 296 women) lubricant use did not lower the chance of conceiving.

dose.effective: For natural conception, lubricant choice appears not to matter in cohort data; if wanted, pick an isotonic 'fertility-friendly' product. For semen collection (semen analysis, IUI, IVF), use none or a clinic-approved isotonic lubricant (Pre-Seed did not change motility, ROS or DNA damage in a crossover trial).
dose.studied_range: In vitro lubricant concentrations of 5-12.5% in semen for 10 min to 4 h; cohorts of natural conception attempts.
dose.timeframe: In vitro motility falls within 10-30 minutes of contact.
dose.notes: Saliva is one of the worst performers in vitro. Paraben preservatives at lubricant concentrations raised sperm ROS in vitro.

entries.mechanism: Hyperosmolar, acidic or viscous gels and preservatives (parabens, glycerol) impair motility and can raise mitochondrial ROS and oxidative DNA adducts in vitro; isotonic, pH-matched gels avoid this.
entries.interactions: Relevant mainly when sperm quality is already marginal or for samples collected for assisted reproduction.
entries.caveats: In vitro tests expose washed sperm to lubricant directly, unlike intercourse where most sperm enter cervical mucus quickly. Cohort data rely on self-reported lubricant type; no randomized fertility trial exists.
entries.debate: Lab studies show many lubricants impair motility or chromatin [env-anderson1998, env-agarwal2008, env-tulandi1982, env-mackenzie2019], with 'sperm-friendly' products performing best [env-mowat2014, env-tomlinson2023] and parabens adding oxidative stress [env-samarasinghe2018]. Real-world data disagree with the lab: no lubricant type reduced fecundability in a 6,467-woman cohort [env-mcinerney2018] or in a smaller diary study [env-steiner2012]. Reviews conclude the question is unresolved and that a randomized trial is needed [env-mesen2014, env-gumerova2024].

key_numbers.label: Fecundability ratio, any lubricant in fertile window

entries.title: Personal lubricants and sperm

entries.headline: Farm workers exposed to organophosphate/carbamate pesticides have higher SDF; high-residue produce seems to cancel the benefit of fruit and vegetables.

dose.effective: Use protective equipment for occupational spraying; wash produce; choose lower-residue or organic options for high-residue items if affordable.
dose.studied_range: Occupational cholinesterase-inhibiting exposure; dietary residues by produce type.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Do not cut fruit and vegetables to avoid pesticides; the net effect of produce is positive or neutral.

entries.mechanism: Organophosphates generate ROS and lipid peroxidation in testis and disrupt the HPG axis.
entries.interactions: See [high-fruit-vegetable-intake].
entries.caveats: Small cross-sectional occupational studies; dietary findings come from one cohort.
entries.title: Pesticides (occupational and dietary)

entries.headline: PFAS stay in blood for years (half-lives 2.7-5.3 years) and are linked to weaker vaccine responses, higher cholesterol, lower birth weight and some cancers; NASEM advises testing likely-exposed people with extra screening above 2 and 20 ng/mL, and regular plasma or blood donation measurably lowered serum PFOS in an RCT.

dose.effective: If likely exposed (contaminated water, firefighting foam, PFAS work), ask for a serum test: NASEM sum of 7 PFAS <2 ng/mL = usual care; 2-20 ng/mL = cut exposure plus lipid screening; >20 ng/mL = also thyroid testing and kidney/testicular cancer and ulcerative colitis checks. Cut intake by treating contaminated tap water ([water-filtration]). To speed elimination: plasma donation every 6 weeks for 12 months lowered PFOS by 2.9 ng/mL (blood every 12 weeks: 1.1 ng/mL); prescription cholestyramine 4 g three times daily for 12 weeks lowered PFOS by 60% in highly exposed adults.
dose.studied_range: Donation RCT in firefighters with PFOS >=5 ng/mL; cholestyramine trials in residents with PFOS ~50-190 ng/mL.
dose.too_much: EFSA tolerable weekly intake: 4.4 ng/kg body weight per week for PFOA+PFNA+PFHxS+PFOS; NASEM serum sum >20 ng/mL = increased risk.
dose.timeframe: Years: after clean water was supplied, serum PFHxS, PFOS and PFOA fell only 13%, 20% and 26% per year.
dose.notes: Donate blood or plasma only if eligible and for its own sake; PFAS reduction is a side benefit. Bile-acid sequestrants have GI side effects and interfere with absorption of other drugs; trials are small and only in highly exposed people. Women eliminate some PFAS faster (menstruation, pregnancy, breastfeeding).

entries.mechanism: PFAS bind serum albumin and liver fatty-acid proteins, activate PPAR-alpha and other nuclear receptors, alter lipid and bile-acid handling, and in cells and animals raise ROS and modulate NF-kB and immune cell signalling. Human oxidative-stress marker data are mixed.
entries.interactions: Blood or plasma donation also lowers iron stores (relevant to [iron-excess]). Bile-acid sequestrants block enterohepatic recycling of PFAS. Shares food-contact and water routes with [plastics-chemicals].
entries.caveats: Most health links are observational; kidney function, menstruation, pregnancy and breastfeeding all change serum PFAS and can create reverse-causation artefacts. Elimination studies measure blood levels, not health outcomes.
entries.debate: Clinical relevance: NASEM concluded PFAS are linked to cancers, thyroid dysfunction, cholesterol changes and lower birth weight and set serum action levels [env-nasem2022]; EFSA based its intake limit on reduced vaccine antibodies in children [env-efsa2020, env-grandjean2012]. On cholesterol, a 2025 bias-focused meta-analysis found positive pooled links driven by cross-sectional studies, with longitudinal estimates near null [env-hussey2025]. Oxidative stress: PFOS tracked higher 8-isoprostane in pregnancy [env-siwakoti2024] and 8-OHdG in adults [env-lin2020], but a meta-analysis found PFAS-oxidative stress associations mostly inconsistent [env-chen2023]. Elimination: donation lowers PFOS [env-gasiorowski2022] and sequestrants lower it more [env-moller2024, env-andersson2025], but no study shows a health benefit, and the firefighter treatment-program data are uncontrolled [env-delaere2025]. A fibre trial hinted at falling long-chain PFAS but only in a secondary analysis [env-schlezinger2025].

entries.title: PFAS ('forever chemicals')

entries.headline: A Singapore preconception cohort found 5-10% lower fecundability per quartile of some PFAS and Chinese clinic studies link PFAS to PCOS and poorer embryo quality, but older time-to-pregnancy links were likely reverse causation, and PFAS did not track AMH or follicle counts.

dose.effective: No fertility intervention tested. For likely-exposed women, see [pfas] (testing, water filtration). Plasma donation and bile-acid sequestrants lower serum PFAS but have not been studied for fertility and sequestrants are not tested in pregnancy planning.
dose.studied_range: Plasma PFOS ~4-13 ng/mL in fertility cohorts; follicular fluid PFOA ~5-7 ng/mL.
dose.too_much: NASEM serum sum >20 ng/mL = increased general health risk.
dose.timeframe: Years (PFAS half-lives 2.7-5.3 years).
dose.notes: PFAS cross readily into follicular fluid (65-92% of serum levels). Pregnancy and breastfeeding lower a woman's PFAS, which is why parity confounds time-to-pregnancy studies.

entries.mechanism: PFAS in follicular fluid may disrupt steroidogenesis, PPAR signalling and follicular lipid metabolism; one IVF study linked PFOA to altered follicular sphingolipids and organonitrogen metabolites.
entries.interactions: Coexists with other persistent pollutants; in one ovarian-tissue study organochlorines, not PFAS, tracked a smaller ovarian reserve. Women's PFAS falls with each pregnancy and breastfeeding period.
entries.caveats: Mostly case-control or single-centre clinic studies; PCOS itself alters menstruation and therefore PFAS excretion (reverse causation).
entries.debate: Time to pregnancy: the Danish birth cohort found longer TTP with PFOS/PFOA [env-fei2009], but the link appeared only in parous women in Norway [env-whitworth2012], the original authors raised reverse causation [env-fei2012], and a systematic review judged it most likely not causal [env-bach2016]. A preconception cohort that avoids this bias still found modestly lower fecundability [env-cohen2023]. PCOS: a mixture of PFAS, led by newer alternatives, was associated with PCOS [env-zhan2023], whereas an earlier study found only one congener associated [env-wangw2019]. IVF: follicular PFOA tracked poorer embryo quality [env-xu2025], but another IVF study found no clear outcome pattern [env-hong2022]; PFAS were not associated with AMH or follicle density in ovarian tissue [env-bjorvang2021].

entries.title: PFAS and female fertility

entries.headline: Pooled data link PFAS to slightly lower progressive motility and more sperm DNA fragmentation (r = 0.14 across 14 studies), but the effects are small, individual studies disagree, and a 604-man study found no consistent SDF effect.

dose.effective: No sperm-specific intervention tested. If exposure is likely, see [pfas] for testing and exposure reduction.
dose.studied_range: General-population serum PFOS ~5-25 ng/mL; occupational groups higher.
dose.too_much: NASEM serum sum >20 ng/mL = increased general health risk (not a fertility-specific threshold).
dose.timeframe: PFAS half-lives are years, so serum (and any sperm effect) changes slowly.
dose.notes: Effect sizes are correlations of about 0.06-0.14, i.e. small at the individual level.

entries.mechanism: PFAS reach the testis and seminal plasma; in animals they lower testosterone, disrupt Sertoli and Leydig cells and raise oxidative stress.
entries.interactions: Occurs alongside other persistent pollutants (PCBs, organochlorines) that confound associations; see [plastics-chemicals] for short-lived endocrine disruptors.
entries.caveats: Cross-sectional, single-sample designs; many congener-by-endpoint tests invite chance findings.
entries.debate: A 2026 meta-analysis found consistent inverse links with motility and DNA integrity [env-dinisio2026] and an earlier one found PFOA/PFNA linked to lower progressive motility [env-wangh2023a]; Danish young men with high PFOS+PFOA had fewer normal sperm [env-joensen2009]. Against this, a 604-man study found no consistent link with SCSA DNA fragmentation [env-specht2012], the LIFE study found associations in varying directions [env-louis2015], and a systematic review found little consistent evidence in men [env-bach2016].

entries.headline: PGT-A does not raise live birth per woman and can lower it: in a 1212-woman NEJM trial cumulative live birth was 77.2% with PGT-A vs 81.8% without; it lowers miscarriage per transfer (HFEA green for that) but HFEA rates it red for having a baby, and it roughly doubles IVF cost.

dose.effective: Not recommended routinely (ESHRE, HFEA). Distinct from PGT-M/PGT-SR for known genetic conditions, which are not add-ons.
dose.studied_range: Trophectoderm biopsy of day 5-6 blastocysts with NGS; older trials used day-3 or polar-body biopsy.
dose.too_much: Embryos labelled aneuploid or mosaic may be discarded although some could make healthy babies; some couples end with no transferable embryo.
dose.timeframe: Adds a freeze-all cycle and weeks of delay before transfer.
dose.notes: Per-transfer success looks higher because poor embryos are filtered out before transfer; the fair comparison is live birth per started cycle.

entries.mechanism: Selects embryos without whole-chromosome errors, which rise steeply with maternal age because of cohesin loss in eggs (see [maternal-age]). It cannot create euploid embryos, only choose among those already made, and a 5-10-cell biopsy may misrepresent the embryo (mosaicism).
entries.interactions: Most relevant with advanced [maternal-age]; does not fix egg quality. Combining with [time-lapse-egg] or [assisted-hatching-egg] adds nothing proven.
entries.caveats: Aneuploid calls are very accurate at predicting failure [fer-tiegs2021], which is why the debate is about efficacy per woman, not about test validity.
entries.debate: Supporters cite fewer miscarriages and shorter time to pregnancy in older women (Rubio RCT: miscarriage 2.7% vs 39%, delivery per first transfer 52.9% vs 24.2%) and the STAR post hoc gain at 35-40 [fer-rubio2017, fer-munne2019], plus near-perfect predictive value of aneuploid calls [fer-tiegs2021]. Critics point to unchanged or lower cumulative live birth [fer-yan2021, fer-munne2019, fer-cornelisse2020, fer-iwarsson2026], viable mosaic embryos being discarded (the mosaic study was run by a PGT company) [fer-capalbo2021], and per-transfer reporting that hides losses [fer-paulson2019]. HFEA red for live birth, green for miscarriage [fer-hfea2026]; ESHRE: not for routine use [fer-eshre2023addons].

factors.name: Plastics chemicals (phthalates, BPA)
aliases: Endocrine disruptors: phthalates and bisphenol A

entries.headline: Cutting canned and plastic-packaged food can halve urinary BPA and DEHP within 3 days (a can of soup a day raised urinary BPA more than 10-fold), but one randomized diet trial backfired on contaminated food, and no trial shows a health or fertility benefit from lowering exposure.

dose.effective: Biggest proven exposure levers: avoid canned foods and drinks (canned soup daily: urinary BPA 20.8 vs 1.1 ug/L), avoid drinking from polycarbonate bottles (+69% BPA in 1 week), eat mostly fresh, minimally packaged food (3 days: BPA -66%, DEHP metabolites -53 to -56%), and use phthalate/paraben-free personal-care products (3 days: MEP -27%, methyl/propyl paraben ~-44%).
dose.studied_range: Exposure-reduction interventions lasting 1 meal to 1 week; outcomes are urinary metabolites only.
dose.too_much: EFSA (2023) tolerable daily intake for BPA: 0.2 ng/kg body weight per day (cut 20,000-fold from 4 ug/kg); EFSA estimates average diets exceed it 100-1000-fold. Other agencies (BfR, FDA) have not adopted this value.
dose.timeframe: BPA and phthalates clear within hours to a day (canned-meal BPA peaks at ~4 h and is back to baseline by 24 h), so changes show in urine within 1-3 days; any sperm effect would need ~3 months.
dose.notes: 'BPA-free' often means BPS or BPF, which show similar hormonal activity in lab and animal studies (regrettable substitution). Hidden contamination of foods and spices can undo careful swaps.

entries.mechanism: Bisphenols bind estrogen receptors and phthalate metabolites act anti-androgenically; in cells and animals both raise mitochondrial ROS and NADPH oxidase activity and cause lipid peroxidation. In pregnant women, urinary phthalate metabolites track urinary 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane.
entries.interactions: Overlaps heavily with ultra-processed and packaged diets, so diet quality ([mediterranean-diet]) confounds most associations. Shares sources with [microplastics] (heated plastic food contact). Persistent chemicals are covered separately under [pfas].
entries.caveats: Single spot-urine samples misclassify exposure to short-lived chemicals. Exposure-reduction studies are tiny (20-100 people) and short, and none measured a health outcome. Fertility associations are inconsistent and sometimes point in opposite directions within the same cohort.
entries.debate: Exposure reduction: a fresh-food intervention cut BPA and DEHP by half or more [env-rudel2011], but a randomized catered-diet trial saw DEHP rise about 25-fold because coriander and milk were contaminated, arguing that individual action is limited without regulation [env-sathyanarayana2013]. Safe dose: EFSA cut the BPA TDI 20,000-fold on immune endpoints [env-efsa2023], a move endorsed by academic endocrinologists who criticize the German BfR and US FDA for keeping higher limits [env-vomsaal2024]. Semen: one meta-analysis found BPA's link to motility vanished after publication-bias correction [env-castellini2022], while another found small falls in concentration and count [env-lu2024]; for phthalates only MBP, MBzP and semen DEHP tracked lower concentration [env-wangh2023b]. Fecundity: one cohort found bisphenols and phthalates prolonged time to pregnancy [env-charifson2024], while another found several phthalates linked to shorter time to pregnancy [env-blaauwendraad2025]. IVF: BPA is linked to lower fertilization and embryo quality but not to pregnancy rates [env-yuan2025]. Substitutes: BPS/BPF carry similar hazard signals with large data gaps [env-denbraversewradj2020, env-mhaoutykodja2024].

entries.title: Plastic-associated chemicals (phthalates, bisphenols)

entries.headline: Higher urinary phthalate and BPA levels are linked to more sperm DNA damage (about 10-18% more Comet damage per interquartile rise).

dose.effective: Practical reduction: avoid heating food in plastic, prefer glass/steel containers, eat less ultra-processed and canned food, choose fragrance-free personal care products.
dose.studied_range: General-population urinary levels (median BPA 1.3 ng/mL).
dose.timeframe: Urinary levels fall within days; any sperm effect would take ~3 months.
dose.notes: No intervention trial shows that lowering exposure improves SDF.

entries.mechanism: Anti-androgenic and estrogenic receptor effects plus induction of oxidative stress in germ cells.
entries.interactions: Exposure falls naturally with a less processed diet ([mediterranean-diet]).
entries.caveats: Single-centre cross-sectional studies with spot urine samples; inconsistent replication.

entries.title: Endocrine disruptors: phthalates and bisphenol A

entries.headline: In the EARTH IVF cohort, women in the top quartile of urinary DEHP metabolites had fewer eggs and about 19 percentage points lower live birth per cycle than the bottom quartile.

dose.effective: Lower exposure: eat more fresh, less ultra-processed and packaged food; avoid heating food in plastic; choose fragrance-free personal-care products.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of urinary phthalate metabolites (spot urine samples).
dose.too_much: No established threshold; risk scaled with quartile.
dose.timeframe: Urinary levels vary day to day, reflecting recent exposure; follicles develop over ~3 months, so reduce exposure across that window.
dose.notes: Single EARTH cohort with 256 women; replication is limited.

entries.mechanism: Anti-androgenic and endocrine-disrupting effects on granulosa-cell steroidogenesis; animal studies show follicular oxidative stress and atresia.
entries.interactions: Often co-occurs with [plastics-chemicals] exposure from packaged food.
entries.caveats: Urine levels fluctuate day to day, so single samples misclassify exposure; confounding by diet quality is possible.

entries.title: Phthalates (DEHP and related plasticizers)

entries.headline: Each log-unit increase in urinary BPA was associated with 12% fewer eggs retrieved in IVF; BPA causes egg aneuploidy in animals, but human outcome data are small and inconsistent.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure: fewer canned foods, avoid polycarbonate containers and heating food in plastic, minimise thermal-paper receipts.
dose.studied_range: Urinary BPA < 0.4 to 25.5 ug/L.
dose.timeframe: Reduce exposure across the ~3-month follicle-growth window.
dose.notes: Human data come from small IVF cohorts at one clinic.

entries.mechanism: Estrogen-receptor activity; in animals disrupts meiotic spindle formation and steroidogenesis and increases oxidative stress.
entries.interactions: [plastics-chemicals] come from similar sources.
entries.caveats: Small cohorts (84 women); human evidence is not strong enough to quantify live-birth effects.

entries.title: Bisphenol A (BPA)

entries.headline: PCOS carries measurable systemic oxidative stress (malondialdehyde about 47% higher, glutathione about 50% lower than controls, independent of weight); fertility problems are mainly ovulatory, and IVF outcomes are worse when PCOS coexists with obesity.

dose.effective: Management per the 2023 international guideline: healthy lifestyle first, then evidence-based medical and fertility treatment. In overweight women, losing 5% or more of body weight improved insulin, SHBG and cycles in an early study.
dose.studied_range: Weight loss studies 5-22% of body weight; lifestyle RCTs mostly 3-12 months.
dose.timeframe: Metabolic and ovulatory improvement over 3-6 months of weight loss.
dose.notes: Insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism, not oocytes per se, drive most of the problem; egg quality in lean, ovulating PCOS is often normal.

entries.mechanism: Hyperinsulinaemia and hyperandrogenism alter the follicular environment; chronic low-grade inflammation and lower antioxidant reserve (glutathione, paraoxonase-1) increase lipid peroxidation. Obesity adds lipotoxicity and further insulin resistance.
entries.interactions: Strongly interacts with [excess-adiposity] and [glycemic-control]; supplements studied mainly in PCOS: [myo-inositol], [n-acetylcysteine]. Weight loss is covered by [weight-loss].
entries.caveats: Raised oxidative markers in blood do not prove oxidative damage to eggs is the cause of infertility in PCOS; most infertility is anovulation, which is treatable. Lifestyle RCTs in PCOS have not reported live birth (Cochrane 2019 found none).
entries.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

entries.headline: An oral fern extract that modestly raises the skin's tolerance to UV: in 9 volunteers a single 7.5 mg/kg dose reduced sunburn redness, sunburn cells and DNA dimers, but the evidence is small trials, and there are no large trials showing less photoaging or fewer skin cancers.

dose.effective: No established dose; the key photoprotection study used a single 7.5 mg/kg dose (about 500 mg for a 70 kg adult) before UV exposure.
dose.studied_range: Single pre-exposure doses in photoprotection studies; daily use as an adjunct in small trials for melasma, vitiligo, polymorphous light eruption and atopic dermatitis.
dose.too_much: No safety signal in reviews; long-term data are limited.
dose.timeframe: Hours (taken before sun exposure).
dose.notes: An adjunct only; it does not replace [sunscreen].

entries.mechanism: The extract's polyphenols are thought to scavenge ROS; in human skin biopsies it reduced UV-induced CPDs, sunburn cells and mast-cell infiltration, with a trend toward preserved Langerhans cells.
entries.interactions: Similar systemic-photoprotection niche to dietary carotenoids ([tomatoes-lycopene]); neither approaches the protection of [sunscreen].
entries.caveats: The landmark study had 9 participants without a placebo group. Effect sizes are small (a modest rise in the dose needed to burn).
entries.debate: A 2025 systematic review describes strong therapeutic potential across many skin conditions [skb-zundell2025], but its evidence base is 21 small studies spread over six conditions; the core photoprotection data come from tiny within-person studies [skb-middelkamphup2004]. No independent large RCT has tested hard outcomes.
entries.title: Polypodium leucotomos extract (oral fern extract)

entries.headline: In one 70-man RCT, pomegranate-fruit extract plus galangal tablets for 3 months raised the total number of motile sperm by 62%, vs 20% on placebo; it has not been replicated and pregnancy was not measured.

dose.effective: Daily standardised pomegranate-extract plus galangal tablets (Punalpin) for 3 months.
dose.studied_range: 3 months.
dose.timeframe: About 3 months (one spermatogenic cycle plus transit).
dose.notes: The extract was standardised for punicalagins, punicalin and ellagic acid; effect of pomegranate alone is unknown.

entries.mechanism: Not established in humans; candidates are ellagitannin-derived metabolites (urolithins, metabotype-dependent) and galangal's acetoxychavicol acetate.
entries.interactions: Overlaps [male-antioxidant-combination]. Urolithin production varies by metabotype (see [urolithin-a]).
entries.caveats: Single trial; participants were men whose semen did not meet sperm-bank standards, not infertile couples; no pregnancy or DNA-fragmentation outcomes.

entries.title: Pomegranate fruit extract (with galangal)

entries.headline: A famous 10-patient study reported dramatic falls in LDL oxidation and carotid thickness, but an 18-month RCT in 289 people found no effect on carotid progression and a meta-analysis found no lipid effect.

dose.effective: Not established; 240 mL/day was ineffective for carotid progression overall.
dose.studied_range: 50-240 mL/day for up to 3 years.
dose.too_much: Juice adds free sugar.
dose.notes: Punicalagins are converted by gut bacteria to urolithins, but people differ: across trials 25-80% make only urolithin A, 10-50% also make isourolithin A/urolithin B, and 5-25% make none, and the mix shifts with age. Purified urolithin A bypasses this (see [urolithin-a]).

entries.mechanism: Ellagitannins (punicalagin) -> ellagic acid -> urolithins; raised paraoxonase-1 in the small study.
entries.interactions: Ellagitannin source like [walnuts-nuts] and [blackberries]; downstream metabolite evidence is under [urolithin-a]. A pomegranate-plus-galangal extract increased motile sperm in one RCT (see [pomegranate-extract-sperm]).
entries.caveats: Industry-funded small studies drove early enthusiasm; possible benefit only in exploratory subgroups with high oxidative stress.

entries.headline: IARC classifies processed meat as carcinogenic (Group 1) and red meat as probably carcinogenic (2A); heme iron catalyses lipid peroxidation and N-nitroso compound formation in the gut, with fecal N-nitroso compounds rising linearly with red-meat intake.

dose.effective: Keep processed meat rare and red meat to a few modest portions per week.
dose.studied_range: 0-420 g/day red meat in controlled feeding (dose-response for fecal N-nitroso compounds); white meat at 420-600 g/day had no effect.
dose.too_much: Each 50 g/day of processed meat raised colorectal cancer risk ~18% (IARC). Highest vs lowest heme intake: colon cancer RR 1.18.
dose.timeframe: Fecal markers change within days; cancer risk over years.
dose.notes: Meat eaten with red-wine polyphenols or polyphenol-rich spices produced less postprandial MDA in animal and human meal studies.

entries.mechanism: Heme iron catalyses peroxidation of dietary PUFA in the stomach and colon, producing malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal, and promotes endogenous N-nitrosation; processed meats add nitrite and pre-formed nitrosamines; high-heat cooking adds HCAs and PAHs.
entries.interactions: Worse with [high-temperature-cooking]; partly offset by [herbs-spices] and polyphenol-rich foods eaten in the same meal.
entries.caveats: Oxidative mechanism evidence is strongest for the gut lumen; effects on systemic markers are less studied. For sperm, only processed meat (not unprocessed red meat) has been linked to worse semen; see [unprocessed-red-meat].

entries.headline: Processed meat is the meat signal for sperm: men eating the most had fewer normal-shaped sperm (1.7 points) and, in young men, about 78 million fewer sperm per ejaculate. Unprocessed red meat was not linked to worse semen.

dose.effective: Keep processed meat (bacon, ham, sausages, deli meats) to less than one serving a week; replace with fish or legumes.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of intake in 155 clinic patients.
dose.too_much: Highest quartile associated with worse morphology.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.

entries.mechanism: Heme iron, nitrites and advanced glycation/lipoxidation products may increase oxidative stress; may also mark a Western diet.
entries.interactions: Replace with [omega3-fish] or unprocessed meat/poultry; see [unprocessed-red-meat].
entries.caveats: Observational only, small effects, and confounding by overall diet and abstinence time is possible (the young-men study noted heavy meat eaters also had shorter abstinence). The finding is specific to processed meat; see [unprocessed-red-meat].

entries.headline: Fasts of 2-10+ days push ketones into the millimolar range and lowered lipid peroxidation (TBARS) in uncontrolled cohorts, but half or more of the weight lost is lean tissue and water, uric acid rises 100-200 umol/L, and no controlled trial shows lasting oxidative stress or health benefit beyond weight loss.

dose.effective: No proven effective dose. Medically supervised Buchinger-type fasts of 5-10 days at 200-250 kcal/day, or water-only fasts, have been studied; a refeeding period of at least half the fast length is used in clinics.
dose.studied_range: 2-21 days, water-only or 75-250 kcal/day, usually 1-2 times per year.
dose.too_much: Beyond ~5 days of little or no intake, refeeding-syndrome criteria apply (NICE: >5 days plus another risk factor, or >10 days alone). Risks: hyponatraemia, orthostatic hypotension, arrhythmia, gout and urate stones, gallstones, lean-mass loss. Never unsupervised with diabetes medication, low BMI, eating disorder, pregnancy, gout or kidney disease.
dose.timeframe: Ketosis from day 2-4; systemic proteome changes appear only after ~3 days; most weight is regained within weeks.
dose.notes: Ketonaemia reaches roughly 2-4 mmol/L by day 3-5 in many adults (higher in lean people and with exercise) and keeps rising for ~2-3 weeks.

entries.mechanism: Glycogen depletion (largely by ~24-42 h), lipolysis and ketogenesis; insulin and IGF-1 fall, growth hormone rises ~5-fold. Beta-hydroxybutyrate signalling (HDAC inhibition) and lower substrate flux may reduce ROS production; the rise in uric acid, an antioxidant, inflates total antioxidant capacity readings.
entries.interactions: Exercise during a fast speeds ketosis; light activity was used to protect muscle in the 10-day trial. Does not replace sustained [calorie-restriction] or [weight-loss]. Avoid stacking with [vigorous-exercise-low-energy] in women.
entries.caveats: Evidence comes mostly from clinic cohorts run by fasting-clinic staff, without control groups. 'Autophagy peaks at day 2-3' is extrapolated from mice; human muscle and blood studies show ambiguous flux changes. TAC increases partly reflect uric acid.
