entries.title: Prolonged (multi-day) fasting

entries.headline: The most sedentary quarter of adults had about 2.6x the mortality of the least sedentary in accelerometer studies, and walking breaks in sitting cut post-meal glucose and insulin by a moderate amount (SMD about -0.5); direct evidence that sitting itself raises oxidative stress is weak.

dose.effective: Break up sitting every 20-30 min with 2-5 min of light walking (better than just standing); aim to replace sitting with any movement. About 60-75 min/day of moderate activity offset the extra mortality of sitting 8+ h/day.
dose.studied_range: Acute crossover trials: 2-min light or moderate walking every 20-30 min over 5-9 h; cohorts: under 4 to over 8 h/day sitting.
dose.too_much: More than 8 h/day sitting combined with low activity; more than 20 h/week TV was linked to 44% lower sperm concentration in young men.
dose.timeframe: Glucose and insulin effects within a single day; insulin resistance appears within days of bed rest or step reduction.
dose.notes: Even high activity only attenuated, not eliminated, the risk tied to heavy TV viewing, perhaps because TV time travels with snacking and other habits.

entries.mechanism: Inactive muscle takes up little glucose (less GLUT4 translocation, lower lipoprotein lipase activity); repeated post-meal glucose and triglyceride spikes drive mitochondrial superoxide and NADPH oxidase activity. Over time, lost fitness, fat gain and inflammation add chronic ROS sources. Short-term disuse lowers mitochondrial content without raising muscle H2O2.
entries.interactions: Countered by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [post-meal-walking] and [exercise-snacks]; worsens [glycemic-control] and [excess-adiposity]. In men, prolonged sitting may add scrotal heat ([everyday-scrotal-heat]).
entries.caveats: Bed rest cut insulin sensitivity 42% but did not raise mitochondrial H2O2 or oxidative markers, so 'sitting causes oxidative stress' is not established directly; the one oxidative crossover study used a crude marker (d-ROMs) and only showed trends. Sedentary-time associations with mortality are rated weak in umbrella reviews and are hard to separate from low activity and poor health.
entries.debate: Whether sitting is an independent risk or mainly a marker of low activity is debated. A harmonised meta-analysis of 1 million adults found 60-75 min/day of moderate activity eliminated the excess mortality of high sitting time (but not of high TV time) [exr-ekelund2016]; accelerometer data still show a steep gradient for sedentary time [exr-ekelund2019], while an umbrella review graded the sedentary-mortality evidence as weak [exr-rahmati2025]. For metabolism, activity breaks lower glucose and insulin versus continuous sitting [exr-loh2020, exr-dunstan2012, exr-buffey2022], but when energy expenditure was matched the advantage of breaks over a single continuous bout was small for glucose and absent for insulin and triglycerides [exr-loh2020]. Direct oxidative effects are unproven: disuse lowered mitochondrial capacity without increasing muscle H2O2 [exr-dirks2020, exr-edwards2021], and the only sitting/oxidative crossover trial was small with borderline results [exr-takahashi2015].

entries.headline: Two or more years of PPIs is linked to B12 deficiency (OR 1.65), iron deficiency (OR 2.49) and low magnesium (RR 1.43) in observational studies, but the 17,598-person COMPASS RCT found no excess harm over 3 years except slightly more gut infections.

dose.effective: As prescribed (e.g. omeprazole 20-40 mg/day, pantoprazole 40 mg/day), ideally at the lowest effective dose and for a defined duration.
dose.studied_range: Pantoprazole 40 mg/day for ~3 years (COMPASS); >=2 years' supply in case-control studies.
dose.too_much: Associations strengthen above ~1.5 pills/day and with longer use (iron deficiency OR 4.27 at >1.5 pills/day for >=10 years).
dose.timeframe: Nutrient effects appear over years; iron-deficiency association weakens after stopping.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Ask the prescriber how to step down rather than stopping on your own. On long-term use, ask whether B12, iron (ferritin) and magnesium checks make sense.

entries.mechanism: Gastric acid frees food-bound B12 and keeps non-heme iron soluble, so chronic acid suppression reduces their absorption; magnesium loss reflects impaired intestinal uptake. Higher gastric pH also lets oral bacteria colonize the gut and reduces microbial diversity [med-imhann2016].
entries.interactions: Adds to the B12 drain of [metformin]. Iron deficiency interacts with [iron-excess] advice (supplementing iron when deficient is different from excess). Microbiome shifts overlap [antibiotics-microbiome] and may affect polyphenol metabolism ([dietary-fiber-microbiome]).
entries.caveats: Observational associations are prone to confounding by indication and illness; the RCT used pantoprazole in older adults with cardiovascular disease and did not measure nutrient levels.
entries.debate: Harms: large case-control studies link long-term PPIs to B12 and iron deficiency [med-lam2013, med-lam2017] and a meta-analysis to hypomagnesemia [med-cheungpasitporn2015]; a B12 meta-analysis found only a modest, heterogeneous association with no difference in serum B12 in most studies [med-choudhury2023], and the COMPASS RCT found no excess harms besides enteric infection [med-moayyedi2019]. Sperm: a Dutch registry linked PPI use 6-12 months earlier to threefold odds of low motile sperm count [med-huijgen2016], while a US clinic study of 248 users found no effect [med-keihani2018b].
entries.title: Proton-pump inhibitors & acid suppressants

entries.headline: Chronic stress and depression are associated with higher oxidative damage markers (depression: F2-isoprostanes effect size ~0.5), but causality and the size of any modifiable effect are uncertain.

dose.effective: Treat depression and anxiety with proven methods (therapy, medication when indicated, exercise, sleep); reduce chronic stressors where possible.
dose.studied_range: Cross-sectional comparisons of high vs low perceived stress and depressed vs non-depressed groups.
dose.timeframe: Unknown for oxidative markers.
dose.notes: Exercise and sleep improvements are the best-evidenced stress interventions that also affect oxidative stress.

entries.mechanism: Chronic stress raises cortisol and catecholamines, increases metabolic rate and inflammatory signalling (NF-kB), and is associated with lower telomerase activity; catecholamine auto-oxidation produces ROS.
entries.interactions: Stress worsens [short-sleep], drinking ([alcohol]), smoking and eating, which are likely bigger oxidative contributors than stress itself.
entries.caveats: The famous Epel 2004 study was cross-sectional in 58 women; it shows association, not cause. Confounding by health behaviours is likely in most studies.
entries.title: Chronic psychological stress and depression

entries.headline: A high salivary alpha-amylase stress marker was linked to 29% lower fecundability in one cohort, but a meta-analysis of 3583 IVF patients found pre-treatment anxiety or depression did not affect pregnancy rates.

dose.effective: Stress management for wellbeing (counselling, CBT, mindfulness, exercise); not proven to raise pregnancy rates.
dose.notes: Reassure people that stress caused by infertility does not ruin their IVF chances.

entries.mechanism: Sympathetic and HPA-axis activation can suppress GnRH/LH and raise systemic oxidative stress, but direct evidence of oocyte damage in humans is lacking.
entries.interactions: Linked with [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Reverse causation (infertility causes stress) is likely in many studies; avoid blaming patients.
entries.title: Psychological stress

entries.headline: Marketed for 'mitochondrial biogenesis', PQQ raised muscle PGC-1alpha but not aerobic performance in a 23-man trial; cognition trials are small and manufacturer-linked.

dose.effective: No proven clinical dose; 20 mg/day is typical
dose.studied_range: 0.2-0.3 mg/kg in a 10-person study; 20-21.5 mg/day for 6-12 weeks
dose.too_much: EFSA judged up to 20 mg/day safe for healthy adults, excluding pregnant and breastfeeding women
dose.timeframe: Trials ran 6-12 weeks
dose.notes: The proposed supplement dose is at least 250 times typical dietary intake.

entries.mechanism: A redox-cycling quinone made by bacteria and present in trace amounts in foods. In animals it influences mitochondrial biogenesis signalling (PGC-1alpha) and acts as a redox cofactor; it is not a confirmed vitamin in humans.
entries.interactions: Often sold with [coq10]; no evidence for the combination. Exercise is a far stronger trigger of mitochondrial biogenesis ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]).
entries.caveats: Human data are tiny and short. The 'longevity vitamin' label is a hypothesis, not evidence.
entries.debate: Supporters cite lower CRP and IL-6 in a 10-person study [lon-harris2013], better cognitive test scores in two small Japanese RCTs of branded PQQ products [lon-itoh2016, lon-shiojima2022], and Ames's proposal of PQQ as a longevity vitamin [lon-ames2018]. In the only exercise trial, PQQ raised PGC-1alpha protein but did not improve aerobic performance beyond training alone [lon-hwang2020]. EFSA addressed safety, not efficacy [lon-efsa2017pqq].
entries.title: Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ)

entries.headline: At 500 mg/day or more, quercetin lowers blood pressure by about 4/3 mmHg in pooled RCTs, but it did not reduce colds in a 1002-person trial, improves endurance by a trivial ~2%, and left oxidative-stress markers unchanged even when it lowered blood pressure.

dose.effective: 500-1000 mg/day for blood-pressure effects.
dose.studied_range: 100-1250 mg/day for 2-12 weeks; senolytic protocols used 1000-1250 mg for 3 days with dasatinib.
dose.too_much: Long-term safety above 1000 mg/day beyond 12 weeks is not established; quercetin alters the bioavailability of some drugs, and animal data raise kidney concerns.
dose.timeframe: Blood pressure change within 4 weeks.
dose.notes: Quercetin glucosides from onions were 52% absorbed vs 24% for the aglycone used in most pills; almost all circulates as conjugates.

entries.mechanism: Quercetin conjugates act on vascular signalling (nitric oxide availability, NADPH oxidase) rather than by scavenging radicals in plasma; in senolytic regimens it is paired with the kinase inhibitor dasatinib.
entries.interactions: Same flavonol class as [fisetin]. Flavonol foods overlap [green-tea], [black-tea] and onions in [garlic-alliums]. Unlike resveratrol, 1000 mg/day for 2 weeks did not blunt mitochondrial markers in untrained men (see [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements]).
entries.caveats: The often-quoted '~1% bioavailability' understates absorption from onion glucosides, but plasma levels stay low-micromolar. The infection benefit appeared only in a post-hoc subgroup. Dasatinib plus quercetin trials are small and mostly open-label; the one RCT (bone) missed its primary endpoint, and quercetin was not detected in CSF in the Alzheimer's pilot.
entries.title: Quercetin (supplement; onions, capers, apples, tea)

entries.headline: Rapamycin is the most reproducible drug for extending mouse lifespan, but in humans the year-long PEARL trial (5-10 mg weekly) found no change in its primary outcome, visceral fat; it is a prescription immunosuppressant with real risks.

dose.effective: No proven longevity dose in humans; PEARL used 5 or 10 mg compounded rapamycin once weekly
dose.studied_range: Weekly 5-10 mg (PEARL, 48 weeks); low-dose everolimus or combined TORC1 inhibitors for 6 weeks in immune-function trials
dose.too_much: Transplant-level daily dosing causes immunosuppression, infections, raised cholesterol and triglycerides, and impaired glucose control (mTORC2 disruption in mice)
dose.timeframe: Immune effects after 6 weeks; PEARL ran 48 weeks
dose.notes: Prescription-only; off-label use should be medically supervised with monitoring of lipids, glucose and blood counts. Compounded products vary in bioavailability.

entries.mechanism: Inhibits mTORC1, the nutrient-sensing kinase that drives growth and suppresses autophagy; this mimics aspects of calorie restriction. Chronic exposure also disrupts mTORC2, which causes insulin resistance. Effects on oxidative stress are indirect, through improved mitochondrial quality control.
entries.interactions: Has many drug interactions; review all medicines with a prescriber. Overlaps conceptually with energy restriction and exercise, which also lower mTORC1 signalling.
entries.caveats: Human data are short and mostly surrogate. The off-label user survey is self-selected and partly authored by people with commercial interests in longevity medicine.
entries.debate: Mouse data are robust: rapamycin extended lifespan even when started late in life [lon-harrison2009], and low-dose mTOR inhibitors improved vaccine responses and reduced infections in older adults [lon-mannick2014, lon-mannick2018]. But PEARL missed its primary endpoint, with benefits only in subgroups [lon-moel2025]; a systematic review found some immune and cardiovascular improvements but more infections and higher lipids in patients [lon-lee2024]; and insulin resistance via mTORC2 is a known mechanism-based risk [lon-lamming2012]. Supporters cite a survey of 333 off-label users as evidence of safety [lon-kaeberlein2023], but that design cannot detect benefits or uncommon harms.
entries.title: Rapamycin (sirolimus), off-label for longevity

entries.headline: A glass of red wine contains well under 1 mg trans-resveratrol, oral resveratrol is almost entirely conjugated before it reaches blood, and urinary resveratrol levels did not predict mortality; the ethanol itself raises lipid peroxidation in a dose-dependent way.

dose.effective: No antioxidant reason to drink. If you drink, wine polyphenols taken with a fatty meal may limit postprandial lipid oxidation in the stomach (animal data).
dose.studied_range: Resveratrol supplements in trials range from tens to thousands of mg; a 25 mg oral dose left <5 ng/mL free resveratrol in plasma.
dose.too_much: Alcohol raises urinary isoprostanes dose-dependently; see [alcohol].
dose.notes: Trans-resveratrol ~0.18 mg/100 mL (about 0.3 mg per 150 mL glass), so reaching supplement doses would take hundreds of glasses.

entries.mechanism: Resveratrol is absorbed (~70%) but rapidly sulfated and glucuronidated; wine's other polyphenols (anthocyanins, flavan-3-ols) are similar to those in grapes and berries without the ethanol.
entries.interactions: Ethanol counteracts the polyphenols; grapes, berries or dealcoholised wine provide the polyphenols without it. Supplement-dose resveratrol is covered under [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements]: meta-analyses find no overall blood-pressure effect and only trivial or very-low-certainty metabolic effects, and 250 mg/day blunted training gains in older men.
entries.caveats: Associations of urinary resveratrol metabolites with better lipids in PREDIMED are cross-sectional and confounded by wine drinking patterns.

key_numbers.label: Total polyphenols, chromatography, red wine (sum of compounds)
Free resveratrol in plasma after 25 mg oral dose

entries.title: Red wine and resveratrol

factors.name: Refined sugar, sugary drinks & high-GI meals

entries.headline: A 75 g glucose drink more than doubled leukocyte ROS generation at 2 h in healthy people and lowered plasma vitamin E; large post-meal glucose and triglyceride spikes drive transient oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction.

dose.effective: Limit sugary drinks and large refined-starch meals; pair carbohydrates with fiber, protein, fat and vinegar or acidic foods.
dose.studied_range: 75 g oral glucose; single high-fat or high-carbohydrate meals.
dose.too_much: Repeated large spikes; sugar-sweetened beverages.
dose.timeframe: Peaks at 1-3 h after the meal.
dose.notes: Cream (fat) and casein (protein) also raised leukocyte ROS, so the size of the meal matters, not only sugar.

entries.mechanism: Nutrient surges increase leukocyte NADPH oxidase (p47phox) and mitochondrial superoxide; hyperglycemia fuels AGE and polyol pathways and NF-kB activation.
entries.interactions: Additive with [overfeeding]. Blunted by [whole-grains], [legumes], [dietary-fiber-microbiome] and polyphenol-rich foods with the meal (e.g. [tomatoes-lycopene], [herbs-spices]).
entries.caveats: Acute leukocyte ROS assays are not the same as chronic tissue damage; whether postprandial spikes in non-diabetic people cause disease independent of overall diet is debated.

key_numbers.label: Peak leukocyte (PMNL) ROS after 75 g glucose

entries.title: Refined sugar and high-glycemic meals

entries.headline: Young men drinking 1.3+ sugary drinks a day had about 10 points lower progressive motility.

dose.effective: Under one sugary drink a week; water, unsweetened tea or coffee instead.
dose.studied_range: <0.2 to >=1.3 servings/day.
dose.too_much: >=1.3 servings/day associated with lower motility.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Caffeinated soft drinks also looked worse than coffee in reviews.

entries.mechanism: Glycaemic load drives insulin resistance, advanced glycation end-products and inflammation.
entries.interactions: Linked with [excess-adiposity].
entries.caveats: Cross-sectional, single semen sample; association only in lean men.
entries.title: Sugar-sweetened beverages

entries.headline: Donating lowers iron stores, and donors live longer, but most of that is the 'healthy donor effect': in 1.2 million donors the 18.6% lower mortality per annual donation shrank to 7.5% after adjustment, a large cohort found no heart benefit, and frequent donation often causes iron deficiency.

dose.effective: Donate for altruism, not as a health intervention. Standard whole-blood intervals (in the UK about 12 weeks for men and 16 for women), with ferritin checks or iron supplementation for frequent donors.
dose.studied_range: One donation removes ~200-250 mg iron. RCT of 550-800 mL phlebotomy in metabolic syndrome; donation intervals of 8-16 weeks (INTERVAL).
dose.too_much: Each week shorter donation interval lowered ferritin ~5-6.5% and raised low-haemoglobin deferrals; frequent donors reported more tiredness and restless legs.
dose.timeframe: Ferritin falls within months of regular donation.
dose.notes: Therapeutic phlebotomy for haemochromatosis is a medical treatment and is clearly beneficial in that condition; this entry is about healthy people.

entries.mechanism: Removes iron (as haemoglobin) and thereby lowers ferritin and, in theory, the labile iron available for Fenton chemistry. Short-term blood-pressure falls after phlebotomy may reflect volume and haemodynamic effects rather than iron.
entries.interactions: Lowers [iron-status-ferritin]; can cause [iron-deficiency], especially in young women and frequent donors.
entries.caveats: Donors are pre-screened for good health and continue donating only while healthy, so observational comparisons overstate benefits. No study has shown that donation reduces oxidative-stress outcomes or disease in healthy people.
entries.debate: For a benefit: the Kuopio cohort found 88% fewer heart attacks in recent donors [nut-salonen1998], a small RCT of phlebotomy in metabolic syndrome lowered systolic BP by 16.6 mmHg [nut-houschyar2012] (commentary noted design drawbacks [nut-manco2012]), and FeAST suggested fewer cancers [nut-zacharski2008]. Against: the 38,244-man Health Professionals cohort found no CHD benefit despite lower ferritin [nut-ascherio2001], FeAST was null for death and CV events [nut-zacharski2007], and Scandinavian and Dutch data show a strong healthy donor effect [nut-ullum2015, nut-atsma2011]. INTERVAL showed the harms side: more symptoms and iron deficiency with frequent donation [nut-diangelantonio2017, nut-kaptoge2019, nut-vandenhurk2018].

entries.title: Regular blood donation

entries.headline: Muscle-strengthening is associated with 10-27% lower mortality, with the biggest drop at about 30-60 min/week and the best results when combined with aerobic exercise (41% lower vs neither); it reliably builds strength (about 25-30% in older adults) and fights sarcopenia, while its 'antioxidant' effects are small.

dose.effective: 2-3 sessions/week (about 30-60 min/week total) on non-consecutive days, covering major muscle groups; 1-3 sets of 8-12 reps at a load you could lift a couple more times. Older adults benefit most from progressively heavier loads.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: 0 to 150+ min/week; RCTs in older adults: 2-3 sessions/week for 8-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Some cohorts show the mortality benefit fading above about 60 min/week (J-shape), but the largest cohort found no upturn. Rapid jumps in volume caused a 7-fold rise in urinary isoprostanes and a performance drop in an overreaching study.
dose.timeframe: Strength gains within 4-8 weeks; muscle mass in 8-12 weeks; antioxidant enzyme changes (glutathione peroxidase) in 8-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Do it in addition to aerobic activity: in NIH-AARP weight training was not associated with lower mortality in people doing no aerobic exercise. Avoid high-dose vitamin C/E and post-workout cold plunges if muscle gain is the goal.

entries.mechanism: Mechanical tension and metabolic stress activate mTOR and satellite cells; local ROS and NOX-derived signals contribute to hypertrophy signalling (p38, ERK, p70S6K, which vitamin C/E blunted). Added muscle increases glucose disposal, lowering glycemic oxidative stress, and repeated sessions modestly up-regulate glutathione peroxidase.
entries.interactions: High-dose vitamin C/E blunted lean-mass and bone-density gains in older men and hypertrophy signalling in younger adults ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]); post-workout [cold-water-immersion] blunted strength gains. Strength appears to feed fitness: genetic analyses suggest grip strength raises [cardiorespiratory-fitness], not the reverse. Combines with [aerobic-exercise-moderate].
entries.caveats: Mortality data are self-reported and observational; people who lift weights differ in many ways. In older adults, muscle and function benefits are well proven by RCTs, but mortality benefit is not. Meta-analysis found a small decrease in SOD and no change in catalase, so 'strength training is an antioxidant' is an overstatement.
entries.debate: Whether 'more is worse' is disputed. Two meta-analyses found J-shaped curves with maximal benefit at about 30-60 min/week [exr-momma2022, exr-shailendra2022], echoed in older women [exr-kamada2017]; but the largest single cohort (216,339 older adults) found any weight training lowered mortality with no clear upturn, just diminishing returns [exr-shailendra2024], and the J-shape rests on few people at high volumes with wide confidence intervals. An umbrella review rated the resistance-training mortality evidence only 'suggestive' [exr-rahmati2025]. On causality, Mendelian randomization supports grip strength protecting against coronary disease and AF [exr-tikkanen2018], while grip strength's mortality association comes from observational data [exr-leong2015]. For oxidative stress, only glutathione peroxidase rose reliably [exr-cordeiro2025]; a 2026 meta-analysis in older adults found redox data from just 6 trials with moderate-to-high bias [exr-chenhuichen2026].

entries.title: Resistance (strength) training

entries.headline: Despite the sirtuin story, resveratrol supplements show trivial or very-low-certainty metabolic effects in meta-analyses, 250 mg/day blunted training gains in older men, and pterostilbene 250 mg/day lowered blood pressure but raised LDL by 17 mg/dL.

dose.effective: None established for health outcomes.
dose.studied_range: Resveratrol 10 mg to 2 g/day; pterostilbene 100-250 mg/day for 6-8 weeks.
dose.too_much: Gram doses cause nausea, diarrhoea and weight loss. Avoid around training if adaptation is the goal. See [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements] for embryo-transfer concerns.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Food supplies well under 1 mg/day (see [red-wine-resveratrol]); supplements are a pharmacological, not dietary, exposure.

entries.mechanism: Resveratrol activates AMPK and indirectly SIRT1 and acts as a mild hormetic stressor at low micromolar levels; in muscle it can dampen the reactive-oxygen signalling that drives training adaptation.
entries.interactions: Can antagonise exercise adaptation (contrast [quercetin], which did not blunt mitochondrial markers short-term). Part of the broader [isolated-polyphenol-supplements] picture.
entries.caveats: Positive single trials exist (150 mg/day in 11 obese men; 200 mg/day for memory; 500 mg/day augmenting muscle response to training in 65-80-year-olds), but other trials were null, and in the 52-week Alzheimer's trial (up to 1 g twice daily) brain-volume loss was greater on resveratrol. Exercise results conflict by age, dose and training type.

LDL change, pterostilbene 125 mg twice daily
Systolic BP change, pterostilbene 125 mg twice daily

entries.title: Resveratrol and pterostilbene supplements

entries.headline: The only human data are an uncontrolled 20-man pilot of a multivitamin with 150 mg/day resveratrol, which reported motility rising from 48% to 59%; with no placebo group the effect cannot be attributed to resveratrol.

dose.effective: Not established.
dose.studied_range: 150 mg/day resveratrol within a multivitamin for 3-6 months.
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.

entries.mechanism: Proposed SIRT1 and mitochondrial effects in sperm, from animal work.
entries.interactions: Overlaps [male-antioxidant-combination]; see [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements] for general resveratrol evidence.
entries.caveats: Uncontrolled, small, multi-ingredient, no pregnancy outcomes; regression to the mean is likely.
entries.title: Resveratrol (multivitamin-based) for sperm

entries.headline: Resveratrol may improve some follicular markers (an 800 mg/day RCT in PCOS raised oocyte maturity without changing pregnancy rates), but it suppresses endometrial decidualization, and 200 mg/day during embryo-transfer cycles was associated with lower pregnancy (OR 0.54) and more miscarriage (OR 2.60).

dose.effective: Not recommended while trying to conceive or around embryo transfer.
dose.studied_range: 200 mg/day (retrospective IVF cohort); 800 mg/day for 60 days (PCOS RCT, 56 women).
dose.too_much: Any use in the luteal phase or early pregnancy (possible anti-implantation effect; teratogenicity not excluded).
dose.notes: A clear example where an 'anti-ageing' antioxidant may harm the uterus even if it helps the ovary.

entries.mechanism: SIRT1 activation and antioxidant effects in the ovary; in endometrium it down-regulates the CRABP2-RAR pathway, inhibiting decidualization needed for implantation.
entries.interactions: Sirtuin-pathway overlap with [nmn-nad].
entries.caveats: Harm signal is retrospective; benefit signal is a single small RCT on surrogate outcomes.

key_numbers.label: Clinical pregnancy, resveratrol during transfer cycles

entries.title: Resveratrol

factors.name: Reused deep-frying oil and frequent fried food

entries.headline: Repeatedly heated PUFA-rich oils accumulate polar compounds and genotoxic aldehydes such as 4-HNE, part of which survives digestion; frequent fried-food eaters have about 22-28% more coronary and major cardiovascular events in meta-analyses, but a Spanish cohort frying in olive or sunflower oil found no link, and in US cohorts body weight explained much of it.

dose.effective: Eat deep-fried food occasionally rather than daily; at home, fry in a stable oil at no more than ~180 °C, filter and store it covered and dark between uses, and discard it when it darkens, foams, smokes at normal temperature or smells acrid. An air fryer or oven-frying sidesteps most of the oil.
dose.studied_range: Fried food from <1 to ≥7 times/week in cohorts; domestic frying up to ~27 h of oil use.
dose.too_much: The legal discard limit used in a Portuguese frying study was 25% total polar compounds; fried food ≥1 serving/day was linked to 8% higher all-cause mortality in older US women.
dose.timeframe: Postprandial exposure with each meal; disease associations over years.
dose.notes: Restaurant and fast-food oils are the main source of heavily reused oil. Fried chicken and fried fish were the items most linked to mortality in the Women's Health Initiative.

entries.mechanism: Hydrolysis, oxidation and polymerisation during frying generate free fatty acids, hydroperoxides, epoxides, polymers and alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehydes (4-hydroxy-2-nonenal, acrolein). Some aldehydes stay bioaccessible after digestion and can modify proteins, deplete glutathione and activate NF-kB in gut, liver and vessel walls; animals fed reheated oils develop higher blood pressure and vascular inflammation.
entries.interactions: Oil type matters ([cooking-oil-choice]); fried starchy foods also carry [acrylamide]; fried meat adds HCAs ([high-temperature-cooking]); frequent fried food tracks with weight gain ([excess-adiposity]).
entries.caveats: Human evidence is observational and confounded by fast-food patterns, salt and body weight; direct human evidence that reused oil raises oxidative damage is sparse. Much mechanistic evidence comes from rodents fed large amounts of oil heated many times.
entries.debate: A meta-analysis found higher major CVD (RR 1.28) and CHD (RR 1.22) with the most fried food but no rise in CVD or total mortality and high heterogeneity [kcc-qin2021]; the Women's Health Initiative linked fried chicken and fish to mortality [kcc-sun2019]. Against this, the Spanish EPIC cohort found no association whether olive or sunflower oil was used [kcc-guallarcastillon2012], and US cohort associations were largely explained by weight, hypertension and cholesterol [kcc-cahill2014]. Mechanistic concern rests on oil chemistry and animal work [kcc-guillen2009, kcc-goicoechea2008, kcc-ng2014].

entries.headline: Riboflavin's FAD form powers glutathione reductase, which recycles oxidised glutathione; subclinical deficiency is probably common but rarely measured, and in people with the MTHFR 677TT genotype 1.6 mg/day lowered systolic blood pressure by 5.6 mmHg.

dose.effective: RDA 1.3 mg/day men, 1.1 mg/day women (1.4 pregnancy). Dairy, eggs, meat, fortified cereals, almonds and mushrooms.
dose.studied_range: 1.6 mg/day in the MTHFR trials.
dose.too_much: No UL has been set (IOM); excess is excreted in urine.
dose.timeframe: Status (EGRac) improves within weeks; BP effect seen at 16 weeks.
dose.notes: At risk: low dairy intake (some vegans), older adults, alcohol use disorder, adolescents, pregnancy. Best status marker is the erythrocyte glutathione reductase activation coefficient (EGRac).

entries.mechanism: FAD is the cofactor of glutathione reductase (GSSG -> 2 GSH, using NADPH), of MTHFR in folate metabolism, and of mitochondrial complex II and fatty-acid oxidation enzymes. Low riboflavin therefore weakens glutathione recycling and one-carbon metabolism.
entries.interactions: Works with folate and B12 in homocysteine metabolism [vitamin-b12-folate-status]; supports the glutathione system targeted by [n-acetylcysteine] and [glynac].
entries.caveats: Evidence for oxidative-stress outcomes is mechanistic; the human trial evidence is for blood pressure in a specific genotype, from one research group.
entries.debate: Proponents argue subclinical deficiency is widespread and under-recognised [nut-mcnulty2023], supported by global intake models showing >4 billion people under-consume riboflavin [nut-passarelli2024]. The blood-pressure benefit [nut-wilson2013] has been studied mainly by one group in genotype-selected patients and lacks independent replication; no outcome trials show oxidative-stress benefits in replete people.

key_numbers.label: Global share with inadequate riboflavin intake

entries.title: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) status

factors.name: Sauna, hot tubs & hot baths
aliases: Saunas, hot tubs and hot baths

entries.headline: Frequent sauna use is linked to lower cardiovascular death and inflammation in Finnish cohorts, and heat therapy improves vascular function in trials, but direct oxidative-stress benefits are unproven; sauna clearly impairs sperm (reversibly).

dose.effective: Cohort 'high' group: 4-7 sessions/week, sessions longer than 19 min, in a traditional Finnish sauna (hot and dry, ~80-90 C as in the sperm study); trial: 40.5 C hot-water immersion for 60 min, 4-5x/week for 8 weeks.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: 1 to 4-7 sessions/week, <11 to >19 min; sperm study: 2 x 15 min/week at 80-90 C for 3 months.
dose.too_much: Men trying to conceive should avoid sauna: 2 sessions/week at 80-90 C for 3 months reduced sperm count and motility and damaged chromatin; avoid alcohol in the sauna; caution with unstable heart disease, pregnancy and low blood pressure.
dose.timeframe: Vascular changes in 8 weeks; sperm recovered ~6 months after stopping.
dose.notes: Cohort men who used saunas more often were also fitter and healthier; benefits may partly reflect that.

entries.mechanism: Heat stress induces heat-shock proteins, increases shear stress and nitric oxide production (like exercise), and may trigger mild hormetic ROS signalling. For testes, heat disrupts spermatogenesis and increases sperm oxidative/chromatin damage.
entries.interactions: Partially mimics [aerobic-exercise-moderate] vascular effects but is not a substitute for exercise. Cross-link to sperm area: heat is a strong, reversible harm to sperm.
entries.caveats: The KIHD cohort found no association between sauna frequency and GGT (the oxidative-stress proxy studied) despite lower CRP. Oxidative claims for sauna are mostly extrapolation.
entries.title: Sauna bathing (Finnish sauna) and passive heat

entries.headline: Regular sauna or hot-tub use reversibly damages sperm count, motility and chromatin packaging; effects take 3-6 months to clear.

dose.effective: Avoid while trying to conceive. Harm shown with sauna at 80-90 C for 15 min twice a week for 3 months, and with scrotal water at 43 C for 30 min on 10 occasions.
dose.studied_range: Sauna 80-90 C x 15 min, 2x/week, 12 weeks; scrotal bath 43 C x 30 min, daily or every 3 days, 10 sessions; habitual hot tubs/baths.
dose.too_much: Testes work best about 2-4 C below core temperature; any wet heat above ~40 C held for 30 min is a risk. Daily (consecutive) exposure was worse than intermittent.
dose.timeframe: Recovery by about 16 weeks after short exposure and fully by 6 months after 3 months of sauna use.
dose.notes: If you will not give it up, keep sessions short, sit with the scrotum away from hot surfaces, and stop for at least 3 months before trying.

entries.mechanism: Scrotal hyperthermia disrupts histone-to-protamine exchange and mitochondrial function in developing sperm, raises heat-shock and hypoxia gene expression and triggers apoptosis, making DNA more susceptible to oxidative breaks.
entries.interactions: Adds to [varicocele] and [everyday-scrotal-heat]. Same pathway as [febrile-illness].
entries.caveats: Trials are small (10-20 normozoospermic men), but they are interventional with clear reversal, so causality is convincing. Benefits of sauna for cardiovascular health are real; this is a temporary trade-off.

key_numbers.label: Total motile count rise after stopping hot tubs (responders)

entries.title: Saunas, hot tubs and hot baths

entries.headline: Secondhand smoke raises coronary heart disease risk about 30%, and even brief exposures produce vascular and oxidative effects averaging 80-90% of active smoking.

dose.effective: Keep home and car completely smoke-free; avoid indoor smoky venues.
dose.studied_range: Experimental exposures of 30 min to a few hours; cohort exposure from household smoking.
dose.too_much: No safe level identified for cardiovascular effects; 30 min of exposure impaired coronary flow reserve in healthy nonsmokers.
dose.timeframe: Acute vascular effects within minutes to hours.
dose.notes: Ventilation and smoking in another room do not remove the exposure.

entries.mechanism: Sidestream smoke contains the same radical-generating tar and oxidant gases as mainstream smoke; tar from secondhand smoke generates H2O2 and breaks DNA in cells.
entries.interactions: Adds to [outdoor-air-pollution] and [indoor-combustion-smoke].
entries.caveats: One cross-sectional study of women with modest exposure (>=15 min, 2 days/week) found no difference in 8-isoprostane, so low-level exposure may not show up on systemic markers even though vascular effects are documented.
entries.title: Secondhand (passive) smoke

entries.headline: The 'toxic seed oil' claim is not supported: across 44 cohorts higher linoleic acid intake was linked to 13% lower total and CVD mortality, blood linoleic acid to lower CVD in 30 cohorts, and RCTs show no rise in inflammatory markers; but omega-6 RCTs on hard outcomes are mixed, and two recovered 1960s-70s trials suggested harm.

dose.effective: Using liquid vegetable oils (including seed oils such as soybean, sunflower, canola/rapeseed, corn) in place of butter, lard and other saturated fats; cohort benefits were seen at higher habitual LA intakes, roughly 5-10% of energy.
dose.studied_range: RCTs raised PUFA from ~5% to ~15% of energy for 1-8 years; cohorts compare top vs bottom LA intake or blood/adipose LA levels.
dose.too_much: No established harm threshold in humans. Repeatedly heated or reused PUFA-rich oil is a separate issue (see [oxidized-frying-oils]).
dose.timeframe: LDL changes within weeks; outcome trials 1-8 years.
dose.notes: The question is what the oil replaces: benefit is seen when it replaces saturated fat, not when added on top of an energy surplus. For high-heat or repeated frying, more oxidation-stable oils are preferable ([cooking-oil-choice]).

entries.mechanism: Linoleic acid lowers LDL cholesterol when it replaces saturated fat and is the precursor of arachidonic acid, but tissue arachidonate barely rises with higher intake. Its bis-allylic hydrogens make LA-rich LDL more oxidizable in vitro, and lowering LA reduces circulating oxidized LA metabolites (OXLAMs); whether this matters clinically is unproven.
entries.interactions: Displacing saturated fat matters more than the oil itself; trans-fat-containing margarines confounded older trials ([trans-fats]). Oleic-rich oils such as [extra-virgin-olive-oil] give LDL that resists oxidation better. Omega-3 status ([omega3-fish]) is a separate lever.
entries.caveats: Cohort associations could be confounded by healthier diets, though biomarker studies reduce reliance on questionnaires. Surrogate oxidative markers (in-vitro LDL oxidizability, OXLAMs) have not been shown to predict outcomes. Claims about hexane extraction, 'industrial' processing or seed oils causing obesity and chronic disease are not backed by outcome studies we could find.
entries.debate: Pro-benefit: an RCT meta-analysis found 19% fewer CHD events when PUFA replaced saturated fat [kcc-mozaffarian2010], cohort and biomarker meta-analyses show lower CHD, CVD and mortality with higher LA [kcc-farvid2014, kcc-marklund2019, kcc-li2020], RCTs show no rise in inflammatory markers [kcc-johnson2012], and the AHA advisory strongly recommends PUFA in place of saturated fat [kcc-sacks2017]; Cochrane found that cutting saturated fat lowered CVD events by 17% [kcc-hooper2020]. Sceptical: recovered data from the Sydney Diet Heart Study showed higher death rates with safflower oil [kcc-ramsden2013] and the Minnesota Coronary Experiment showed no mortality benefit despite lower cholesterol [kcc-ramsden2016]; a meta-analysis restricted to 'adequately controlled' trials found no benefit [kcc-hamley2017]; Cochrane rates omega-6 trial evidence as low quality with little effect on mortality [kcc-hooper2018]; and an opinion piece blames oxidized LA for heart disease [kcc-dinicolantonio2018], whose authors disclose commercial interests. The AHA advisory counters that the Sydney trial used a margarine high in trans fat and the Minnesota trial was short with high turnover [kcc-sacks2017]. Mechanistically, LA-rich LDL oxidizes more readily in vitro [kcc-reaven1993] and LA lowering reduces OXLAMs [kcc-ramsden2012].

CVD mortality per interquintile range of blood LA

All-cause death, Sydney Diet Heart intervention

entries.title: Seed oils and linoleic acid (omega-6)

entries.headline: Selenium is a textbook U-curve: deficiency causes Keshan cardiomyopathy (supplements cut it 86%) and weak sperm midpieces, but in replete people 200 ug/day raised type 2 diabetes (HR 1.55), and 300 ug/day for 5 years raised 10-year mortality (HR 1.59); Cochrane finds no cancer prevention.

dose.effective: RDA 55 ug/day (60 in pregnancy). Selenoprotein P was maximised at about 105 ug/day total intake. Food covers this in North America (wheat, meat, fish, eggs); Brazil nuts are very rich but their selenium content varies widely, so a nut or two is enough. Supplement (50-100 ug/day) only with low intake or low measured status, e.g. parts of Europe, China, vegans in low-selenium regions.
dose.studied_range: 50-300 ug/day selenium yeast or selenomethionine in trials; 100-200 ug/day in male fertility trials.
dose.too_much: UL 400 ug/day (IOM) or 255 ug/day (EFSA 2023, based on hair loss at 330 ug/day in SELECT). Signals of harm in replete people at 200 ug/day (diabetes, high-grade prostate cancer in men with high baseline status) and 300 ug/day (mortality).
dose.timeframe: Plasma selenium plateaus in ~10 weeks; one spermatogenic cycle ~74 days.
dose.notes: Measure plasma/serum selenium or selenoprotein P if in doubt; many 'antioxidant' and fertility blends add 50-200 ug on top of diet.

entries.mechanism: Selenium is the active-site selenocysteine of glutathione peroxidases (including GPX4, the master brake on ferroptosis) and thioredoxin reductases, plus deiodinases for thyroid hormone. Once selenoproteins are saturated, extra selenium accumulates non-specifically (as selenomethionine) with no further antioxidant gain and possible pro-oxidant and insulin-signalling effects. In sperm, GPX4 is cross-linked into the mitochondrial capsule as a structural protein.
entries.interactions: Vitamin E effects on prostate cancer depended on selenium status [vitamin-e-supplement]. Iodine and selenium together support thyroid function [iodine-status]. Selenium in [multivitamin-mineral] and [male-antioxidant-combination] products adds up.
entries.caveats: Benefits are confined to people with low status; most US/Canadian adults are replete. The best-known positive male fertility trial (Safarinejad 2009) carries a 2023 journal Expression of Concern.
entries.debate: U-curve proponents [nut-rayman2012] point to harms in replete people: diabetes in NPC [nut-stranges2007] (editorial: 'more bad news for supplements' [nut-bleys2007]), high-grade prostate cancer when baseline status was high [nut-kristal2014] (with methodological questions raised [nut-frankel2014]) and excess mortality at 300 ug/day [nut-rayman2018]; Cochrane found no cancer benefit [nut-vinceti2018]. Benefits are clear for deficiency (Keshan disease [nut-zhou2018]). For sperm, a low-status Scottish RCT improved motility [nut-scott1998] and meta-analysis of small trials is positive [nut-buhling2019], but the largest positive trial [nut-safarinejad2009] is under an Expression of Concern [nut-jurol2023] and Cochrane rates male antioxidant evidence low to very low certainty [nut-deligny2022].
entries.title: Selenium status and supplements

entries.headline: Selenium helps motility mainly in men with low selenium status; little reason to supplement if diet is adequate.

dose.effective: About 100-200 ug/day only if intake is low (e.g. parts of Europe); 1-2 Brazil nuts provide a similar amount.
dose.studied_range: 3 months of selenium with or without vitamins A, C, E (69 men); MOXI used 200 ug.
dose.too_much: Do not exceed the US tolerable upper intake of 400 ug/day; chronic excess causes selenosis.
dose.timeframe: 3 months.

entries.mechanism: Cofactor of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPx4), which becomes a structural protein of the sperm midpiece and protects against lipid peroxidation.
entries.interactions: Part of [male-antioxidant-combination].
entries.caveats: Small, older trials; benefit limited to deficient men.
entries.title: Selenium

entries.headline: Lower oxidative stress is one of many proposed reasons for these drugs' heart and kidney benefits, but that part is mostly mechanistic; the practical redox-diet point is safety: combined with a ketogenic diet they can cause euglycemic ketoacidosis, sometimes within a week.

dose.effective: As prescribed (e.g. empagliflozin 10-25 mg/day, dapagliflozin 10 mg/day).
dose.studied_range: Case reports involve standard doses; euDKA occurred after one dose in one case and after one week of a ketogenic diet in another.
dose.too_much: Ketogenic or very-low-carbohydrate diets, prolonged fasting, acute illness, surgery and dehydration raise euDKA risk; blood glucose may look normal.
dose.timeframe: Ketoacidosis can develop within days of starting a ketogenic diet on the drug.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Tell the prescriber before starting a ketogenic diet, extended fasting or a very-low-carb plan; seek urgent care for nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or malaise even if glucose is normal.

entries.mechanism: SGLT2 inhibitors make the kidney excrete glucose, causing natriuresis, a shift toward ketone fuel, lower uric acid and less AGE signalling; reduced oxidative stress and inflammation are proposed contributors from mechanistic studies [med-cowie2020]. Insulin-independent glucose loss, high glucagon and volume depletion promote ketogenesis, which a carbohydrate-free diet amplifies [med-peters2015, med-mistry2021].
entries.interactions: Dangerous with [ketogenic-diet], [low-carb-diet] and prolonged [intermittent-fasting]. Part of [glycemic-control] therapy alongside [metformin] and [glp1-agonists].
entries.caveats: No human outcome data show that their oxidative-stress effects matter clinically; the heart-failure and kidney benefits are established on clinical outcomes and are not the subject here.
entries.debate: Which mechanisms explain the cardiorenal benefits is debated, with haemodynamic, natriuretic and metabolic explanations competing with anti-inflammatory and antioxidant ones [med-cowie2020]. On euDKA itself no substantive published disagreement was found: case series agree on the risk and on avoiding ketogenic diets [med-peters2015, med-mistry2021].
entries.title: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin)

entries.headline: Cutting sleep raises oxidative stress in human studies (endothelial oxidative stress after 6 weeks of 1.5 h less sleep; lower glutathione after one sleepless night), but the dramatic 'sleep loss kills via gut ROS' finding is from flies and mice.

dose.effective: 7-9 h per night on a regular schedule (adults; AASM/SRS: 7 h or more).
dose.studied_range: Human studies: one night of total deprivation; 6 weeks of 1.5 h/night restriction; observational comparison of <=6 h vs >8 h.
dose.too_much: Regularly <=6 h was associated with ~12% higher urinary 8-isoprostane; chronic restriction increased endothelial oxidative stress.
dose.timeframe: Glutathione drop after a single night; endothelial changes within 6 weeks.
dose.notes: Consistency matters as well as duration. Treat sleep apnea if present (see [sleep-apnea]).

entries.mechanism: Wakefulness raises metabolic rate and sympathetic tone, consumes glutathione and cysteine, and reduces melatonin (itself a radical scavenger and regulator of DNA repair). In animals, ROS accumulate in the gut with severe deprivation. Short sleep also worsens insulin resistance and appetite regulation.
entries.interactions: Interacts with [shift-work-circadian]. Poor sleep worsens [glycemic-control] and weight gain ([weight-loss]) and impairs recovery from [overtraining-ultraendurance].
entries.caveats: Vaccaro 2020 (Cell) was done in flies and mice with extreme deprivation; antioxidants rescued survival there, which does not mean antioxidant pills replace sleep in humans. Human data are small or observational.
entries.title: Short or insufficient sleep

entries.headline: Sleeping under 6 hours or over 9 hours, or poor sleep quality, is associated with roughly 15-20% lower sperm counts, but estimates are imprecise.

dose.effective: 7-9 hours per night with regular timing.
dose.studied_range: <6 h, 7-8.9 h and >=9 h per night; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index >5 vs <=5.
dose.too_much: Both short and long sleep were associated with lower counts.
dose.timeframe: Unknown; plausibly one spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: No SDF-specific human data.

entries.mechanism: Sleep loss lowers testosterone and raises systemic inflammation and oxidative stress.
entries.interactions: Interlinked with [excess-adiposity].
entries.caveats: Observational; confidence intervals mostly cross zero.
entries.title: Short or poor-quality sleep

entries.headline: Frequent trouble sleeping was associated with about 13% lower monthly chance of conception; shift work is linked to menstrual disruption and night shifts to early miscarriage, but not clearly to infertility.

dose.effective: Aim for 7-9 h/night with a regular schedule; treat insomnia and sleep apnea.
dose.studied_range: Sleep < 6 to >= 9 h/day; shift vs day work.
dose.too_much: Trouble sleeping > 50% of nights: FR 0.87; night shifts: aOR 1.41 for early pregnancy loss.
dose.notes: Melatonin supplements are discussed separately ([melatonin]); they are not a substitute for sleep.

entries.mechanism: Ovarian and pituitary clocks regulate the LH surge; circadian disruption alters melatonin (a follicular antioxidant), cortisol and insulin sensitivity.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [psychological-stress]. The shift-work findings also apply to [shift-work-circadian].
entries.caveats: Observational and confounded by depression and stress; shift work-infertility association lost significance after adjustment.

key_numbers.label: Fecundability, trouble sleeping > 50% of the time

entries.title: Poor sleep and circadian disruption

entries.headline: Soy isoflavones do not change male sex hormones (41-study meta-analysis), and only 25-60% of people carry gut bacteria that convert daidzein to the more potent equol, one likely reason soy trials disagree.

dose.effective: Food amounts; no oxidative-stress dose established.
dose.studied_range: Male hormone trials used soy protein or isoflavone extracts across a wide dose range.
dose.notes: Equol production is a microbiome trait; non-producers get less estrogenic activity from the same soy.

entries.mechanism: Isoflavones are weak estrogen-receptor ligands; equol, made only by some microbiomes, binds more strongly. In-vivo antioxidant effects are not established.
entries.interactions: See [soy] (no effect on male fertility measures) and [soy] for the ART cohort.
entries.caveats: Few trials stratify by equol status, and oxidative-stress outcomes are rarely measured.

key_numbers.label: Share of people able to produce equol

entries.title: Soy foods and isoflavones (equol producers vs non-producers)

entries.headline: Soy does not change male hormones in clinical trials and male soy intake was unrelated to IVF success; one small study linked very high intake to lower concentration.

dose.effective: Normal dietary amounts (1-2 servings/day of tofu, soy milk, edamame) are fine.
dose.studied_range: Up to the highest intake category in 99 clinic patients; 41 clinical studies of hormones.
dose.too_much: Very high intake (top of distribution) associated with 41 million/mL lower concentration in one study, mainly in overweight men.

entries.mechanism: Isoflavones are weak phytoestrogens; hormone-level trials show no feminising effect in men.
entries.interactions: Can replace [processed-meat] as protein.
entries.caveats: The negative association comes from one small cross-sectional study.
entries.title: Soy foods

entries.headline: In a fertility-clinic cohort of 315 women (520 ART cycles), higher dietary soy isoflavone intake was associated with higher live-birth rates (adjusted OR about 1.8); no trial has tested it.

dose.effective: Habitual intakes of 2.6-28 mg/day isoflavones were in the higher-benefit categories.
dose.studied_range: 0-28 mg/day dietary isoflavones (observational).
dose.notes: Equol-producer status was not assessed.

entries.mechanism: Weak estrogen-receptor activity of isoflavones and equol has been proposed to aid endometrial receptivity; unproven.
entries.interactions: See [soy] and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Single observational cohort; residual confounding by diet pattern is likely.

key_numbers.label: Adjusted odds ratio of live birth, 2.6-7.6 mg/day vs none

entries.title: Soy isoflavones and IVF outcomes

factors.name: Spermidine (wheat germ, soy, legumes, mushrooms, aged cheese; supplements)

entries.headline: Higher dietary spermidine tracked with 24% lower mortality per standard deviation in an Austrian cohort, but the only long human trial (12 months of 0.9 mg/day wheat-germ extract) found no memory or biomarker benefit, so the autophagy story is still animal-based.

dose.effective: Not established.
dose.studied_range: About 0.9 mg/day spermidine from wheat-germ extract for 3-12 months.
dose.too_much: No safety concerns at the supplement doses studied.
dose.timeframe: 3-12 months studied.
dose.notes: Supplement doses are small next to total dietary polyamines (Swedish adolescents ate about 316 umol/day of all polyamines, half from fruit). Whole foods are the practical source.

entries.mechanism: Spermidine lowers protein acetylation and induces autophagy; in mice its cardioprotection disappeared when cardiomyocyte autophagy (Atg5) was knocked out. It has no meaningful direct antioxidant role.
entries.interactions: Autophagy induction overlaps conceptually with [calorie-restriction]. Spermidine-rich foods overlap [legumes] and [whole-grains], which confound the cohort association.
entries.caveats: The cohort cannot separate spermidine from the whole-grain, legume and vegetable pattern it marks. The 3-month pilot's benefit (confidence interval touching zero) did not replicate in the 12-month trial. Polyamines support cell growth; long-term cancer implications in humans are unstudied.

key_numbers.label: All-cause mortality HR per 1-SD higher intake

entries.title: Spermidine (wheat germ, soy, legumes, mushrooms, aged cheese; supplements)

entries.headline: Spermidine supplementation restored oocyte quality and fertility in aged mice by enhancing mitophagy, but there are no human data.

dose.effective: Not established.
dose.studied_range: Mouse and pig-oocyte studies only.

entries.mechanism: Ovarian spermidine falls with age in mice; supplementation improved mitophagy and mitochondrial function in oocytes.
entries.interactions: See [spermidine] for general human evidence.
entries.caveats: Animal-only; supplements marketed for egg quality are ahead of the data.
entries.title: Spermidine for oocyte quality

entries.headline: In 35 healthy men, 4 weeks of paroxetine raised sperm DNA fragmentation from 13.8% to 30.3% (abnormal in 50% of men vs 9.7% before) with a normal standard semen analysis; small sertraline and escitalopram studies point the same way and effects appear reversible.

dose.effective: Effects seen at standard antidepressant or premature-ejaculation doses: paroxetine (4 weeks), sertraline 50 mg/day (3 months), escitalopram 10 mg/day (12 weeks).
dose.studied_range: Single-arm or small controlled studies of 25-60 men, 4-12 weeks.
dose.too_much: No dose threshold established; a sperm DNA fragmentation test (rather than a routine semen analysis) is what detects the change.
dose.timeframe: DNA fragmentation rose within 4 weeks; reversal after stopping is expected over about one spermatogenic cycle (~74 days) but timing data are limited.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Untreated depression also lowers couple fertility; men trying to conceive who take SSRIs can discuss a DNA fragmentation test, timing, or alternatives with the prescriber rather than stopping.

entries.mechanism: Proposed mechanisms include serotonin effects on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and epididymal transit, and direct effects on sperm membranes and chromatin; DNA fragmentation without changes in count or motility suggests a post-testicular or chromatin-packaging effect [med-tanrikut2010, med-beeder2020].
entries.interactions: Untreated [psychological-stress] and depression are themselves linked to lower fertility. Ejaculatory delay on SSRIs may lengthen abstinence; see [short-abstinence]. Not known whether [male-antioxidant-combination] offsets the effect.
entries.caveats: Studies are small, mostly uncontrolled, and many are in men treated for premature ejaculation. No study shows lower live-birth rates from paternal SSRI use.
entries.debate: Harm: paroxetine [med-tanrikut2010], escitalopram [med-koyuncu2011] and sertraline (vs behavioural therapy) [med-akasheh2014] all worsened sperm measures, and reviews conclude SSRIs can harm semen quality reversibly [med-beeder2020]. Caution: a frequently cited large study [med-safarinejad2008] is under a 2023 Expression of Concern; a systematic review rated most male studies poor quality [med-sylvester2019]; and in a preconception cohort, male depression rather than medication explained most of a weak fecundability association [med-yland2022], with active depression in men linked to lower conception [med-evanshoeker2018].
entries.title: SSRIs (antidepressants) and sperm DNA

entries.headline: In the largest preconception cohort, severe depressive symptoms lowered the monthly chance of conceiving (FR 0.62) whether or not they were treated, and psychotropic medication itself did not appear to harm fecundability; a possible miscarriage signal with antidepressants remains unresolved.

dose.effective: Standard therapeutic SSRI doses as prescribed.
dose.studied_range: Self-reported antidepressant use in preconception cohorts (957-2146 women) and infertility-trial cohorts (1650 women).
dose.too_much: No dose threshold established.
dose.timeframe: Associations measured per menstrual cycle over 6-12 months of trying.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Guidelines (ACOG 2023) support individualized decisions and SSRIs as first-line drug treatment in pregnancy; stopping an effective antidepressant risks relapse, which itself affects fertility and pregnancy.

entries.mechanism: No established oxidative mechanism; serotonin signalling and the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis may interact, and depression itself affects behaviour, sleep and stress hormones [med-nillni2016].
entries.interactions: [psychological-stress] and [short-sleep] overlap with depression; the male-partner side is covered by [ssris].
entries.caveats: Confounding by the underlying depression is the central problem in every study.
entries.debate: Reassuring: in PRESTO, medication use did not harm fecundability and depression did [med-nillni2016], and a review found insufficient evidence that SSRIs reduce fertility or IVF outcomes [med-sylvester2019]. Concerning: another cohort found lower cycle-specific fecundability with antidepressants after adjusting for depression history (FR 0.66) [med-casillalennon2016], and maternal antidepressant use was associated with first-trimester loss in infertility trials [med-evanshoeker2018]. ACOG supports continuing effective treatment with shared decision-making [med-acog2023].
entries.title: Antidepressants while trying to conceive

entries.headline: Two large RCTs disagree on cancer (PHS II HR 0.92 over 11 years; COSMOS HR 0.97 over 3.6 years), neither cut heart disease or death, and a 390,000-person cohort found no mortality benefit; COSMOS did find a small slowing of cognitive ageing (0.07 SD). It is nutrient insurance for shortfalls, not an antioxidant therapy.

dose.effective: One daily multivitamin/mineral near RDA levels (100% DV range), chosen for need: iron-free for men and postmenopausal women; a prenatal with 400-800 ug folic acid, ~150 ug iodine and ~27 mg iron when trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: Centrum Silver-type formulas in PHS II and COSMOS.
dose.too_much: Avoid 'mega' or 'antioxidant' formulas: preformed vitamin A >3000 ug (10,000 IU), beta-carotene in smokers, vitamin E >=400 IU, selenium >=200 ug, zinc >25-40 mg, folic acid >1000 ug unless prescribed. Stacking several products easily breaches ULs.
dose.timeframe: Cognitive effects over 2-3 years in COSMOS; cancer effect after ~11 years in PHS II.
dose.notes: Most useful for restricted diets (vegan: B12, iodine, zinc), older adults (B12 absorption), heavy drinkers, bariatric surgery, and before/during pregnancy.

entries.mechanism: Corrects marginal shortfalls of cofactors for antioxidant and DNA-maintenance enzymes (selenium for GPx, zinc/copper for SOD1, manganese for SOD2, riboflavin for glutathione reductase, folate/B12 for one-carbon metabolism) rather than scavenging radicals directly.
entries.interactions: Not the same as [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]. Adds to dietary selenium [selenium-supplement] and vitamin A [beta-carotene-supplement]. Prenatal formulas deliver [folic-acid] and [iodine-status]. Iron content matters [iron-excess] [iron-deficiency].
entries.caveats: Trial populations were well-nourished older Americans, so benefits may be larger where diets are poor and smaller where they are good. The PHS II cancer result was a modest effect on one of several endpoints.
entries.debate: Supportive: PHS II cancer reduction [nut-gaziano2012], COSMOS cognitive benefit [nut-vyas2024], USPSTF evidence review showing a small pooled cancer reduction (OR 0.93) [nut-oconnor2022], and lower ovulatory infertility in multivitamin users [nut-chavarro2008]. Sceptical: COSMOS found no cancer or CVD effect [nut-sesso2022], PHS II found no CVD [nut-sesso2012] or cognitive [nut-grodstein2013] benefit, an editorial questioned the PHS II cancer finding given multiple comparisons [nut-bach2012], USPSTF calls the evidence insufficient [nut-uspstf2022], and a 390,124-person cohort found no mortality benefit [nut-loftfield2024] with commentary on their limited value [nut-barnard2024].
entries.title: Standard multivitamin/mineral (nutritional doses)

entries.headline: Statins lower LDL and, in proportion, oxidized LDL (-39% on atorvastatin 80 mg) and F2-isoprostanes, and cut CRP by 37% in JUPITER; only about 1 in 15 muscle complaints on statins is caused by the drug, and CoQ10 for statin muscle pain has conflicting trial evidence.

dose.effective: Prescribed by cardiovascular risk: moderate intensity (e.g. atorvastatin 10-20 mg, rosuvastatin 5-10 mg) or high intensity (atorvastatin 40-80 mg, rosuvastatin 20-40 mg).
dose.studied_range: Rosuvastatin 20 mg (JUPITER, 1.9 years median); atorvastatin 10 vs 80 mg (12 weeks, oxidative markers); simvastatin 20-40 mg (exercise and CoQ10 trials).
dose.too_much: High-intensity regimens give a slightly larger muscle-symptom excess (RR 1.08 vs 1.03); JUPITER saw more physician-reported diabetes.
dose.timeframe: LDL and oxidized LDL fall within weeks; event reduction accrues over 1-5 years; excess muscle symptoms occur mainly in year 1.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. If muscle symptoms appear, ask about a supervised re-challenge or dose change rather than quitting; most symptoms are not drug-caused. CoQ10 (100-600 mg/day in trials) is harmless but not reliably helpful. Most women should stop statins once pregnancy is recognized, but very high-risk patients may continue with their doctor (FDA 2021).

entries.mechanism: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition lowers cholesterol and also isoprenoid intermediates, reducing prenylation of Rho and Rac and hence NADPH oxidase activation and ROS production in cell and animal studies [med-oesterle2017]. In humans the fall in F2-isoprostanes tracked the fall in LDL, implying much of the 'antioxidant' effect follows from removing oxidizable lipoprotein [med-decaterina2002]. The same mevalonate pathway makes coenzyme Q10, which statins lower in blood [med-taylor2015].
entries.interactions: Lower oxidized LDL more than [vitamin-e-supplement] (adding vitamin E to simvastatin added nothing). [coq10] is often taken for statin myalgia with mixed evidence. May blunt gains from [aerobic-exercise-moderate] in one RCT, yet fitness plus statins carried the lowest mortality in a cohort. Similar exercise debate to [metformin]. Complements [mediterranean-diet] and [glycemic-control] for cardiovascular risk.
entries.caveats: Pleiotropic claims come mostly from cells and animals and are hard to separate from LDL lowering. The exercise-blunting finding rests on one small 12-week trial. Statin effects on sperm are probably negligible, though one 17-man pilot found a 31% fall in sperm count on atorvastatin.
entries.debate: CoQ10 for statin myopathy: a 6-trial meta-analysis found no significant effect [med-banach2015] and a well-run RCT in confirmed myalgia found none [med-taylor2015], whereas a 12-trial meta-analysis found reduced pain, weakness and cramps [med-qu2018]; individual-patient data show most muscle complaints on statins are not drug-caused [med-ctt2022]. Exercise: simvastatin abolished fitness and mitochondrial gains in one RCT [med-mikus2013], but statin users who were fit had the lowest mortality [med-kokkinos2013] and atorvastatin did not reduce habitual activity vs placebo [med-panza2016]; reviewers call for trials in healthy users [med-miller2020]. Pleiotropy beyond LDL remains disputed [med-oesterle2017, med-decaterina2002]. Pregnancy: no excess malformations [med-bateman2015, med-vahedianazimi2021, med-dutta2026], but a Taiwan cohort linked use to low birth weight and preterm birth [med-chang2021]. Sperm: a small pilot reported harm [med-ponsrejraji2014]; a systematic review and a large clinic study found no clinically relevant effect [med-anagnostis2021, med-keihani2018a].
entries.title: Statins

entries.headline: Sulfasalazine (2-4 g/day) reliably but reversibly damages sperm, with pregnancies typically about 2.5 months after switching; low-dose methotrexate showed no change in semen or sperm DNA fragmentation and no excess birth defects in 127 children of exposed fathers.

dose.effective: Sulfasalazine 2-4 g/day; low-dose weekly methotrexate as used in arthritis, psoriasis and IBD.
dose.studied_range: Sulfasalazine 2-4 g/day for >2 months; methotrexate in 20 men followed prospectively and 127 Danish births.
dose.too_much: Sulfasalazine at any therapeutic dose for over 2 months; high-dose methotrexate as chemotherapy is a different exposure (see chemo-radiation).
dose.timeframe: Sulfasalazine effects reverse within about 2-3 months of switching; methotrexate data cover the 90 days before conception.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Men on sulfasalazine who are trying to conceive can ask about switching to mesalazine or another agent; the ACR guideline supports continuing low-dose methotrexate in men planning conception.

entries.mechanism: The sulphapyridine part of sulfasalazine is toxic to maturing sperm late in their development (rat data show the same effect with sulphapyridine but not 5-aminosalicylic acid) [med-omorain1984]. Methotrexate barely accumulates in sperm because of low folylpolyglutamate synthetase activity [med-perezgarcia2023].
entries.interactions: Underlying inflammatory disease ([chronic-inflammation]) can itself affect fertility; high-dose cytotoxic treatment belongs under [chemo-radiation]. Folate status ([folate-zinc]) is relevant for methotrexate users.
entries.caveats: Sulfasalazine data are older and small but consistent. Methotrexate data come from 20 men and registry births; high-dose regimens are not covered.
entries.debate: Older advice to stop methotrexate 3 months before conception is contested by a Danish registry (aOR 1.01 for malformations) [med-eck2017] and a prospective semen study [med-perezgarcia2023]; reviews still describe its sperm effect as uncertain and note animal testicular toxicity [med-perezgarcia2020, med-banerjee2019]. For sulfasalazine there is no real disagreement: men on it have lower counts and motility than men on mesalazine [med-banerjee2019, med-toovey1981].
entries.title: Sulfasalazine & methotrexate (bowel and arthritis drugs)

factors.name: Sulforaphane / broccoli extract supplements
aliases: Sulforaphane / broccoli sprouts for egg and ovarian function
Sulforaphane / broccoli sprouts for sperm quality

entries.headline: Product type decides everything: glucoraphanin-only pills convert about 5-20% and very unevenly, whereas preformed (stabilised) sulforaphane or myrosinase-active products deliver about 40-70%; trials at 50-200 µmol/day show mixed results (modest glucose benefit in obese poorly controlled diabetes, small autism effects, several nulls).

dose.effective: Myrosinase-active or stabilised-sulforaphane products supplying roughly 40-150 µmol sulforaphane (about 7-27 mg) per day, the range used in most positive and negative trials.
dose.studied_range: 25-200 µmol/day sulforaphane-equivalent for 4 weeks to 12 months; up to ~340 µmol (60 mg) stabilised sulforaphane for 6 months; glucoraphanin 25-600 µmol/day.
dose.too_much: No serious toxicity in trials up to 200 µmol/day for weeks to months. GI effects (nausea, loose stools, reflux) are the main dose-limiting problem and contributed to drop-outs at 150 µmol/day and with 15-capsule regimens.
dose.timeframe: Hours per dose (pulsatile); clinical effects in trials appeared after 4-18 weeks and faded within weeks of stopping.
dose.notes: Check the label for active myrosinase or stabilised sulforaphane and an assayed µmol figure. A myrosinase-free supplement gave far lower isothiocyanates than 40 g fresh sprouts. Splitting the daily dose keeps blood levels up longer. Conversion is lower in people with higher body mass.

entries.mechanism: Nrf2 activation; human blood-cell HDAC inhibition after sprouts or glucoraphanin supplements in some studies; hepatic gluconeogenesis suppression via NRF2 in the diabetes work. Glucoraphanin without myrosinase depends on gut microbial activity, which antibiotics and bowel cleansing abolish.
entries.interactions: Redundant with [broccoli-sprouts] and [broccoli-seed-powder]. Poor microbial 'converters' gain most from myrosinase-active or preformed forms. Sulforaphane inhibited CYP3A4 and induced conjugating enzymes in human liver cells, and crucifer diets induce UGT1A1 in people: a theoretical interaction with drugs cleared by these enzymes at high supplement doses. In cancer patients, strong Nrf2 activation could theoretically protect tumour cells from chemotherapy; discuss with the oncologist. Not shown to add to [turmeric-curcumin] or [isolated-polyphenol-supplements].
entries.caveats: About half of registered sulforaphane trials remain unpublished. Effects in published trials are inconsistent: 150 µmol/day did not induce Nrf2 targets in COPD lungs; prediabetes trial missed its primary endpoint; autism trials in young children were null; prostate PSA trials missed primary endpoints. Commercial labels are often not independently verified. Long-term high-dose Nrf2 activation has open safety questions (synthetic activator bardoxolone raised heart-failure events).

entries.title: Sulforaphane / broccoli extract supplements

entries.headline: No human trial has tested sulforaphane or broccoli sprouts on sperm DNA fragmentation, motility or fertility; protection is shown only in rodents exposed to toxins, diabetes or high-fat diets and in human sperm treated in the lab.

dose.effective: Unknown for sperm. General-health doses (30-70 g fresh sprouts, or 40-150 µmol sulforaphane/day) are the only human-tested amounts.
dose.studied_range: Rodents: injected or oral sulforaphane for weeks to months; in vitro: 5 µM added to human semen before freezing.
dose.too_much: Not established; in cell culture sulforaphane becomes cytotoxic above about 10-15 µM, far above blood levels from food.
dose.timeframe: One spermatogenic cycle (about 74 days) would be needed to see any effect.
dose.notes: The in vitro cryopreservation result applies to sperm-freezing media, not to eating broccoli.

entries.mechanism: Nrf2-driven antioxidant genes in testis, AMPK-dependent relief of ER stress in sperm, and reduced testicular apoptosis in diabetic or toxin-exposed animals.
entries.interactions: Same redundancy considerations as [broccoli-sprouts] and [sulforaphane-supplements]; no data on combining with other sperm antioxidants such as [n-acetylcysteine].
entries.caveats: All evidence is animal or in vitro; rodent models used toxic exposures (phthalates, diabetes, high-fat diet) and often injected doses. Do not expect measurable improvement in semen analysis from broccoli in healthy men.
entries.title: Sulforaphane / broccoli sprouts for sperm quality

entries.headline: No human trial has tested sulforaphane on egg quality, ovarian reserve, PCOS or IVF outcomes; it protects human granulosa cells and animal oocytes from oxidative stress in the lab, but becomes cytotoxic to granulosa cells at higher concentrations.

dose.effective: Unknown for ovarian outcomes; only general-health doses have been tested in people.
dose.studied_range: In vitro: about 1-5 µM in oocyte maturation or granulosa-cell culture.
dose.too_much: Bovine granulosa cells lost viability above about 15 µM in culture.
dose.timeframe: Follicle development takes about 3 months, so any dietary effect would need at least that long.
dose.notes: In vitro maturation results apply to IVF lab media, not diet.

entries.mechanism: Nrf2 activation (SOD, catalase, GCLC/GCLM, HO-1, NQO1) and AMPK/AKT signalling in granulosa cells and oocytes; reduced ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction and spindle defects after toxin exposure.
entries.interactions: Same redundancy considerations as [broccoli-sprouts] and [sulforaphane-supplements]. The modest glucose-lowering seen in obese people with poorly controlled diabetes ([glycemic-control]) is the only human finding with plausible indirect relevance to PCOS, and it has not been tested in PCOS.
entries.caveats: Cell and animal data only; biphasic (protective at low, harmful at high concentrations) responses argue against high-dose supplementation around conception without data.
entries.title: Sulforaphane / broccoli sprouts for egg and ovarian function

factors.name: Sun/UV exposure (photoaging and skin DNA damage)

entries.headline: Chronic unprotected UV is the main driver of visible skin aging and of skin cancer: a single exposure switched on collagen-degrading MMPs and raised collagen breakdown 58% in human skin, and identical twins with more sun exposure looked older.

dose.effective: Avoid sunburn. Around midday and whenever the UV index is high, use shade, clothing and a hat, plus daily broad-spectrum sunscreen on exposed skin (see [sunscreen]).
dose.studied_range: Experimental studies used single or repeated (every 2 days) erythemal UV doses on buttock skin; twin and cohort data reflect lifetime exposure.
dose.too_much: Any sunburn, tanning beds, and long cumulative outdoor exposure without protection.
dose.timeframe: MMP induction within hours of one exposure, sustained about 7 days with repeated exposure; visible photoaging accrues over years to decades.
dose.notes: Vitamin D: a consensus panel concluded that sunscreen used to prevent sunburn is unlikely to compromise vitamin D status; people with low levels or strict photoprotection needs should test and supplement rather than tan.

entries.mechanism: UVB (290-320 nm) is absorbed directly by DNA, forming cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) and 6-4 photoproducts. UVA (320-400 nm) penetrates deeper into the dermis and is absorbed by cellular chromophores that generate singlet oxygen and superoxide, producing 8-oxo-dG, lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial DNA deletions; in whole human skin UVA also forms CPDs, which outnumber 8-oxo-dG and are repaired more slowly. ROS-activated MAP kinase signalling drives AP-1, which induces MMP-1 (collagenase), MMP-3 and MMP-9 and suppresses new procollagen, while NF-kB drives inflammation. Repeated sub-burning exposures leave behind fragmented collagen: photoaging.
entries.interactions: [tobacco-smoking] and traffic-related [outdoor-air-pollution] add to extrinsic skin aging. Oral antioxidants do not replace UV protection: 30 mg/day beta-carotene ([beta-carotene-supplement]) had no effect on photoaging or skin cancer in Nambour, and the SU.VI.MAX antioxidant capsule raised skin cancer in women. Protection and repair options: [sunscreen], [topical-retinoids], and in high-risk people [nicotinamide].
entries.caveats: Whole-body oxidative-marker effects of ordinary sun exposure are not well documented; the evidence concerns skin. Visible light and near-infrared also generate ROS in skin in lab and biopsy studies, but whether everyday doses cause visible aging is unproven (visible light does matter for melasma and darker skin types). Twin and survey studies are observational and partly self-reported.
entries.debate: Mechanism weighting: the textbook picture of UVA as an 'oxidative' waveband is complicated by evidence that CPDs, not 8-oxo-dG, are the predominant UVA lesion in whole human skin [skb-mouret2006]. Beyond UV: visible light induced ROS and MMP-1 in skin equivalents [skb-liebel2012] and IR-A induced MMP-1 in human skin in vivo [skb-schroeder2008], but Diffey and Cadars argue solar IR doses equal those of furnace workers who show little chronic damage, so IR-protection claims are premature [skb-diffey2016]. Vitamin D: concern that sun avoidance causes deficiency is countered by a consensus review concluding normal sunscreen use does not compromise status [skb-passeron2019], though that panel included cosmetics-industry scientists.
