factors.name: Supplement-drug interactions (anticoagulants, nitrates, St John's wort)

entries.headline: Vitamin E raised haemorrhagic stroke 22% in trials, NAC with nitroglycerin caused symptomatic hypotension and intolerable headache in a third of patients, and St John's wort sped up oral-contraceptive breakdown (breakthrough bleeding in 7 of 12 women); fish oil, by contrast, did not raise bleeding overall in 120,643 trial patients.

dose.effective: Not applicable: this is about avoiding harmful combinations.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin E 50-800 IU/day (stroke trials) and 100-400 IU/day with warfarin; NAC 10 g/day IV or oral with nitroglycerin; high-hyperforin St John's wort (>10 mg hyperforin/day); omega-3 up to 4 g/day purified EPA.
dose.too_much: Vitamin E above ~400 IU/day with anticoagulants; any NAC with nitrate therapy without supervision; any St John's wort with hormonal contraceptives, transplant drugs or other CYP3A substrates; high-dose purified EPA (bleeding RR ~1.5, absolute +0.6%).
dose.timeframe: Interactions act within days of starting the combination.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Bring a list of all supplements to every prescriber and pharmacist; ask before combining supplements with anticoagulants, antiplatelets, nitrates, hormonal contraception or immunosuppressants.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin E may antagonize vitamin K-dependent clotting factors at high doses [med-corrigan1981]; omega-3s alter platelet function without clearly raising bleeding [med-wachira2014]; NAC supplies thiols that potentiate nitroglycerin's vasodilation [med-horowitz1988]; St John's wort's hyperforin induces CYP3A, accelerating breakdown of ethinyl estradiol and progestins [med-hall2003, med-whitten2006].
entries.interactions: Applies to [vitamin-e-supplement], [omega3-fish], [n-acetylcysteine], [turmeric-curcumin] and [curcumin-supplements]. Contraceptive failure from St John's wort parallels the oral-contraceptive interaction of tirzepatide ([glp1-agonists]).
entries.caveats: Curcumin is often listed as a warfarin potentiator, but the evidence is case-level; it was not among the higher-risk items named in a 2021 systematic review of warfarin interactions [med-tan2021]. Vitamin E 400 IU/day did not change prothrombin time in a small warfarin study.
entries.debate: Fish oil: reviews and a 2024 meta-analysis found no increase in clinically significant bleeding even with antithrombotic drugs [med-wachira2014, med-javaid2024], though high-dose purified EPA showed a small dose-related signal [med-javaid2024]. Vitamin E: no prothrombin-time change at <=400 IU/day with warfarin [med-corrigan1981], but a 9-trial meta-analysis found more haemorrhagic strokes [med-schurks2010]. NAC with nitrates: the combination reduced cardiac events in angina trials yet was limited by hypotension and headache [med-horowitz1988, med-ardissino1997]. Warfarin and herbs: most supplements are safe in moderation but dozens potentiate warfarin [med-tan2021].
entries.title: Supplement-drug interactions (anticoagulants, nitrates, St John's wort)

entries.headline: Taurine extended mouse lifespan in a 2023 Science study, but a 2025 NIH study found blood taurine does not fall with age in humans; human trials show only small drops in blood pressure (about 4 mmHg systolic), glucose and triglycerides.

dose.effective: 1.5-3 g/day; 1.6 g/day for 12 weeks lowered clinic systolic BP by 7.2 vs 2.6 mmHg (placebo) in prehypertension
dose.studied_range: 0.5-6 g/day for 5 days to 1 year in RCTs
dose.too_much: Observed safe level 3 g/day for long-term use; no systematic adverse effects in trials up to 6 g/day
dose.timeframe: Blood-pressure and metabolic effects measured at 8-12 weeks; endurance effects seen after a single dose
dose.notes: Diet supplies taurine mainly from meat, fish and shellfish. Mouse doses, scaled per kg of body weight, are much higher than typical human supplement doses. Energy drinks contain taurine plus caffeine and sugar; those are not a sensible source.

entries.mechanism: Taurine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that is not built into proteins. It conjugates bile acids, regulates cell volume and calcium, and modifies mitochondrial tRNAs, which supports translation of respiratory-chain proteins. It is a weak direct antioxidant; its proposed anti-aging effects in mice act through less mitochondrial dysfunction, less cellular senescence, less DNA damage and lower inflammation. In humans it may lower blood pressure partly through hydrogen sulfide and improved endothelial function.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with exercise, which raised blood taurine acutely in the Singh study; there is no evidence that taurine adds to the benefits of [aerobic-exercise-moderate]. Often stacked with [glycine] and [n-acetylcysteine] in 'longevity' blends with no trial of the combination.
entries.caveats: The 'taurine deficiency drives aging' claim rests on mouse and monkey data plus human cross-sectional associations. Monkeys showed health-span markers, not lifespan. Human blood taurine varies with diet and was not consistently lower in older people in larger longitudinal cohorts. No trial has tested taurine on aging outcomes in humans.
entries.debate: Singh et al. reported that circulating taurine declines with age in mice, monkeys and humans and that supplementation extended mouse median lifespan and improved monkey health span [lon-singh2023], a result welcomed as a reason for human trials [lon-mcgaunn2023]. An NIH group led by Fernandez and de Cabo measured taurine longitudinally in three human cohorts, monkeys and mice and found it increased or stayed flat with age, with inconsistent links to health outcomes, arguing taurine is not a universal aging biomarker [lon-fernandez2025]. On the clinical side, a meta-analysis of 25 small RCTs found modest metabolic benefits [lon-tzang2024], consistent with one well-run BP trial [lon-sun2016], but the trials are short and heterogeneous.
entries.title: Taurine

factors.name: Testicular sperm for ICSI when ejaculated SDF stays high

entries.headline: Sperm taken directly from the testis have about 25 percentage points less DNA fragmentation than ejaculated sperm, and pooled studies show higher pregnancy and live birth with ICSI.

dose.effective: Testicular sperm aspiration/extraction (TESA/TESE) for ICSI in non-azoospermic men with confirmed high SDF, usually after failed IVF/ICSI or recurrent miscarriage.
dose.studied_range: 5 studies with paired SDF (143 men); 4 studies, 507 cycles with clinical outcomes.
dose.too_much: Invasive; small risks of bleeding, infection and testicular damage; testicular sperm have higher aneuploidy in some studies.
dose.timeframe: Single procedure at the time of egg retrieval.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM 2024: may consider. EAU: experimental (weak). Try reversible causes and short-abstinence ejaculates first; a meta-analysis found testicular SDF ~9.5 points lower than short-abstinence ejaculates.

entries.mechanism: Much oxidative DNA damage occurs during epididymal transit and storage, where defective sperm and leukocytes generate ROS; testicular sperm bypass this exposure.
entries.interactions: Compare with [short-abstinence], which reduces epididymal storage time non-invasively.
entries.caveats: Evidence is from small, mostly non-randomised studies. Not appropriate as first-line care.
entries.title: Testicular sperm for ICSI when ejaculated SDF stays high

entries.headline: Two large double-blind RCTs (TILT, 1575 women; SelecTIMO, 1731 couples) found no live-birth or cumulative-pregnancy gain from time-lapse culture or time-lapse-based selection; HFEA rates it black (no effect).

dose.effective: No benefit for live birth; harmless if the clinic includes it at no extra cost.
dose.studied_range: Time-lapse incubators with manual or algorithmic (e.g. EEVA, KIDScore) embryo selection.
dose.too_much: No known extra risk; cost only.
dose.timeframe: Embryo culture days 0-5.
dose.notes: Useful as a lab-management tool (undisturbed culture, records), not as a success booster.

entries.mechanism: Continuous imaging avoids taking embryos out of the incubator (stable temperature, pH and oxygen, i.e. less culture stress) and adds timing data for selection.
entries.interactions: Often bundled with AI embryo selection; same lack of live-birth data applies.
entries.caveats: Earlier Cochrane evidence was low quality and inconclusive.
entries.debate: Proponents point to the non-significant +3.6 points with undisturbed culture in TILT [fer-bhide2024]; trialists conclude widespread use 'should be questioned' [fer-kieslinger2023]. Cochrane found low-quality, inconclusive evidence [fer-armstrong2019]; HFEA and ESHRE say it does not improve live birth [fer-hfea2026, fer-eshre2023addons].

entries.title: Time-lapse embryo imaging and incubation

entries.headline: Eating within an 8-10 h window cuts intake by roughly 170-550 kcal/day and gives weight loss similar to calorie counting; when calories are matched (Liu 2022 NEJM, Peters 2025) it adds little or nothing, and 4-6 h windows lowered 8-isoprostane ~35% only alongside ~3% weight loss.

dose.effective: An 8-10 h daily window, ideally early (e.g., 8:00-16:00 or 7:00-15:00), at least 5-6 days/week, for 12 weeks or more.
dose.studied_range: 4-10 h windows, early (ending 14:00-16:00), mid-day or late (12:00-20:00), 4 days to 12 months.
dose.too_much: Windows of 4-6 h increased lean-mass loss (6-h TRE: -1.5 kg lean in 8 weeks); 16:8 without resistance training reduced appendicular lean mass. An observational NHANES analysis linked <8 h eating to CV mortality (HR 2.35) but is heavily confounded.
dose.timeframe: Glucose and insulin changes within 4 days to 5 weeks; weight loss over 3-12 months.
dose.notes: Early windows look better than late ones in some trials (Xie 2022) but not when calories are held constant (Peters 2025). The overnight fast in a 16:8 schedule barely raises ketones (~0.1-0.15 mmol/L).

entries.mechanism: Mainly spontaneous energy reduction. Early windows align meals with daytime insulin sensitivity and lower evening glucose exposure; a longer overnight fast lowers insulin and slightly raises fat oxidation and ketones. eTRF raised blood SIRT1 and LC3A expression in one 4-day study.
entries.interactions: Equivalent to [calorie-restriction] at matched intake; benefits track [weight-loss]. Combine with [resistance-training] and ~1.6 g/kg protein to keep lean mass. Late windows that push dinner close to bedtime may conflict with [short-sleep] and [shift-work-circadian]. Useful as a weight-loss tool in [pcos].
entries.caveats: Many trials are small and short. TREAT (Lowe 2020) found 16:8 alone no better than three meals. Manoogian 2024 found only a -0.10% HbA1c effect in metabolic syndrome. The 2024 AHA abstract (published as Chen 2025) used two days of dietary recall; the <8 h group was ~2% of participants, more often smokers, food-insecure and habitual breakfast-skippers, and the CV association lost significance when <8 h was required on both recall days (HR 1.78, 0.85-3.74).

entries.headline: Smoking roughly doubles plasma F2-isoprostanes, which fall measurably within 2 weeks of quitting. It raises urinary 8-OHdG and turns beta-carotene supplements harmful.

dose.effective: Complete cessation.
dose.too_much: Any smoking
dose.timeframe: F2-isoprostanes fell significantly after 2 weeks of abstinence
dose.notes: Smokers should avoid beta-carotene and high-dose vitamin A supplements.

entries.mechanism: Cigarette smoke delivers large amounts of radicals and oxidants directly and recruits activated inflammatory cells to the lung. Tumours with activating NRF2 mutations are enriched in smokers.
entries.interactions: Strongly interacts with [beta-carotene-supplement] (lung cancer RR 1.18-1.28). NRF2-mutant tumours occur especially in smokers.
entries.caveats: No antioxidant supplement offsets smoking.
entries.title: Tobacco smoking

entries.headline: Smoking roughly doubles circulating F2-isoprostanes in a dose-dependent way; quitting lowers them within 2 weeks and to a new steady state by about 4 weeks, making it the single largest lifestyle lever.

dose.effective: Quit completely. In an RCT, cutting down from ~27 to ~18 cigarettes/day did not lower F2-isoprostanes or any other harm marker except carbon monoxide.
dose.studied_range: Studies compared heavy, moderate and non-smokers; cessation studies followed people from 2 weeks to 1 year.
dose.too_much: No safe level: urinary 8-epi-PGF2a was ~1.7x the nonsmoker level in moderate and ~3.3x in heavy smokers.
dose.timeframe: Isoprostanes fall within days, are ~20-40% lower at 2-3 weeks, and plateau about 4 weeks after quitting; cardiovascular risk falls ~39% within 5 years but takes 10-15+ years to approach never-smoker levels.
dose.notes: Nicotine replacement did not prevent the fall in isoprostanes, suggesting combustion products, not nicotine, drive most of it.

entries.mechanism: Each puff delivers large amounts of free radicals in the gas and tar phases (semiquinone radicals, NO, peroxynitrite, H2O2), plus metals and aldehydes. Smoke also activates neutrophils and vascular NADPH oxidase, depletes vitamin C and E, and uncouples eNOS.
entries.interactions: Effects add to [alcohol], [secondhand-smoke] and [outdoor-air-pollution]. Weight gain after quitting does not cancel the drop in oxidative markers. Smoking is also the main source of cadmium ([heavy-metals]) and worsens [periodontal-disease].
entries.caveats: Five days of 2 g/day vitamin C lowered smokers' isoprostanes in Reilly 1996 (vitamin E alone did not), but that is not a substitute for quitting. Smoking harms sperm parameters (meta-analysis) and is relevant to egg health (cross-link to fertility areas).
entries.title: Smoking tobacco (and quitting)

entries.headline: Smokers average about 9 percentage points higher SDF and lower count, motility and morphology; quitting improves semen within 3-6 months.

dose.effective: Quit completely; harm rises with cigarettes per day (moderate/heavy smokers, roughly >10/day, show larger effects).
dose.studied_range: Light (<10/day) to heavy (>20/day) smokers in clinic and population samples.
dose.too_much: No safe level identified; avoid second-hand smoke too.
dose.timeframe: Semen improved at 3 months and further at 6 months after quitting.
dose.notes: Nicotine replacement is far less harmful than smoking. Vaping data for sperm are sparse.

entries.mechanism: Tobacco smoke delivers oxidants, cadmium, lead and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; seminal leukocytes and ROS rise, antioxidant levels fall, and sperm show more 8-OHdG and strand breaks.
entries.interactions: Stacks with [varicocele] and [outdoor-air-pollution]. Non-responders to stopping heat exposure in one series were mostly smokers. Antioxidant pills do not offset smoking.
entries.caveats: Effects on standard semen parameters are moderate; the clearest harm is on DNA integrity and on offspring and partner health.
entries.title: Tobacco smoking

entries.headline: Smoking is the largest avoidable toxic exposure for eggs: about 60% higher odds of infertility, roughly halved odds of IVF live birth (OR 0.54), lower AMH and twice the risk of early menopause.

dose.effective: Zero. Risk is dose-dependent (cigarettes/day, years smoked, pack-years).
dose.studied_range: Current vs never smokers; dose-response up to >20 cigarettes/day and 15-20+ years.
dose.too_much: Any active smoking. 11-15 pack-years: ~4-fold risk of premature menopause; 15-20 years' duration: much higher.
dose.timeframe: Quitting at least 3 months before trying covers one follicle-growth cycle; menopause-timing risk normalises about 10 years after quitting.
dose.notes: ASRM's 2024 opinion also reviews nicotine and marijuana as potential reproductive harms.

entries.mechanism: Tobacco smoke delivers polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, cadmium and other oxidants that accelerate follicle loss (lower AMH), raise follicular oxidative stress and impair oocyte maturation.
entries.interactions: Adds to [maternal-age]. Cadmium overlaps with [heavy-metals]. Cessation is covered by [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: Evidence is observational, but consistent across designs and dose-dependent, which supports causation.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth per cycle, smokers

entries.title: Cigarette smoking

entries.headline: Quitting removes the biggest avoidable egg toxin; former smokers' excess menopause risk is much smaller than current smokers' and disappears about 10 years after quitting.

dose.effective: Complete cessation, ideally at least 3 months before trying or before IVF stimulation.
dose.studied_range: Former vs current smokers, years since quitting.
dose.timeframe: One follicle-growth cycle (~3 months) for the follicular environment; longer for ovarian-reserve effects.
dose.notes: Lost follicles are not regained, so earlier is better. Use evidence-based cessation support.

entries.mechanism: Removes the exogenous oxidant and toxicant load (PAHs, cadmium) on growing follicles.
entries.interactions: See [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: No RCT has randomised women to quit and measured egg quality; the benefit is inferred from the dose-response and former-smoker data.
entries.title: Stopping smoking

factors.name: Tomatoes and tomato products (cooked with oil)

entries.headline: Lycopene is 2.5-3.8x more bioavailable from tomato paste than fresh tomatoes and needs fat to be absorbed; tomato interventions lower LDL and IL-6, improve FMD, and blunted LDL oxidation after a high-fat meal.

dose.effective: A serving of cooked tomato product (sauce, paste, puree) with a little olive oil most days.
dose.studied_range: 21 intervention trials of tomato products or lycopene; single meals with processed tomato.
dose.timeframe: Postprandial (same meal) for oxLDL; weeks for lipids and FMD.
dose.notes: Tomato puree has ~8x the lycopene of raw tomato per 100 g (USDA). Fat-free dressing gave essentially no carotenoid absorption from salad.

entries.mechanism: Lycopene is a lipid-phase singlet-oxygen quencher carried in LDL; processing breaks cell walls and isomerises lycopene, improving absorption; tomato also supplies vitamin C and naringenin chalcone.
entries.interactions: Pair with [extra-virgin-olive-oil] or avocado; eat with high-fat meals to blunt postprandial oxidation.
entries.caveats: Lycopene supplements lowered systolic BP in pooled trials but tomato products, not pills, gave the lipid and FMD effects. Most trials are short.

key_numbers.label: Lycopene AUC, paste vs fresh tomato

entries.title: Tomatoes and tomato products (cooked with oil)

entries.headline: A placebo-controlled trial of 14 mg/day lycopene improved fast motility and morphology, but missed its primary endpoint; no SDF data.

dose.effective: About 14 mg lycopene/day, roughly half a cup of tomato sauce or passata (content varies by product); cooked tomato with some oil is better absorbed than raw.
dose.studied_range: 14 mg/day lactolycopene for 12 weeks in 60 healthy men.
dose.timeframe: 12 weeks.
dose.notes: Getting lycopene from food also brings other carotenoids and fibre.

entries.mechanism: Lycopene is a potent singlet-oxygen quencher concentrated in the testes and seminal fluid.
entries.interactions: Part of [mediterranean-diet]; included in the MOXI supplement (10 mg), which was null.
entries.caveats: Single small trial in healthy men; primary outcome (motile sperm concentration) not significant (p=0.058).
entries.title: Tomatoes and lycopene

entries.headline: The best-proven topical treatment for photoaging: tretinoin improved 14 of 15 treated faces versus none on vehicle in 16 weeks, retinol 0.4% smoothed fine wrinkles even at age 87, and tretinoin blocked 70-80% of UV-induced collagenase; it does not prevent skin cancer.

dose.effective: Prescription tretinoin cream at night (0.1% in the classic trials; lower strengths if irritated), or over-the-counter retinol (0.4% lotion up to 3 times a week in the elderly-skin trial); build up from every second or third night.
dose.studied_range: Tretinoin 0.1% daily for 16 weeks to 5.5 years; retinol 0.4% up to 3 times weekly for 24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Irritation, redness and peeling (retinoid dermatitis) are common and dose-related. Avoid during pregnancy as a precaution, although first-trimester topical tretinoin exposure showed no excess birth defects in a 106-pregnancy cohort.
dose.timeframe: Visible improvement from about 16-24 weeks, with continued use needed to maintain it.
dose.notes: Retinoids are not antioxidants: they work downstream of UV-generated ROS by blocking AP-1-driven MMPs and rebuilding matrix. Use with daily [sunscreen].

entries.mechanism: Retinoic acid binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors, which antagonize AP-1 (c-Jun/c-Fos). This blocks the UV- and ROS-triggered induction of MMP-1, MMP-3 and MMP-9, while increasing procollagen I and glycosaminoglycan synthesis and normalizing epidermal turnover.
entries.interactions: Complements [sunscreen] (prevention) and [uv-sun-exposure] avoidance; stronger evidence than [topical-vitamin-c] for wrinkles. Oral retinoid-like compounds such as high-dose [beta-carotene-supplement] are a different story and are not a substitute.
entries.caveats: Most photoaging trials are small and vehicle-controlled over months, with clinician-graded outcomes. In the large VATTC trial, high-dose tretinoin did not prevent basal- or squamous-cell carcinoma, and the trial stopped early because of excess deaths in the tretinoin arm.
entries.debate: Efficacy for photoaging is not seriously disputed [skb-weiss1988, skb-kafi2007, skb-fisher1997]. The disputes concern cancer and safety: VATTC showed no prevention of keratinocyte carcinoma [skb-weinstock2012] and an unexpected mortality excess [skb-weinstock2009]; the investigators judged it unlikely to be causal given minor baseline imbalances and no plausible mechanism for a topical cream, but the signal has never been explained. Pregnancy: systemic retinoids are teratogens, yet a prospective cohort found no excess malformations after topical tretinoin [skb-loureiro2005], so advice to avoid it is precautionary.

BCC at 5 years, tretinoin vs vehicle

factors.name: Topical vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid serum), alone or with vitamin E and ferulic acid

entries.headline: Vitamin C only gets into skin as L-ascorbic acid at pH below 3.5 (best at about 20%); small vehicle-controlled trials (7 RCTs, 139 people in total) show modest smoothing of wrinkles and lighter pigment, and a 15% C + 1% E + ferulic acid mix doubled UV protection in pig skin, an add-on to sunscreen rather than a replacement.

dose.effective: 10-20% L-ascorbic acid at pH below 3.5, applied once daily in the morning under sunscreen; the best-studied combination is 15% L-ascorbic acid + 1% alpha-tocopherol + ferulic acid.
dose.studied_range: 5-20% L-ascorbic acid for 3-6 months in clinical trials; 4 days of pretreatment in photoprotection studies.
dose.too_much: Concentrations above 20% did not increase skin uptake; the low pH can sting or irritate.
dose.timeframe: Skin levels saturate after about 3 daily applications and fall with a half-life of about 4 days; visible change needs 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Common derivatives (magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, ascorbyl palmitate) did not raise skin vitamin C in pig skin. L-ascorbic acid is unstable in solution; ferulic acid improved the stability of the C+E formula. Eating or swallowing vitamin C does not deliver comparable skin levels ([vitamin-c-supplement]).

entries.mechanism: Ascorbate is the main water-soluble antioxidant in skin, scavenging UV-generated radicals and regenerating alpha-tocopherol from the tocopheroxyl radical. It is also the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases needed to make stable collagen, and it inhibits tyrosinase, which explains the pigment-lightening effect.
entries.interactions: Synergy with vitamin E and ferulic acid in the same formula. Complements [sunscreen] (blocks photons) by mopping up ROS from the photons that get through, including visible and IR-A light. [topical-retinoids] have stronger evidence for wrinkles.
entries.caveats: The trials are small, short, split-face or split-arm, and often run or funded by the product developers. There are no long-term trials of visible aging and none on skin cancer. 'Doubled photoprotection' means a protection factor of about 8, measured in pig skin, well below a typical sunscreen.
entries.debate: Supporters point to vehicle-controlled improvements in wrinkles and pigmentation [skb-humbert2003, skb-correia2023] and to a 31-study Bayesian pooling showing dose-dependent prevention of UV pigmentation [skb-dedormael2019]. Sceptics note the pooled studies were all run in-house by L'Oreal, the key formulation papers come from the group that developed the C+E+ferulic serum [skb-lin2003, skb-lin2005, skb-pinnell2001], and the only independent systematic review found just 139 participants across 7 trials [skb-correia2023]. No independent large RCT exists.

entries.headline: A teaspoon (2-3 g) of ground turmeric holds roughly 60-100 mg curcumin, and eating it in food produces only nanomolar curcumin conjugates in blood (free curcumin mostly undetectable), so culinary turmeric is a pleasant spice with plausible gut-local effects but no demonstrated systemic antioxidant effect.

dose.effective: No proven systemic dose from cooking. Normal culinary use (about 1/2-2 teaspoons, 1.5-6 g ground turmeric/day in curries) is safe; one small haemodialysis trial used 2.5 g turmeric in juice three times a week.
dose.studied_range: Culinary-level feeding studies used a few grams of turmeric per meal; supplement trials use 80 mg-3 g/day of curcuminoids, mostly far above what food provides.
dose.too_much: Food amounts are within the EFSA ADI of 3 mg curcumin/kg/day (about 210 mg/day for a 70 kg adult). Turmeric is relatively high in soluble oxalate, a consideration for people with calcium-oxalate kidney stones. Cheap or imported ground turmeric can be adulterated with lead chromate.
dose.timeframe: Plasma conjugates peak about 30 min after a turmeric meal and persist for at least 8 h; no long-term human outcome data.
dose.notes: Pure turmeric powder averages about 3% curcumin by weight; most curry powders contain much less and vary widely. Black pepper and fat are often recommended, but in a head-to-head human study piperine-type adjuvants did not significantly raise curcumin exposure at a 207 mg dose. Buy from suppliers that test for lead; avoid unusually bright, cheap loose turmeric from markets with documented adulteration.

entries.mechanism: Curcumin is an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl (Michael acceptor) that can modify KEAP1 Cys151 and activate Nrf2/HO-1 in cells, inhibits NF-kB signalling in vitro, and scavenges radicals in a test tube. In people, food doses are rapidly glucuronidated and sulfated in gut wall and liver; circulating forms are mainly conjugates that lack the parent compound's activity in cell assays. The gut lumen and intestinal wall are the only tissues likely to see meaningful concentrations.
entries.interactions: Redundant with, and far weaker than, food Nrf2 activators such as [broccoli-sprouts] and [broccoli-seed-powder]. Part of the general [herbs-spices] pattern within a [mediterranean-diet]-style or South Asian diet. Not interchangeable with [curcumin-supplements], which deliver 10-100x more curcuminoids in formulations designed to be absorbed. No known meaningful drug interactions at culinary amounts.
entries.caveats: Population associations (e.g. curry eaters with better cognitive scores in Singapore) cannot separate turmeric from the rest of diet and lifestyle. Claims that 'golden milk' or a pinch of pepper turns kitchen turmeric into a systemic antioxidant are not supported by pharmacokinetic data. In-vitro antioxidant capacity of turmeric says nothing about in-vivo effect. Lead chromate adulteration has been documented in turmeric from Bangladesh, India and Pakistan and has caused childhood lead poisoning in the US.

factors.name: Unneeded iron supplements / excess iron intake

entries.headline: Iron pills taken without a deficiency mostly pass unabsorbed into the colon, where 19 mg/day raised faecal free-radical production by ~40% and, in infant trials, shifted gut bacteria toward pathogens and inflammation; genetic studies link lifelong higher iron to shorter lifespan and more diabetes.

dose.effective: Take iron only to correct documented deficiency (ferritin below ~30 ug/L, or below ~50 ug/L with symptoms such as fatigue), then stop or reduce once ferritin is replete. Most iron-replete men and postmenopausal women need no supplemental iron; a multivitamin 'for men' or '50+' formula without iron is the sensible default.
dose.studied_range: 19 mg/day ferrous sulfate for 2 weeks (adults, gut markers); 2.5-12.5 mg/day in infant micronutrient powders; >100 mg/day high-dose supplements (cross-sectional microbiome data).
dose.too_much: IOM UL 45 mg/day elemental iron (GI side effects); EFSA set no UL but a safe level of 40 mg/day total iron for adults including pregnancy. Untargeted iron in malaria-endemic settings raised severe illness and death in young children. Never self-supplement with known or suspected haemochromatosis.
dose.timeframe: Gut changes within 2 weeks; systemic store build-up over years.
dose.notes: Absorption is regulated (hepcidin) but there is no excretion route, so stores accumulate in iron-replete people, especially men. Vitamin C taken with iron raises non-heme absorption; tea, coffee and calcium lower it.

entries.mechanism: Unabsorbed ferrous iron in the colon catalyses Fenton chemistry (Fe2+ + H2O2 -> hydroxyl radical) and lipid peroxidation, and favours iron-hungry Enterobacteriaceae over bifidobacteria and butyrate producers. Systemically, surplus iron expands the labile iron pool that feeds Fenton reactions and ferroptosis.
entries.interactions: Heme iron from red and processed meat acts similarly in the gut [processed-red-meat]. Do not pair high-dose vitamin C with iron in people with high stores [vitamin-c-status]. Overlaps with [iron-status-ferritin]; the opposite risk is [iron-deficiency]. Multivitamins often contain 8-18 mg iron [multivitamin-mineral].
entries.caveats: Faecal radical generation is an ex vivo assay and the infant microbiome trials were done in low-income settings with high pathogen loads; adult outcome data are thin. The harm signal is for iron the body does not need: in deficient people, including many pregnant women, iron is clearly beneficial.
entries.debate: Harm from untargeted iron is shown by infant trials (Pemba mortality [nut-sazawal2006]; Kenyan microbiome and calprotectin [nut-jaeggi2015]) and by gut-biology commentaries [nut-weiss2015, nut-simonytesjodin2019], with Mendelian randomization suggesting lifelong higher iron shortens lifespan [nut-daghlas2021]. On the other side, a 2023 meta-analysis found daily iron in iron-replete pregnant women still reduced iron-deficiency anaemia and low birthweight [nut-hansen2023], and EFSA could not identify a dose-response for chronic disease, setting only a conservative safe level [nut-efsa2024iron]. Adult evidence for harm at typical multivitamin doses (8-18 mg) is lacking.

entries.headline: Not linked to worse semen quality. In young US men unprocessed red meat showed no association with any semen measure, and a Chinese case-control study linked higher unprocessed meat intake to lower odds of poor motility (OR 0.61). The negative meat signal for sperm comes from processed meat.

dose.effective: No evidence-based target. Normal portions of unprocessed red meat are compatible with sperm health; cooking method may matter more than the meat itself.
dose.studied_range: Food-frequency quartiles/tertiles of habitual intake.
dose.timeframe: ~2-3 months (one spermatogenic cycle) for any dietary change to show in semen.
dose.notes: Red meat is a dense source of zinc, vitamin B12, iron and carnitine, which sperm production needs. That matters most if intake is low (e.g. restrictive diets). In men who were not deficient, adding 30 mg/day zinc (with folic acid) did not improve semen or live birth in the large FAZST trial.

entries.mechanism: No direct human evidence that red meat improves spermatogenesis or spermiogenesis. The plausible route is nutrient supply (zinc, B12, iron, carnitine) in people with low intake. The oxidative concerns that apply to processed meat (nitrites, preformed N-nitroso compounds) do not apply to fresh meat, while high-heat or stir-fry cooking can add oxidized products.
entries.interactions: Contrast with [processed-meat]. High-heat cooking was associated with worse motility in the case-control study. Extra zinc on top of an adequate diet did not help ([folate-zinc]).
entries.caveats: Two observational studies with different populations; no trials. The case-control result could reflect overall diet or recall bias. Absence of harm is not proof of benefit.
entries.title: Unprocessed red meat (beef, pork, lamb)

entries.headline: Repeated night-time oxygen drops and re-oxygenation act like ischemia-reperfusion; CPAP treatment raised total antioxidant capacity in a meta-analysis.

dose.effective: Get tested if you snore loudly, stop breathing during sleep, or have daytime sleepiness; use CPAP or other prescribed therapy nightly.
dose.studied_range: CPAP studies of weeks to months.
dose.timeframe: Changes within weeks to months of consistent CPAP use.
dose.notes: Weight loss often reduces apnea severity.

entries.mechanism: Cycles of hypoxia and re-oxygenation activate NADPH oxidase and xanthine oxidase and cause mitochondrial ROS bursts, much like ischemia-reperfusion injury.
entries.interactions: Strongly linked to [weight-loss]; worsened by [alcohol] at night.
entries.caveats: Total antioxidant capacity is a crude marker; studies are heterogeneous.
entries.title: Untreated obstructive sleep apnea

factors.name: Urolithin A (supplement; gut metabolite of ellagitannins in pomegranate, berries, walnuts)

entries.headline: In company-funded RCTs, 500-1000 mg/day of urolithin A for 1-4 months improved muscle endurance or strength (about 12% for leg strength) and lowered CRP and acylcarnitines in older and middle-aged adults, but most primary endpoints were not met and trained runners gained no performance.

dose.effective: 500-1000 mg/day purified urolithin A (the Mitopure product in all major trials).
dose.studied_range: 250-1000 mg/day for 4 weeks to 4 months.
dose.too_much: No safety signal up to 1000 mg/day for 4 months; long-term data lacking.
dose.timeframe: Plasma and muscle biomarker changes by 4 weeks; muscle endurance differences at 2 months.
dose.notes: Ellagitannin foods only yield urolithin A if your gut bacteria can make it: across trials 5-25% of people make none and 10-50% partly divert to isourolithin A/urolithin B, and the distribution shifts with age. Taking urolithin A directly bypasses this metabotype problem.

entries.mechanism: Urolithin A, made by gut bacteria from ellagic acid, induces mitophagy (selective removal of damaged mitochondria) and mitochondrial gene expression; it is not a meaningful radical scavenger at the concentrations reached in plasma.
entries.interactions: Food precursors overlap [pomegranate], [walnuts-nuts], [blackberries] and [berries-other], but only help producers. Unlike high-dose vitamins C and E, there is no sign that it blunts training adaptations; in trained runners it lowered creatine kinase.
entries.caveats: All major human trials were sponsored by the manufacturer. In the 66-person JAMA Network Open trial the primary endpoints (6-minute walk, maximal muscle ATP production) were null; in the middle-aged trial peak power (primary) was null. Oxidative-damage markers have not been measured directly. The immune study reports 4-week changes in cell phenotypes, not infections.

entries.headline: Repairing a clinical varicocele lowers SDF by about 7 percentage points on average, and more when SDF starts high.

dose.effective: One procedure (microsurgical subinguinal varicocelectomy is the reference technique) in men with a palpable varicocele plus abnormal semen or high SDF.
dose.studied_range: 19 studies, 1070 men; SCSA, TUNEL and SCD all showed reductions.
dose.timeframe: Re-test semen/SDF about 3-6 months after surgery; one spermatogenic cycle is ~64-74 days.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: consider varicocelectomy in men trying to conceive with palpable varicocele, infertility and abnormal semen (not azoospermia). EAU adds that the female partner should have good ovarian reserve, because the benefit takes months.

entries.mechanism: Removes venous reflux, restoring testicular cooling and oxygenation and cutting seminal ROS, which lowers oxidative DNA damage in newly made sperm.
entries.interactions: Lifestyle changes ([tobacco-smoking], [sauna]) should be made in parallel. If the female partner is older, time may favour going straight to ART, optionally with [testicular-sperm-icsi] or short abstinence [short-abstinence].
entries.caveats: The SDF drop is solid; the pregnancy benefit is less certain (Cochrane: pregnancy RR 1.55, low certainty; live birth uncertain). Not useful for subclinical varicocele with normal semen.
entries.title: Varicocele repair (microsurgical varicocelectomy or embolisation)

factors.name: Vigorous exercise and high-intensity interval training (HIIT)

entries.headline: Minute for minute, intervals raise VO2max and muscle mitochondria more than steady moderate exercise (about +1-3 mL/kg/min extra VO2max; 1.7-3.9x more mitochondrial gain per hour), and vigorous training improved redox markers where gentle training did not; total mitochondrial gains converge when volume is matched.

dose.effective: 75-150 min/week of vigorous activity, or 2-3 interval sessions/week, e.g. 4 x 4 min at 85-95% HRmax with 3 min easy between (similar to the ~90%-of-peak-heart-rate intervals used in Generation 100), or 4-6 x 4-6 min at >90% HRmax (Paulsen 2014). Sprint intervals (3 x 20 s all-out) work too.
dose.studied_range: Trials: 2-4 sessions/week for 2-16 weeks; Generation 100 used 2 sessions/week for 5 years in 70-77-year-olds.
dose.too_much: Oxidative load rises with intensity x volume. Ramping HIIT to daily hard sessions over 4 weeks cut mitochondrial respiration and worsened glucose tolerance. Keep hard sessions to about 2-3 per week with easy days between.
dose.timeframe: VO2max and mitochondrial gains within 2-6 weeks; antioxidant-enzyme changes in 6-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Intensity is one of the surest ways to abolish fitness 'non-response'. People with heart disease should get medical clearance first.

entries.mechanism: Higher intensity recruits more fibres and produces larger calcium, AMP/AMPK and ROS signals per minute (NOX2-derived ROS were required for full HIIT adaptation in mice), driving PGC-1alpha, Nrf2 and mitochondrial protein synthesis. Volume is a separate driver of mitochondrial content, while relative intensity matters more for mitochondrial respiratory function. Excess intensity x volume leads to sustained ROS, glutathione depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction.
entries.interactions: Same caution about [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training] (resveratrol blunted HIIT gains in two trials). Combines with [resistance-training]. The most efficient route to [cardiorespiratory-fitness]. Excess volume leads to [overtraining-ultraendurance]. In men, the one large semen RCT found moderate continuous training beat HIIT for sperm markers.
entries.caveats: Hard mortality data for HIIT specifically are thin: Generation 100's HIIT advantage was not statistically significant. Many HIIT-vs-moderate comparisons are small, short and not matched for energy. 'Zone 2 is special' and 'only intensity matters' are both overstatements.
entries.debate: Intensity versus volume is a live argument. MacInnis, Skelly and Gibala argue intensity matters more for mitochondrial content [exr-macinnis2019, exr-macinnis2017a], while Bishop's group argues volume matters more [exr-bishop2019, exr-granata2018]. A 353-study meta-regression found similar total mitochondrial gains for continuous (23%), HIIT (27%) and sprint training (27%) after adjustment, with intervals far more time-efficient [exr-molmen2025]. A 2025 review rejects the popular claim that 'Zone 2' is uniquely good for mitochondria in the general public [exr-storoschuk2025]. HIIT beats moderate training for VO2max by a small margin in healthy adults [exr-milanovic2015] and a larger one in cardiometabolic patients [exr-weston2014], but gives similar fat loss [exr-wewege2017]. For redox markers, vigorous protocols looked better [exr-torresrojo2025], but the meta-analysis held only 7 RCTs, and HIIT and moderate exercise carried the lowest risk of large oxidative damage when volume was moderate [exr-zhou2022].

entries.headline: Correcting B12 or folate deficiency is essential (anaemia, neuropathy, neural tube defects), and folic acid cut first stroke by 21% in unfortified China; but lowering homocysteine with B vitamins did not prevent heart attacks or death in 71,422 trial participants, and high-dose folic acid plus B12 raised cancer in Norway. Women with higher B12 and folate before IVF had ~26 points higher live birth.

dose.effective: Folate RDA 400 ug DFE/day; anyone who could become pregnant: 400-800 ug folic acid daily from at least 1 month (ideally 3) before conception [folic-acid]. B12 RDA 2.4 ug/day; vegans need a reliable source every day (fortified foods or a B12 supplement); adults over 50 should get B12 from fortified foods or supplements.
dose.studied_range: Folic acid 0.4-5 mg/day; B12 0.4-1 mg/day in homocysteine-lowering trials.
dose.too_much: Folic acid UL 1000 ug/day (IOM and EFSA): high folic acid can mask B12 deficiency and let neuropathy progress. Norwegian trial of 0.8 mg folic acid + 0.4 mg B12 saw more cancer; 1 mg/day folic acid did not prevent adenomas and may have raised advanced lesions. No UL for B12.
dose.timeframe: Homocysteine falls within weeks; neural tube closes by day 28 after conception.
dose.notes: At risk of B12 deficiency: vegans, older adults (atrophic gastritis), metformin users (B12 ~57 pmol/L lower), long-term PPI or H2-blocker users (OR 1.65), bariatric surgery, pernicious anaemia, nitrous oxide use. Serum B12 is imperfect; methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are functional markers.

entries.mechanism: Folate (as 5-methyl-THF) and B12 (methionine synthase) remethylate homocysteine to methionine, sustaining SAM-dependent DNA methylation and thymidine synthesis for DNA repair. Homocysteine not remethylated can enter transsulfuration (B6-dependent) to cysteine, the rate-limiting precursor of glutathione. Elevated homocysteine auto-oxidises, generating H2O2, and impairs endothelial nitric oxide.
entries.interactions: Riboflavin is the FAD cofactor of MTHFR [riboflavin]. Folic acid is the core of [profertility-diet] and [folic-acid]. High-dose folic acid in men: [folate-zinc]. NAC and glycine bypass the transsulfuration route to glutathione [n-acetylcysteine] [glynac].
entries.caveats: The homocysteine hypothesis largely failed for heart attacks; benefits concentrate where folate status is low (unfortified populations). Fertility data are observational and from a fortified population.
entries.debate: Cochrane finds homocysteine lowering does not prevent MI or death but modestly reduces stroke [nut-marticarvajal2017]; CSPPT showed a 21% stroke reduction in an unfortified population [nut-huo2015], which an editorial argued outweighs earlier null trials [nut-stampfer2015]. Safety concerns come from excess cancer with folic acid + B12 in Norway [nut-ebbing2009] (editorial urged caution on interpretation [nut-drake2009]) and a possible rise in advanced adenomas [nut-cole2007], although EFSA judged cancer links insufficient while keeping the 1000 ug UL [nut-efsa2023folate]. For eggs, higher serum folate/B12 predicted IVF live birth [nut-gaskins2015] and folic acid predicted fecundability [nut-cueto2016], but no RCT tests B12 for fertility.

factors.name: Vitamin C + E in pregnancy to prevent pre-eclampsia

entries.headline: Four large RCTs (VIP, WHO, US MFMU, DAPIT; about 14,700 women) found vitamin C 1000 mg + E 400 IU did not prevent pre-eclampsia, and pooled data show more low birthweight, gestational hypertension and term rupture of membranes.

dose.effective: None; do not take high-dose C+E for pre-eclampsia.
dose.studied_range: 1000 mg vitamin C + 400 IU vitamin E daily from 9-22 weeks.
dose.too_much: Low birthweight RR 1.15 (VIP); term prelabour rupture of membranes RR 1.77 (Cochrane).
dose.timeframe: From second trimester to delivery in trials.
dose.notes: A standard prenatal vitamin at RDA levels is different and fine.

entries.mechanism: Placental ischaemia-reperfusion and syncytiotrophoblast stress generate oxidative stress in pre-eclampsia, but the disease is driven upstream by defective placentation and antiangiogenic factors that bulk antioxidants do not correct.
entries.interactions: Same failure pattern as [vitamin-c-e-combined] in fertility and cardiovascular trials; [aspirin-preeclampsia-egg] works through a different mechanism.
entries.caveats: A textbook antioxidant paradox: strong biomarker rationale, null hard outcomes.
entries.debate: DAPIT authors suggested women with low antioxidant status might still benefit (pre-eclampsia 15% vs 19%, NS) [fer-mccance2010], and Cochrane found less placental abruption (RR 0.64) [fer-rumbold2015e]. But the large trials were null [fer-poston2006, fer-villar2009, fer-roberts2010], including in low-nutrition populations, and meta-analysis found no benefit with some harms [fer-condeagudelo2011].
entries.title: Vitamin C + E in pregnancy to prevent pre-eclampsia

factors.name: Vitamin C + E supplements (fertility trials)
aliases: Vitamin E and vitamin C supplements

entries.headline: An uncontrolled study found 1 g vitamin C + 1 g vitamin E for 2 months lowered SDF and boosted the next ICSI's pregnancy rate, but controlled trials of similar mixes are null.

dose.effective: If used before ICSI for high SDF: about 500-1000 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E daily for 2-3 months, under medical advice.
dose.studied_range: 1 g C + 1 g E daily for 2 months (38 men).
dose.too_much: Vitamin C contributed to opening protamine disulphide bridges (sperm decondensation) in one study; vitamin E above 1000 mg/day raises bleeding risk.
dose.timeframe: 2-3 months.
dose.notes: Both are in MOXI at lower doses, which was null.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin C is the main water-soluble antioxidant of seminal plasma; vitamin E protects PUFA-rich membranes from lipid peroxidation.
entries.interactions: See [male-antioxidant-combination] and [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Greco 2005 was a before-after comparison after a failed cycle, so regression to the mean and cycle-to-cycle variation can explain much of the effect.
entries.title: Vitamins C and E

entries.headline: Vitamin E (600 mg/day) lowered follicular oxidative markers in a tiny study, and supplement use was associated with slightly shorter time to pregnancy in some subgroups, but there is no convincing RCT evidence of more live births.

dose.effective: Meet needs from food (nuts, seeds, vegetable oils, fruit, vegetables); routine high-dose supplements are not supported.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin E 600 mg/day (Tamura); vitamin C and E in mixed antioxidant trials in the Cochrane review.
dose.too_much: No benefit shown, so there is no reason to take high-dose supplements.
dose.notes: Typical prenatal vitamins already contain modest amounts.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin E is the main lipid-phase chain-breaking antioxidant; vitamin C regenerates it. Neither targets mitochondrial ROS production.
entries.interactions: Part of [female-antioxidant-supplements].
entries.caveats: Classic antioxidant paradox: big mechanistic story, no clinical proof.
entries.title: Vitamin E and vitamin C supplements

factors.name: Vitamin C foods (citrus, kiwi, peppers, strawberries)

entries.headline: Plasma vitamin C saturates near 200 mg/day (white cells saturate at 100 mg), easily reached from foods; extra beyond that is excreted and high-dose pills show no mortality benefit.

dose.effective: About 200 mg/day from food: e.g. 1 red pepper, or 2 kiwifruit, or 1 orange + 1 cup strawberries.
dose.studied_range: 30-2500 mg/day in depletion-repletion pharmacokinetics.
dose.too_much: Doses above ~400 mg/day have no evident value; at 1000 mg/day oxalate and urate excretion rise (kidney stone risk).
dose.timeframe: Steady state in 2-3 weeks.
dose.notes: Benefit is concentrated in people with low intake (smokers, low produce eaters).

entries.mechanism: Ascorbate is the main water-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant and regenerates vitamin E; kiwifruit also raised lymphocyte DNA resistance to H2O2 ex vivo beyond what its vitamin C explained.
entries.interactions: Vitamin C enhances non-heme iron absorption (good if iron-deficient; avoid iron + vitamin C supplements in iron overload, see [iron-excess]). High-dose vitamin C + E blunted exercise adaptation (covered in exercise sections).
entries.caveats: In the Cochrane review vitamin C supplements had no effect on mortality; beta-carotene and vitamin E increased it.

key_numbers.label: Dose at which plasma vitamin C plateaus

entries.title: Vitamin C foods (citrus, kiwi, peppers, strawberries)

entries.headline: Plasma vitamin C rises steeply between 30 and 100 mg/day and plateaus by about 200 mg/day; about 7% of Americans (more among smokers and low-income groups) are deficient, but once tissues are saturated, extra vitamin C did not lower F2-isoprostanes at any dose up to 2500 mg/day.

dose.effective: About 100-200 mg/day from food (e.g. one red pepper, two kiwifruit, or an orange plus a cup of strawberries). Smokers need at least 35 mg/day more than non-smokers. RDA 90 mg men, 75 mg women.
dose.studied_range: 30-2500 mg/day in inpatient depletion-repletion pharmacokinetics.
dose.too_much: UL 2000 mg/day (IOM; diarrhoea). Doses above ~400 mg/day have no evident value; oxalate excretion rises at 1000 mg/day, and supplements are linked to kidney stones in men. EFSA set no UL.
dose.timeframe: Steady state in 2-3 weeks.
dose.notes: At risk of deficiency: smokers, low fruit and vegetable intake, alcohol use disorder, restrictive diets, dialysis.

entries.mechanism: Ascorbate is the main water-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant, regenerates vitamin E, and is a cofactor for collagen and carnitine synthesis and iron absorption. Tissue and white-cell uptake is transporter-limited, so above saturation extra intake is excreted.
entries.interactions: Food sources are covered in [vitamin-c-foods]; pills in [vitamin-c-supplement]. Raises non-heme iron absorption (useful in [iron-deficiency], unhelpful with high [iron-status-ferritin]). High-dose C plus E belongs to [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: The 'more is better' view rests on observational associations; in saturated people neither oxidative-stress biomarkers nor outcomes improve with more.
entries.debate: Levine's pharmacokinetic studies argue for ~200 mg/day and no value above ~400 mg [nut-levine1996, nut-levine2001], while Carr and Frei argued from epidemiology for ~120 mg/day [nut-carr1999]; the IOM settled on 75-90 mg [nut-iom2000]. Both camps agree megadoses add nothing for replete people, and limited evidence links vitamin C supplements to kidney stones [nut-oconnor2022].

entries.title: Vitamin C status (deficiency vs saturation)

entries.headline: No effect on cardiovascular disease, cancer or mortality in large RCTs. Shortens colds by about 8% and halves cold risk only under extreme physical stress. About 1 g/day doubles kidney-stone risk in men.

dose.effective: Body stores saturate with diet alone: cells saturate at ~100 mg/day and plasma at ~1,000 mg/day. 1-2 servings of fruit or vegetables rich in vitamin C cover the steep part of the curve (30-100 mg).
dose.studied_range: 120 mg/day (SU.VI.MAX) to 500 mg/day (PHS II) for outcomes; 200 mg to 2 g/day for colds
dose.too_much: ≥1,000 mg/day: about twice the kidney-stone risk in men (RR 1.95); 1 g/day blunted endurance-training adaptations.
dose.timeframe: Outcome trials ran for ~8 years with no effect
dose.notes: Oral absorption is tightly controlled (1.25 g oral peak ~135 µmol/L vs ~885 µmol/L IV), so megadoses mostly end up in urine. Pharmacological levels need IV dosing.

entries.mechanism: Water-soluble electron donor that regenerates vitamin E and is a cofactor for many enzymes. A true antioxidant at physiological levels, but once someone is replete, extra intake does not raise tissue levels and cannot compete with peroxiredoxins and GPx for H2O2. Large doses can blunt ROS-dependent training signals (PGC-1α, mitochondrial biogenesis).
entries.interactions: Taken around training it can cancel adaptive signalling, the same issue as [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]. Combined with vitamin E it showed no benefit in PHS II. Correcting deficiency is useful; adding more on top of a vegetable-rich diet adds nothing measurable.
entries.caveats: The 'megadose vitamin C' claims come from oral pharmacokinetics that cannot reach the plasma levels seen with IV dosing. Cold prevention works only for marathon runners, skiers and soldiers in subarctic conditions. Kidney-stone risk is relevant for men and people prone to stones.
entries.title: Vitamin C supplements (ascorbic acid)

entries.headline: In a 330-man RCT, high-dose vitamin D did not improve semen quality in men with low vitamin D, though live birth rose in a small oligozoospermic subgroup.

dose.effective: Correct deficiency (25OHD <50 nmol/L) for general health; not a sperm treatment.
dose.studied_range: 300,000 IU loading dose then 1400 IU/day plus 500 mg calcium for 150 days.
dose.too_much: Avoid chronic intake above 4000 IU/day without monitoring.
dose.timeframe: 150 days studied.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin D receptors are present in testis and sperm; proposed effects on calcium signalling and inhibin B.
entries.caveats: The subgroup benefit is hypothesis-generating only.
entries.title: Vitamin D

entries.headline: Vitamin D-replete women had about 33% higher odds of IVF live birth than deficient women, but RCTs of supplementation in deficient women improved only chemical pregnancy, not clinical pregnancy.

dose.effective: Test 25(OH)D and correct deficiency with a clinician; there is no evidence that extra vitamin D helps women who are already replete.
dose.studied_range: Observational: replete vs deficient/insufficient 25(OH)D; 5 RCTs of supplementation in deficient women.
dose.too_much: Avoid unsupervised megadoses.
dose.timeframe: Correct deficiency before IVF or trying, within the 3-month preparation window.
dose.notes: Benefit, if any, is limited to correcting deficiency.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin D receptors are present in granulosa cells and endometrium; vitamin D influences AMH signalling and immune tolerance.
entries.interactions: Part of [profertility-diet].
entries.caveats: Observational links are confounded by overall health, BMI and outdoor activity; RCT evidence is small.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, replete vs deficient

entries.title: Vitamin D (correcting deficiency)

entries.headline: No cardiovascular or cancer benefit in more than 100,000 trial participants. 400 IU/day raised prostate cancer by 17%, hemorrhagic stroke by 22-74% and heart failure by 13%, and high doses slightly raise mortality.

dose.effective: No supplemental dose has shown an outcome benefit; get vitamin E from food (nuts, seeds, plant oils).
dose.studied_range: 50 mg/day (ATBC) to 400 IU/day (HOPE, SELECT) or 600 IU every other day (WHS); 200-3,200 IU in biomarker studies
dose.too_much: ≥400 IU/day: +39 deaths per 10,000 (meta-analysis); risk rises above ~150 IU/day. Prostate cancer HR 1.17 at 400 IU/day (SELECT).
dose.timeframe: Lowering F2-isoprostanes needed ≥1,600 IU/day for 16 weeks; outcome trials ran 4.5-10 years
dose.notes: Doses used in outcome trials (400 IU) were too low to change oxidative-stress markers but high enough for bleeding effects. USPSTF grade D (recommends against).

entries.mechanism: Lipid-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant in membranes and LDL. In replete people extra intake does not lower lipid peroxidation at practical doses. The pattern of more hemorrhagic and fewer ischemic strokes is consistent with an antithrombotic effect, though the exact mechanism was not established in these trials.
entries.interactions: Effect on prostate cancer depended on selenium status (risk raised in low-selenium men) [selenium-supplement]. Combined with vitamin C it blunted exercise-induced insulin-sensitivity gains [vitamin-c-supplement]. Combined with NAC it accelerated tumour growth in mice [n-acetylcysteine].
entries.caveats: Observational data (supplement users had less heart disease) were confounded by healthy-user bias, and RCTs reversed the conclusion. WHS showed a 24% reduction in CV death as a secondary outcome, which was not replicated. Hemorrhagic stroke risk matters for people on anticoagulants.
entries.title: Vitamin E supplements (alpha-tocopherol)

entries.headline: A 10-15 minute walk after each main meal lowered post-meal glucose 12% more than one daily 30-minute walk in type 2 diabetes (22% after dinner), and post-meal exercise reliably blunts glucose spikes (effect size about -0.3); oxidative-stress benefits are inferred, not measured directly.

dose.effective: 10-15 min of easy-to-brisk walking after each main meal, especially the largest (often evening) meal; longer bouts (over 30 min) did more in meta-analysis.
dose.studied_range: Crossover trials: 2-min walks every 20-30 min, 10 min after each meal, 3 x 15 min post-meal, up to 60 min.
dose.too_much: None known at walking intensity.
dose.timeframe: Acute: lowers the glucose curve of that meal and 24-h mean glucose; long-term HbA1c effects are not well established.
dose.notes: Effects are biggest in people with type 2 diabetes, prediabetes or obesity and after carbohydrate-heavy meals. Light walking beat standing breaks. Evidence on the ideal start time is inconsistent.

entries.mechanism: Contracting muscle takes up glucose independently of insulin (AMPK, NOX2-ROS and calcium-mediated GLUT4 translocation), flattening the post-meal glucose and triglyceride peaks that drive mitochondrial superoxide, NADPH oxidase activation and AGE formation.
entries.interactions: Directly supports [glycemic-control] and blunts spikes from [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] meals. A practical way to break [sedentary-time]. Complements, but does not replace, [aerobic-exercise-moderate].
entries.caveats: Most trials are short crossover studies with continuous glucose monitors in small groups; long-term outcome trials are lacking. Oxidative-marker evidence is limited to small studies with crude markers.
entries.debate: That post-meal activity lowers glucose is well replicated [exr-reynolds2016, exr-dipietro2013, exr-kang2023, exr-buffey2022, exr-dunstan2012]. Debated: whether timing or just total movement matters. Breaks beat continuous exercise only modestly once energy expenditure is matched [exr-loh2020], and one meta-analysis found longer bouts mattered more than early start times [exr-kang2023]. Whether lower glucose spikes translate into less oxidative stress in people is mostly inferred; a small crossover found only trends in a crude oxidative marker [exr-takahashi2015].

entries.title: Walking after meals

entries.headline: A handful a day (30 g) lowers LDL and apoB and, in PREDIMED, cut major CVD events by ~28%; walnuts improved endothelial function, but direct oxidation markers were unchanged in several trials.

dose.effective: 30 g (a small handful) of mixed nuts or walnuts daily.
dose.studied_range: 30 g/day mixed nuts (PREDIMED); walnuts replacing ~32% of monounsaturated-fat energy for 4 weeks; 26 walnut trials (1059 people).
dose.too_much: Calories; walnut-enriched diets did not cause weight gain in trials.
dose.timeframe: 4 weeks for lipids and endothelial function.
dose.notes: Walnuts are rich in alpha-linolenic acid and gamma-tocopherol.

entries.mechanism: Lipid lowering (fewer oxidizable LDL particles), gamma-tocopherol, ellagitannins (converted to urolithins), ALA.
entries.interactions: Walnut PUFAs are oxidizable; store nuts cool and dark. Overlaps with [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: In the walnut endothelial trial, oxidation biomarkers did not differ from the Mediterranean control diet; in PREDIMED the nut arm did not improve LDL oxidation traits (the EVOO arm did).

entries.title: Walnuts and other nuts

entries.headline: Two RCTs found that adding 60-75 g of nuts a day improved sperm vitality, motility and morphology, and one also lowered sperm DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: 60 g/day mixed nuts (walnuts, almonds, hazelnuts) or 75 g/day walnuts (about a large handful to two handfuls), added to the usual diet.
dose.studied_range: 60 g/day for 14 weeks (FERTINUTS, n=119); 75 g/day walnuts for 12 weeks (n=117).
dose.too_much: 75 g walnuts is about 490 kcal; swap for other snacks to avoid weight gain. Avoid if allergic.
dose.timeframe: 12-14 weeks.
dose.notes: Unsalted, unroasted or dry-roasted nuts were used. Walnuts are rich in alpha-linolenic acid (plant omega-3).

entries.mechanism: Provides ALA omega-3, vitamin E, polyphenols, magnesium, selenium and zinc; raised blood omega-3 and correlated with lower sperm aneuploidy; FERTINUTS showed lower SDF and miR-34b-3p expression.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [mediterranean-diet] and [omega3-fish].
entries.caveats: Healthy young men on Western diets; not infertile men; no pregnancy outcomes; FERTINUTS was partly funded by the nut industry.
entries.title: Walnuts and mixed nuts

factors.name: Wasabi, horseradish and mustard (allyl and other short-chain isothiocyanates)

entries.headline: Pungent condiments supply isothiocyanates that are well absorbed (in animals) and concentrate in urine, and one 72-person RCT found a wasabi 6-MSITC extract improved memory in older adults, but there are no human oxidative-stress or disease trials.

dose.effective: Not established; culinary amounts.
dose.studied_range: Wasabi 6-MSITC supplement for 12 weeks; cabbage meals for allyl isothiocyanate kinetics.
dose.too_much: Large amounts irritate the gut.
dose.notes: Isothiocyanates form only when the plant's myrosinase acts on crushed tissue, so freshly grated root or prepared mustard delivers them; lightly cooked cabbage gave more allyl isothiocyanate than fully cooked.

entries.mechanism: Allyl isothiocyanate and 6-MSITC are electrophiles that conjugate glutathione and activate Nrf2; allyl isothiocyanate is excreted as an N-acetylcysteine conjugate concentrated in urine.
entries.interactions: Mustard powder also restores myrosinase activity to cooked broccoli: see [mustard-seed-myrosinase]. Same pathway as [broccoli-sprouts] and [watercress-peitc].
entries.caveats: Bioavailability figures for allyl isothiocyanate come mainly from animals. The memory trial is a single study with improvement in 2 of several cognitive domains. Erucin (rocket) and sulforaphene (radish) have essentially no human outcome data.
entries.title: Wasabi, horseradish and mustard (allyl and other short-chain isothiocyanates)

entries.headline: 85 g/day of raw watercress for 8 weeks cut lymphocyte DNA damage by 17% (oxidative purine damage by 24%, more in smokers), and watercress or pure PEITC shifted a tobacco lung carcinogen toward detoxification in smokers.

dose.effective: About 85 g (a large bowl) of raw watercress daily.
dose.studied_range: 85-170 g/day for 3 days to 8 weeks; pure PEITC 40 mg/day for 1 week.
dose.timeframe: Carcinogen-metabolism shift within 2-3 days; DNA-damage changes at 8 weeks.
dose.notes: Eat raw or barely wilted so chewing releases PEITC via the plant's myrosinase. Watercress also doubled plasma lutein and raised beta-carotene, so not all of the effect is PEITC.

entries.mechanism: PEITC inhibits cytochrome P450 activation of the tobacco nitrosamine NNK and, like other isothiocyanates, conjugates glutathione and activates Nrf2-driven phase II enzymes; the carotenoids add lipid-phase antioxidant capacity.
entries.interactions: Same pathway family as [broccoli-sprouts], [cruciferous-other] and [moringa]. The carotenoid boost overlaps [leafy-greens].
entries.caveats: Trials are small; in the 82-smoker PEITC trial the change in carcinogen activation was only 7.7%. The exercise study had 10 men. There are no cancer-outcome data.

entries.title: Watercress (phenethyl isothiocyanate, PEITC)

entries.headline: Each 90 g/day (3 servings) of whole grain is associated with ~19% lower CHD and 17% lower all-cause mortality; the oxidative-stress link is indirect, through lower glycemic spikes and fermentable fiber.

dose.effective: 3 servings (90 g) per day or more; associations continued up to ~210-225 g/day.
dose.studied_range: Cohort intakes; RCTs show lower body weight, blood pressure and cholesterol with higher fiber and whole grain.
dose.timeframe: Long-term.
dose.notes: Oats contain avenanthramides and beta-glucan; most grain phenolics (ferulic acid) are bound to fiber and released by gut bacteria.

entries.mechanism: Fiber-bound ferulic acid released in the colon, short-chain fatty acids, lower glycemic load.
entries.interactions: Replaces [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] carbohydrate.
entries.caveats: Observational for hard outcomes; refined grains and white rice showed little association.

entries.title: Whole grains

entries.headline: About 17% of the world is at risk of low zinc intake, and infertile men have lower seminal zinc, yet zinc supplements in replete people do little: 30 mg zinc plus folic acid did nothing for semen or live birth in 2370 men, and doses of 50 mg/day already depress copper-dependent SOD1, with 100+ mg/day causing copper-deficiency anaemia and myelopathy.

dose.effective: RDA 11 mg/day men, 8 mg/day women (11-12 in pregnancy/lactation). Get it from meat, shellfish (oysters), dairy, legumes, seeds and whole grains; vegans may need up to ~50% more because phytate blocks absorption. If supplementing, 8-15 mg/day in a multivitamin with ~1-2 mg copper.
dose.studied_range: 15-66 mg/day elemental zinc in trials; 30 mg/day in FAZST; 50 mg/day lowered SOD1 in 6 weeks.
dose.too_much: UL 40 mg/day (IOM), 25 mg/day (EFSA). Chronic intake above these induces copper deficiency (anaemia, neutropenia, myelopathy that mimics B12 deficiency); zinc-containing denture creams and long-term cold lozenges are recognised causes.
dose.timeframe: Copper status falls within weeks at high zinc; semen changes need ~74 days.
dose.notes: At risk of deficiency: vegans, older adults, alcohol use disorder, malabsorption (Crohn's, coeliac, bariatric surgery), diuretics. Serum zinc is an insensitive marker and falls with inflammation.

entries.mechanism: Zinc and copper together form the active site of cytosolic SOD1 (copper is catalytic, zinc structural). Zinc also induces metallothionein, protects protein thiols, competes with iron and copper for Fenton-active sites and stabilises sperm chromatin. Excess zinc induces intestinal metallothionein that traps copper, lowering SOD1 and ceruloplasmin activity.
entries.interactions: FAZST combined zinc with high-dose folic acid [folate-zinc]. High zinc impairs copper and possibly iron status [iron-deficiency]. Zinc appears in many fertility blends [male-antioxidant-combination] [multivitamin-mineral].
entries.caveats: Small meta-analysed trials reporting lower CRP or MDA after zinc are heterogeneous and contested. Benefits in sperm come mainly from small trials in men with low zinc.
entries.debate: A meta-analysis reported zinc lowers CRP, TNF-alpha and MDA [nut-hosseini2021], but a published critique flagged search and methodological flaws [nut-jafari2021] (authors replied [nut-hosseini2021b]). For sperm, low seminal zinc in infertile men and small positive trials [nut-zhao2016] contrast with the large null FAZST trial, which also slightly raised DNA fragmentation [nut-schisterman2020] and did not alter sperm methylation [nut-jenkins2022]. Harms of excess zinc are uncontested [nut-fosmire1990, nut-jaiser2010, nut-fischer1984].

mechanisms.name: Aitken's two-step hypothesis of sperm DNA damage
mechanisms.description: Step 1: defective spermiogenesis leaves sperm with poor histone-to-protamine replacement, retained cytoplasm and loose chromatin. Step 2: oxidative stress (from the sperm's own mitochondria, from leukocytes, or from heat and toxicants) attacks this vulnerable DNA, forming 8-OHdG; OGG1 excises the lesion, leaving abasic sites that break into the strand breaks measured as SDF.

mechanisms.name: Cohesin loss and egg aneuploidy
mechanisms.description: Eggs pause in meiosis I from before birth until ovulation. The cohesin complexes that hold chromosome pairs together are not replaced, so they erode over decades; in older women this centromeric cohesion loss drives chromosome mis-segregation, giving a U-shaped aneuploidy curve with a steep rise after the mid-30s. This is the main reason age dominates egg quality, and it is not an oxidative process that antioxidants are known to fix.

mechanisms.name: Declining NAD+ in ageing oocytes
mechanisms.description: In mice, oocyte NAD+ falls with age; restoring it with NMN improved mitochondrial function, spindle assembly and fertility. Human evidence is lacking.

mechanisms.name: Direct radical scavenging by dietary antioxidants
mechanisms.description: The classic idea is that vitamin C, vitamin E, carotenoids and polyphenols protect us by reacting with free radicals before those radicals reach lipids, proteins or DNA. This chemistry is real in the test tube, but in the body it is limited by kinetics, concentration and location. Peroxiredoxins and glutathione peroxidases remove H2O2 and lipid hydroperoxides so quickly, and are present in such amounts, that small-molecule antioxidants cannot capture a meaningful share of peroxide inside cells. Forman, Davies and Ursini conclude that in vivo radical scavenging is kinetically ineffective as a defence, and that enzymatic two-electron reduction of hydroperoxides is the real mechanism. Sies states that the main role in antioxidant defence is played by enzymes, not small molecules. Vitamin E as the chain-breaking antioxidant in membranes, and vitamin C, are genuine exceptions, but their effect plateaus once deficiency is corrected. Oral vitamin C is tightly controlled: plasma is saturated at about 1 g/day, and cells at about 100 mg/day. Vitamin E reduced F2-isoprostanes only at 1,600-3,200 IU/day, far above trial doses. Polyphenols reach only about 0-4 µmol/L in plasma, mostly as conjugated metabolites. That is negligible next to urate and ascorbate, and the rise in plasma 'antioxidant capacity' after eating flavonoid-rich food is explained by uric acid. Food ORAC values therefore do not predict in vivo effects, and USDA withdrew its ORAC database in 2012. Direct scavenging may still matter locally in the gut lumen, where polyphenol concentrations are much higher. Elsewhere, the benefits of plant foods are better explained by signalling (Nrf2, NF-kB) and by the microbiome.

mechanisms.name: Endothelial nitric oxide
mechanisms.description: Flavanols, anthocyanin metabolites and dietary nitrate raise nitric-oxide bioavailability; flow-mediated dilation (FMD) is the most reproducible human outcome for polyphenol foods and partly reflects reduced vascular superoxide.

mechanisms.name: Ferroptosis (iron-dependent lipid-peroxidation death)
mechanisms.description: Ferroptosis is a regulated cell death driven by iron-catalysed peroxidation of polyunsaturated membrane lipids when the selenoprotein GPX4 and its substrate glutathione are depleted (e.g. by cystine deprivation). It links labile iron, selenium status and glutathione supply to tissue damage in models of neurodegeneration, kidney and liver injury, and to sperm and granulosa-cell damage in iron overload; human clinical evidence remains indirect.

mechanisms.name: Follicular fluid oxidative stress
mechanisms.description: Follicular fluid surrounds the maturing egg. Higher ROS, lipid peroxidation and 8-OHdG (oxidative DNA damage) in follicular fluid are associated with degenerate oocytes, fertilization failure and poor embryos. Obesity raises follicular insulin, triglycerides and CRP. These markers are research tools, not validated clinical tests.

mechanisms.name: Folliculogenesis timeline (why 3 months)
mechanisms.description: A resting follicle takes several months to reach the preantral stage, then about 70-85 more days to grow to the selectable 2-5 mm stage and ovulate. The egg ovulated in a given month has therefore been developing in the follicular environment of the preceding ~3 months, which is the window lifestyle changes can influence.

mechanisms.name: Free-radical (oxidative damage) theory of aging and its revision
mechanisms.description: In 1956 Denham Harman proposed that aging is caused by the slow build-up of damage from free radicals made during normal metabolism, and in 1972 he pointed to mitochondria as both the main source and the main target. The theory dominated aging research for decades and is the origin of the idea that antioxidant supplements should slow aging. Direct genetic tests in mice largely failed it. Mice with half the mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (Sod2+/-), or with Gpx1 deleted on top of that, had more oxidative DNA and protein damage and more cancer but lived just as long. Overexpressing SOD, catalase or both did not extend lifespan. Of 18 antioxidant-gene manipulations tested by one group, only Sod1 deletion changed lifespan (it shortened it, mainly through liver cancer). Naked mole-rats, which live more than 28 years, carry more lipid, protein and DNA oxidation than mice from a young age. Mice that accumulate mitochondrial DNA mutations age prematurely without producing more ROS. Large antioxidant-supplement trials in humans did not lower mortality. The main exception is catalase targeted to mitochondria, which extended mouse lifespan by about 5 months and reduced cardiac aging and cancer burden, suggesting that oxidative damage in specific places contributes to specific age-related diseases. Current views split three ways. Defenders such as Barja argue an updated mitochondrial version still explains why long-lived species have low mitochondrial ROS production and oxidation-resistant membranes. Sies and others reframe ROS as signals, with low levels ('eustress') needed for health. Gladyshev argues oxidative damage is just one part of a broader 'deleteriome', the sum of all the by-products of imperfect biological processes that accumulate with age.

mechanisms.name: Glutathione system and endogenous antioxidant enzymes
mechanisms.description: The enzymatic network does almost all of the body's antioxidant work. Superoxide dismutases (SOD1 in the cytosol, SOD2 in mitochondria, SOD3 outside cells) convert superoxide to H2O2. Catalase, the selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidases and the six peroxiredoxins reduce H2O2 and lipid hydroperoxides to water and alcohols. Glutathione reductase and the thioredoxin/thioredoxin reductase system regenerate these enzymes using NADPH. Glutathione (GSH), a tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine and glycine, is the most abundant non-protein thiol, at millimolar concentrations inside cells. Its synthesis is limited by cysteine supply and by glutamate-cysteine ligase, which is itself an Nrf2 target. This is why Nrf2 activators raise glutathione and why cysteine donors such as NAC can raise it in people who are short of it. In older adults, red-cell glutathione and its synthesis rate were about half those of young adults, and F2-isoprostanes were higher. Glycine plus NAC restored these values, and a small 16-week RCT reported metabolic and functional improvements. NAC at 1,200 mg/day improved exercise performance and oxidative markers only in people with low baseline glutathione. In replete people it blunted training signals, and in mouse tumour models it accelerated cancer progression and metastasis by raising tumour glutathione. Measuring the GSH/GSSG ratio needs immediate thiol trapping with N-ethylmaleimide, because GSSG is otherwise greatly overestimated. Selenium status matters for GPx activity, but in replete people extra selenium brings no benefit and may raise diabetes risk.

mechanisms.name: Gut microbial metabolism of polyphenols
mechanisms.description: Most anthocyanins, flavan-3-ol oligomers, chlorogenic acids and ellagitannins reach the colon, where bacteria convert them into phenolic acids, valerolactones and urolithins that circulate for up to 48 h. Inter-individual differences in this metabolism are large and partly explain variable responses.

mechanisms.name: Hormesis, mitohormesis and xenohormesis
mechanisms.description: Hormesis describes a two-phase dose response: a low dose of a stressor triggers protective adaptations, while a high dose causes harm. Mild stressors such as heat, exercise, caloric restriction and some phytochemicals extend lifespan or increase stress resistance in many animal models. 'Mitohormesis' applies this idea to mitochondrial ROS. The transient rise in ROS during exercise or energy restriction triggers lasting increases in antioxidant enzymes, mitochondrial biogenesis and insulin sensitivity, and antioxidant supplements can block these responses. In humans, vitamin C plus vitamin E abolished the gain in insulin sensitivity from four weeks of training, and vitamin C alone blunted mitochondrial biogenesis. Calabrese argues that Nrf2 activation is a common mechanism of hormesis and stresses that the maximal response is modest and capped. Sulforaphane shows a biphasic pattern in vitro: low micromolar levels increased cell proliferation and migration, including in cancer cell lines, while higher levels inhibited them. 'Xenohormesis' proposes that animals evolved to sense plant stress molecules such as polyphenols and isothiocyanates as signals to prepare their own defences. This would explain why such compounds act through signalling pathways and not as stoichiometric scavengers. Forman and colleagues call the electrophilic version 'para-hormesis'. The implications for guidance are that occasional, moderate challenges are the goal, that more stimulus is not always better, and that antioxidant megadoses around training can cancel the benefit.

mechanisms.name: Hormonal regulation (melatonin, cortisol, catecholamines)
mechanisms.description: Melatonin, suppressed by light at night, supports repair of oxidative DNA lesions; cortisol and catecholamines from chronic stress or cold raise metabolic rate and inflammatory signalling.

mechanisms.name: How oxidative stress is measured in diet trials
mechanisms.description: Validation work found plasma/urinary F2-isoprostanes and MDA measured by mass spectrometry, and urinary 8-OHdG, to be the most reliable general markers; TBARS, 'total antioxidant capacity' (TAC, FRAP, ORAC of plasma) and many ELISA kits are non-specific. Even 8-iso-PGF2alpha can rise from enzymatic COX activity during inflammation. Many positive food trials rely on the weaker markers.

mechanisms.name: Hyperglycaemia, glycation and advanced glycation end-products (AGEs)
mechanisms.description: High glucose drives oxidative stress through several linked routes. Brownlee proposed a unifying mechanism: hyperglycaemia makes the mitochondrial electron transport chain overproduce superoxide, which partly inhibits GAPDH and diverts glycolytic intermediates into four damaging pathways.
